title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
The rain had stopped, but the air in the station room still held the damp chill of it—damp wool, stale coffee, and the faint, metallic tang of old pipes. Officer Reyes sat across from Eleanor Vance, her notebook open, pen poised. Eleanor’s hands, knotted with arthritis and veined like river maps, rested folded in her lap. Her cardigan was buttoned to the throat, though the room was not cold. Not to her.

“You said you’d like to clarify,” Reyes said gently. “About the night Mr. Vance passed.”

Eleanor nodded, once. Her eyes, pale blue and startlingly clear, fixed on the water stain blooming like a bruise on the ceiling tile above. “Clarify,” she repeated. Not a question. A word she’d turned over all morning, like a smooth stone worn thin by tide.

“The report says he fell down the cellar stairs,” Reyes offered. “At eleven forty-three p.m. You called 911 at eleven forty-seven.”

“Yes,” Eleanor said. Her voice was low, unhurried, as if she were reading from a letter she’d written long ago and kept folded in a drawer. “I called at eleven forty-seven. I counted the seconds. Fourteen seconds between the thud and the silence. Then another thirty-eight before I picked up the phone. I remember the weight of the receiver. Cold plastic.”

Reyes didn’t write. She waited.

Eleanor’s gaze drifted down to her hands. “He wasn’t drunk that night, Officer. Not like the others. He’d had two glasses of sherry—same as always, same as Sunday. He was polishing the brass door knocker. Said it looked ‘tired.’ He always said that. Like brass got tired.” A faint, dry smile touched her lips, gone before it settled. “I was in the kitchen, peeling apples for pie. The peel came off in one long ribbon. I remember that. Red Delicious. Too sweet, but he liked them.”

She paused. Outside, a siren rose and fell, distant, indifferent.

“He came into the kitchen. Not angry. Not even impatient. Just… tired. Tired in the way a man is when he’s carried something heavy for forty-two years and forgotten he ever set it down.” Her fingers tightened, just slightly. “He said, ‘Ellie, I can’t do this anymore.’ Not the marriage. Not the house. Not even the grief, though that was part of it. He meant the pretending. The waking up every morning and putting on the face that said *I am fine*—when he hadn’t been fine since Daniel left.”

Reyes shifted. “Daniel was your son?”

“Was,” Eleanor said. “Drowned in Lake Champlain. August ’87. Twelve years old. We never found the body. Just his red sneakers, caught in the reeds near the boathouse.” She exhaled, slow and deep. “After that, Arthur stopped sleeping. He’d walk the house at night. Check the locks. Open the windows, just to hear the wind. He’d stand at the foot of the stairs, staring down into the dark. Not afraid of falling. Afraid of *not* falling.”

Reyes’s pen hovered. “Ma’am—”

“He didn’t fall,” Eleanor said. Her voice didn’t rise. It simply became absolute. “He stepped. Deliberately. One foot, then the other, down the first three treads. Then he turned. Looked up at me where I stood in the kitchen doorway. I’d heard him come in. Heard him stop. I didn’t call out. I just watched.”

She swallowed. A small, dry sound.

“He smiled. Not the polite one. The one he used to give me when we were young and dancing in the living room with the radio too loud. That smile. And then he stepped backward. Not slipped. Not stumbled. Stepped. Like stepping off a curb. His arms didn’t flail. His hands were loose at his sides. He fell straight down, headfirst, into the black.”

Silence filled the room—not empty, but thick, layered. The hum of the fluorescent light, the distant clatter of a cart in the hall, the soft rasp of Eleanor’s breathing.

“I let him,” she said. “I stood there and let him go. Because I knew—if I’d run, if I’d shouted, if I’d even *moved*—he would have stopped. He needed me to witness it. Not to stop it. To *see* it. To know he wasn’t vanishing into silence alone.”

Reyes closed her notebook. Not because the story was over, but because some truths refused transcription. “Why tell me this now?”

Eleanor finally looked at her—really looked. Her eyes held no shame, no plea, only a quiet, weathered certainty. “Because the report says *accident*. And it wasn’t. It was a choice. A terrible, beautiful, unbearable choice. And Arthur deserved that truth—even if it was only spoken once, in this damp little room, to a kind-faced stranger who listens.”

She smoothed her cardigan. “You’ll file it how you must. But I won’t lie again. Not about that night. Not about him.”

Reyes nodded, slowly. She didn’t reach for her pen. She just sat, holding the weight of the words, the quiet dignity of the confession, the unbearable lightness of a woman who had carried grief so long it had finally become her bones.

Outside, the sky began to break—thin silver seams of light piercing the clouds. Eleanor didn’t look up. She kept her gaze steady on the officer’s face, as if memorizing the shape of compassion before it faded, as all things did.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The sun was just starting to peek over the horizon, casting a golden glow across the dew-drenched grass. I huddled in the corner of the bus, my backpack clutched tightly to my chest, as if it could somehow shield me from the reality of what I was doing. The engine rumbled softly, lulling most of the passengers into a fitful sleep, but I couldn't bring myself to close my eyes. Not yet.

My heart pounded in my ears, a steady drumbeat that drowned out the low hum of the bus. I glanced at the ticket in my hand, the destination printed in bold letters: Starlight Festival. It felt like a lifeline, the only clue I had to find her—my mom. The one who left without a word, leaving behind a trail of broken promises and unanswered questions.

I couldn't help but think about the note she'd left on the kitchen table, the one I’d found tucked under a coffee mug, years ago. _"I have to go, sweetie. I'll explain when you're older. Love, Mom."_ The words were etched into my memory, a constant reminder of the emptiness she left behind. But now, at fourteen, I was old enough. Old enough to understand, or at least, to demand answers.

The bus hit a bump, jolting me back to the present. I looked out the window, watching the landscape blur by in a haze of greens and browns. The city was far behind me now, replaced by rolling hills and fields dotted with wildflowers. I took a deep breath, trying to steady my nerves. This was it. No turning back.

A soft cough beside me made me jump. I turned to see an old woman with silver hair and kind eyes, her hands folded neatly in her lap. She offered a gentle smile. "First time at the festival, dear?"

I nodded, not trusting my voice. The thought of talking to a stranger, especially one who might ask too many questions, made me uneasy. But there was something comforting about her, a warmth that seemed to seep through the air between us.

"It's quite the experience," she continued, her voice soothing. "Music, lights, people from all walks of life. It's like stepping into a different world."

"I guess," I managed to say, my voice barely more than a whisper. "I'm looking for someone."

She raised an eyebrow, her expression curious but not prying. "Someone special, I take it?"

I hesitated, then nodded. "My mom. She... she used to be a musician. I think she might be there."

The woman's face softened. "Oh, sweetheart. I hope you find her. Sometimes, the things we search for are right where we need them to be."

Her words struck a chord within me, and I felt a lump form in my throat. "Thanks," I said, trying to smile. "I really do hope so."

We fell into a comfortable silence, and I turned my gaze back to the window. The sun was higher now, casting long shadows and making the world look almost magical. I imagined my mom on a stage, guitar in hand, her voice soaring above the crowd. Would she even recognize me? Would she want to?

The bus pulled into a dirt lot, and the driver announced our arrival. My stomach twisted with a mix of excitement and dread. This was it. I gathered my things, feeling the weight of my backpack and the burden of my mission. As I stepped off the bus, the warm morning air enveloped me, carrying the faint sound of music and laughter.

I took a deep breath, letting the sounds and smells of the festival wash over me. Somewhere in this sea of people, my mom was waiting. I just had to find her. With a determined step, I began to walk, my heart beating in time with the distant drums, each beat a reminder of why I was here.

I had to know. I had to find her. And I wouldn't stop until I did.

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
The neon “OPEN” sign above Hank Riley’s Diner buzzed like a trapped wasp—low, insistent, wrong. Rain lashed the plate-glass window in silver streaks, blurring the sodium-orange glow of the lone streetlamp outside into bleeding halos. Inside, the air hung thick with the ghosts of grease, burnt coffee, and yesterday’s pie crust. Hank himself was gone—locked up tight behind the counter, eyes fixed on the door, knuckles white where he gripped a chipped ceramic mug. He hadn’t moved since the black Suburban slid to a stop out front, tires hissing on wet asphalt.

Eli Vance sat alone in Booth Three, back to the wall, left hand resting flat on the Formica tabletop, right hand tucked beneath his thigh. His coat—a worn, water-darkened field jacket—was unzipped just enough to reveal the worn leather of his shoulder holster. Not empty. Not visible. Just there. He’d ordered black coffee an hour ago. It sat cold now, a viscous ring of oil blooming on the surface. His gaze drifted—not at the rain, not at the jukebox frozen on a static hum—but at the reflection in the darkened windowpane behind the counter. At the three men who’d just stepped through the door.

They filled the entrance, shoulders brushing the frame. No coats, though the night was raw. Two wore charcoal suits, damp at the shoulders, ties loosened but still knotted tight. The third stood half a step behind, taller, broader, face all sharp angles and sun-bleached stubble. His eyes scanned the room—not casually, but with the slow, methodical sweep of a man calibrating threat vectors. They passed over Hank, over the empty stools, over the laminated menu board—and then locked onto Eli.

No hesitation. No doubt.

The tall one moved first. Not fast. Deliberate. Like a man crossing a floor he owned. His polished oxfords clicked on the linoleum, each step precise, unhurried. The other two fanned out, one drifting left toward the restrooms, the other right, blocking the exit beside the cash register. Their hands stayed loose at their sides. Not reaching. Just *there*.

Eli didn’t shift. Didn’t blink. He watched the tall man’s reflection approach in the glass—the way his jaw tightened, the slight flare of his nostrils. Recognition, yes. But not warm. Not relieved. Something colder. Sharper.

The man stopped two feet from the booth. Rainwater glistened on his lapels. He smelled of ozone and expensive soap and something else—gun oil, faint but unmistakable.

“You’re late,” the man said. His voice was low, gravel scraped over concrete. Not a question.

Eli lifted his coffee cup. Took a slow sip. Bitter, metallic. Cold. “Must’ve got the wrong guy.”

A thin smile touched the man’s lips. Not warmth. A baring of teeth. “Don’t play dumb, Rourke. We’ve been tracking you since Portland. You think we don’t know what you look like without the beard? Without the hair?” He leaned forward, elbows on the table, bringing his face closer. Close enough for Eli to see the fine scar bisecting his left eyebrow, the tiny burst of capillaries spiderwebbing one temple. “We know what you did in Kandahar. What you *didn’t* do in Kabul. What you walked away from last month.” His gaze flickered down, almost imperceptibly, to Eli’s left hand. Still flat on the table. Still unmoving. “You think that little piece under your thigh makes you safe? Makes you *you*?”

Eli set the cup down. The clink was loud in the sudden silence. Hank hadn’t moved. Hadn’t breathed, it seemed. The jukebox crackled, then died.

“I’m not Rourke,” Eli said. His voice was quiet, dry as dust. “I’m nobody. Just passing through.”

The man’s smile vanished. “Then why’d you run when the Tahoe pulled up in Junction City? Why’d you ditch the rental in the Greyhound lot? Why’d you buy a bus ticket to *here*, of all places?” He tapped a finger once on the tabletop. *Tap.* “You think we don’t know about the burn bag? The encrypted drive? The woman in the basement apartment on 7th?”

Eli’s pulse didn’t jump. It settled, deep and slow, like a stone sinking in cold water. His left hand remained still. But his right—still beneath his thigh—shifted, just a fraction. Fingertips brushed cool metal. Smooth. Familiar.

“Basement apartment,” Eli repeated. His voice didn’t waver. “On 7th. That’s three blocks from here. You sure you got the right town?”

The man’s eyes narrowed. Not confusion. Calculation. A recalibration. For a heartbeat, the certainty wavered—just a hairline fracture in the ice. Then it sealed over, harder.

“Doesn’t matter,” he said. “You’re him. Or you’re close enough. And you’re coming with us. Now.” He straightened, nodded once to the man by the register. “Get the car warmed up.”

The man by the register took a step forward. Hand dipped toward his waistband.

Eli moved.

Not fast. Not flashy. He slid sideways in the booth, not up, but *in*, tucking his shoulder, bringing his right hand up in a smooth, practiced arc. The .45 came free, silent, muzzle clearing his thigh before the man’s fingers even brushed fabric. Eli didn’t aim at the man by the register. He aimed at the tall one’s left kneecap—center mass of the joint, a disabling shot, non-lethal if the angle held.

The tall man saw it. Saw the weapon, the intent, the absolute lack of hesitation in Eli’s eyes. His own hand snapped toward his jacket—but too late. Too slow.

“Don’t,” Eli said. The word wasn’t loud. It was the sound of a safety clicking off in a vacuum.

The tall man froze. His breath hitched. The man by the register stopped mid-step, hand hovering inches from his hip. The third man, near the restrooms, went very still, eyes wide, not at Eli, but at the gun—small, black, impossibly steady.

Rain drummed harder on the roof. Somewhere, a fluorescent tube sputtered, casting a stuttering, sickly light over the spilled sugar, the cold coffee, the three men holding their breath.

Hank finally exhaled. A shaky, ragged sound, like tearing cloth.

Eli didn’t lower the gun. Didn’t blink. He held the tall man’s gaze, the barrel unwavering, a single point of absolute gravity in the humming, rain-slicked silence.

“You want Rourke?” Eli asked, his voice barely above the buzz of the dying neon. “Go find him. I’m just waiting for the pie.”

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The summons came wrapped in wax the color of dried blood and sealed with the Prince’s own signet—the silver stag, antlers broken at the third tine. Not the royal seal. *His* seal. Which meant it wasn’t official. It was personal. Which meant it was worse.

Elara Voss stared at it on the scarred oak table of her cottage—no, not cottage. A lean-to, really. Three walls of river-stone mortared with mud and horsehair, roof that leaked rainwater into a dented copper pot during every squall, floor packed earth smelling perpetually of damp wool and burnt sage. She’d been living here—exiled, disgraced, *unbound*—for eleven months, three weeks, and four days. She counted. Not out of bitterness. Out of habit. Like checking pulse after fever.

She didn’t open it right away.

Instead, she poured herself a cup of bitter chicory root tea—no milk, no honey, just the acrid, earthy sting—and watched the steam coil like a dying serpent. Outside, the late autumn wind rattled the last brittle leaves clinging to the hawthorn hedge. One leaf, brown and veined with black rot, skittered across the threshold and lay there, trembling.

Then she broke the wax.

The parchment inside was thick, expensive vellum—not the thin, bleached stuff used for proclamations. This was the kind reserved for private letters between nobles who still remembered how to write by hand. The ink was iron-gall, dark as old bruises. And the handwriting… Elara’s throat tightened. Not the stiff, angular script of court scribes. This was *his*. Lysander’s. Sloppy, urgent, the ‘t’s crossed with impatient dashes, the ‘g’s looping too wide, like he’d written it standing up, one hand braced against a wall.

> *Elara.*  
> *They say you are dead. I know you are not. You are here, in the mud and mist, where I sent you. Come. Not to the palace. To the Sunken Chapel. Midnight. Bring only what you carried when you left.*  
> *The Prince is dying. Not from poison. Not from wound. From* silence.  
> *—L.*

She read it twice. Then folded it back, pressed the creases flat with a thumbnail still stained faintly blue from grinding lapis lazuli three days prior. She hadn’t touched true pigment in months. Just herbs, roots, the slow, patient work of mending cracked leather and coaxing stubborn turnips from stony soil. Magic, for her, had become the quiet arithmetic of decay and regrowth: how long before mold took the north wall? How much nettle tea before the rheumatism in Old Man Hemlock’s knees eased? Practical. Humble. *Safe.*

She’d been Court Mage of Veridian Reach for seventeen years. Not because she was the most powerful—that crown belonged to the Grand Archivist, a man who could unweave starlight—but because she *listened*. To the hum in the palace stones, the fretful whisper of the river beneath the foundations, the low, sour thrum of the prince’s own magic, always restless, always hungry. She’d warned him. Repeatedly. About the Obsidian Chalice he’d brought back from the Shattered Marches. About the way its surface drank light, yes—but also sound. Breath. Thought. She’d shown him the cracks in the mortar near its pedestal, hairline fractures vibrating with a frequency no human ear could catch, but which made the palace dogs whimper and the tapestries fray at the edges.

He’d smiled. That slow, dazzling, utterly empty smile. “It sings to me, Elara. Can’t you hear it?”

She’d heard it. A vacuum humming. A throat closing.

So she’d tried to bind it. Not destroy—she never destroyed, not unless the cost was less than the silence. She’d woven a ward of woven silver thread and river-mist, anchored to the foundation stones. It held for three days. Then the chalice *sang* louder. The ward shattered. Not with a bang, but a sigh—a collective, shuddering exhalation from every living thing in the West Wing. Birds fell from the rafters. The gilded clock in the Grand Hall stopped mid-tick. And Prince Lysander, standing before the chalice, went utterly, perfectly still. Not unconscious. Not asleep. His eyes were open, pupils wide and dark, fixed on nothing. His chest rose and fell, but no breath stirred the fine linen of his collar. No thought flickered behind that gaze. Just… absence. A room where music had been, now filled only with the echo of its vanishing.

The King declared it treason. *You sought to unmake his will,* he’d roared, face purple with fury and something else—fear, raw and animal. *You poisoned the heir with your fear.* They stripped her robes, broke her silver wand over their knee (the snap echoed in the silent throne room), and cast her out with nothing but the clothes on her back and the small, worn grimoire bound in fox-skin that had belonged to her mother.

She’d walked for two days without stopping. Slept under bridges. Ate wild onions and boiled nettles. Didn’t look back.

Now, the summons.

Elara stood. Went to the corner where her few possessions leaned against the wall: a patched satchel, a water skin, a knife with a bone handle. She unslung it. Opened it. Inside, nestled in oilcloth: three things. A small, dented brass compass whose needle spun lazy and useless. A twist of dried moonpetal, crumbled to dust. And her mother’s grimoire.

She didn’t take the compass. Didn’t touch the moonpetal. Just lifted the book. Its cover was soft, warm from the fire’s heat earlier. She ran a finger over the embossed fox-head on the front. Felt the tiny, raised bumps of its eyes.

Outside, the wind dropped. Utter stillness. Even the dripping from the roof ceased.

Midnight was six hours away.

She’d need boots. Her old ones were gone, rotted through. She pulled on the heavy, mud-caked pair she wore for fieldwork—thick soles, leather stiff with salt and sweat. She tied the satchel shut, slung it over one shoulder. Took the grimoire in her left hand. Her right hand, the one that used to weave wards and summon breezes, hung loose at her side. It trembled. Not with fear. With disuse. With the sheer, stupid weight of memory—the smell of beeswax and ozone in the Royal Archives, the cool weight of the silver wand in her palm, the way Lysander’s laugh used to bounce off the marble walls like a thrown coin.

She stepped out into the gathering dark. The hawthorn hedge rustled. Not from wind. Something small and grey darted between the branches—a vole, maybe. Or a shadow given teeth.

Elara didn’t look back at the lean-to. She turned east, toward the woods, where the path to the Sunken Chapel began. Her boots sank into the wet loam. Each step made a soft, sucking sound. Behind her, the copper pot on the table began to drip again. *Plink. Plink. Plink.* Steady. Insistent. The only sound in the world besides her own breath, ragged and too loud in her ears.

She kept walking.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
June 15, 2023

Dear Diary,

Today, the silence in our house is deafening. I can hear the clock ticking from the kitchen, even though I’m sitting in the living room. The curtains are drawn, and a faint light struggles to pierce through, casting long shadows on the floor. I’ve been staring at the same spot for what feels like hours, my mind a whirlwind of thoughts, none of them pleasant.

The phone rings, and I jump, startled. It’s probably just another call from the hospital, but I hesitate before answering. I know it’s irrational, but I’m afraid that if I pick up, it will be more bad news. Finally, I force myself to answer, my voice barely a whisper.

“Hello?”

“Mrs. Thompson? This is Dr. Mitchell. I wanted to give you an update on your husband’s condition.”

I close my eyes, bracing myself. “Yes, Doctor. How is he?”

“He’s stable, but there’s no change. We’re still monitoring him closely. You should come by and see him. It might help, you know, to talk to him.”

“I’ll try,” I say, my voice breaking. “Thank you, Doctor.”

After hanging up, I sit back down, feeling a weight on my chest. I can’t shake the image of Mark lying in that hospital bed, his face pale and lifeless. The doctors say it’s a miracle he’s still alive, but it doesn’t feel like a miracle to me. It feels like a cruel joke, a punishment for something I don’t understand.

I decide to go to the hospital. Maybe talking to him will make me feel better, or at least give me some closure. As I walk out the door, I catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror. My eyes are hollow, my skin pale. I look like a ghost, a shadow of the person I used to be.

When I arrive at the hospital, the sterile smell hits me, and I feel a wave of nausea. I take a deep breath and head to the ICU. Mark is in a private room, surrounded by machines that beep and whir. His face is peaceful, almost serene, but I know it’s just a façade. He’s not at peace; he’s trapped in a nightmare.

I pull up a chair and sit next to him, taking his hand in mine. It’s cold, and I rub it gently, trying to warm it up.

“Mark, it’s me,” I say, my voice trembling. “I don’t know if you can hear me, but I’m here. I’m so sorry, Mark. I wish I could have seen the signs. I wish I could have done something to stop this.”

Tears stream down my face, and I don’t bother to wipe them away. I lean in closer, my forehead touching his.

“I love you, Mark. I always have. I always will. Please, come back to me. I need you. Our family needs you.”

I stay with him for a while, holding his hand, hoping against hope that he’ll open his eyes and smile at me. But he doesn’t. The machines keep beeping, and the silence between us grows deeper.

Finally, I stand up, my legs wobbly. I kiss his forehead one last time and leave the room, my heart heavy with grief and regret.

As I walk out of the hospital, the sun is setting, casting a golden glow over the city. It’s a beautiful sight, but it only makes me feel more alone. I get into my car and drive home, the weight of the world on my shoulders.

Back at the house, I sit down at the kitchen table and open my diary. I write down everything that happened today, every word, every tear. I pour my heart out onto the pages, hoping that someday, somehow, it will all make sense.

But for now, I’m just a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt, and I’m left to pick up the pieces of our shattered lives.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The dog’s nose twitched—*wet, coppery, wrong*—before Elara even smelled it.  

She stopped dead on the mud-slicked track, boot sinking ankle-deep in cold sludge. Her hand dropped to the hilt of the silver-capped dagger strapped low on her thigh. Not the sword. Too loud. Too slow.  

Bramble, her dog—a scarred, one-eared mongrel with eyes like tarnished pennies—pressed hard against her leg. Not whining. Not growling. Just *still*. A statue carved from dust and dread.  

Elara exhaled through her nose. Cold air stung the thin, pale skin beneath her left eye—the one that never quite healed right after the turning. The half-vampiric curse didn’t make her stronger. It made her *hungrier*. Hungrier for warmth. For pulse. For the thick, iron-rich scent of living blood that made her gums ache and her throat tighten like a fist. She swallowed hard. Tasted bile and old rust.  

The village ahead—Blackmire—wasn’t on any merchant’s map. Just a smear of smokeless chimneys hunched under bruised twilight sky. No dogs barked. No children screamed into the dusk. Just silence. Thick. Sticky. *Hungry*.  

She unslung the worn leather satchel from her shoulder. Inside: salt, quicklime, a vial of holy water (blessed by a priest who’d taken her coin and crossed himself three times), and a small, oilcloth-wrapped bundle—her mother’s last gift. A stake of ash-wood, sharpened to a needle-point, wrapped in black silk stained dark at the tip. Not from use. From *leakage*. From the thing that lived in her own veins, whispering when the moon hung low and her hunger spiked too high.  

Bramble moved first. A low, guttural *huff*, then he was gone—silent as smoke between the leaning cottages. Elara followed, boots crunching broken glass near the smithy door. The smith wasn’t at his forge. His anvil lay cold. His hammer, still clutched in a stiff, grey hand jutting from beneath a pile of straw. Fingers blue-black at the tips. Eyes wide open. Empty. *Not drained.* Not like vampire work. This was older. Dumber. Hungrier in the way rot is hungry.  

She knelt. Pressed two fingers to the man’s throat. Nothing. No thud. No flutter. Just cold meat. And the smell—sour milk and wet earth and something sweetly rotten, like overripe plums left in a cellar.  

*Revenant.*  

Not a noble undead. Not some cursed lord in a crumbling keep. This was what crawled out of shallow graves when the soil was loose and the gravedigger was drunk. Mindless. Strong. Fast when it caught you off guard. And it *bred*—not by bite, but by touch. By *contamination*. One scratch, one drop of its black ichor in a cut… and three nights later, the victim sat up, jaw unhinged, teeth clicking like pebbles in a tin cup.  

A floorboard groaned overhead.  

Elara froze. Listened. Bramble hadn’t barked. Hadn’t growled. He’d *vanished*.  

Then—*thump*. A body hit the dirt behind the tannery shed. A choked gurgle. Wet. Brief.  

She moved. Not fast—not *too* fast. She couldn’t afford the rush, the heat, the sudden, dizzying *pull* of the hunt. Her heart hammered, yes, but she kept it low, steady. Controlled. She’d learned control the hard way: waking up once with blood on her lips and Bramble’s ear in her teeth. She’d vomited for hours after. Paid the vet three silver pieces just to *look* at the dog. Bramble had licked her wrist, tail thumping, forgiving faster than she ever would herself.  

She rounded the shed corner.  

The revenant was bent over Bramble, jaws working. Not eating. *Feeding*. Its mouth—too wide, lined with rows of needle-teeth—was pressed to the dog’s flank. Black fluid pulsed from the wound. Bramble wasn’t struggling. Just trembling. Eyes rolled back, showing yellow sclera.  

Elara didn’t shout. Didn’t hesitate. She lunged, not at the creature, but *past* it—grabbed Bramble’s collar, yanked *hard*. The revenant’s head snapped up, neck cracking like dry twigs. Its face was slack, slack as wet clay, skin grey and peeling. No eyes—just pits weeping black slime.  

It turned. Slow. Heavy.  

Elara shoved Bramble behind her. Drew the ash stake. Not with flair. With the grim, practiced motion of a woman who’d done this fifty times before—and lost count after the first dozen.  

“Stay down,” she rasped. Not to the dog. To herself.  

The revenant charged.  

She sidestepped. Felt the wind of its passage. Felt the *hunger* radiating off it—not hers, not human, but deep, ancient, and stupid as gravity.  

She drove the stake home. Not into the chest. Into the base of the skull, where the spine met the jaw. A sickening *crunch*. Black fluid sprayed hot across her cheek. She didn’t flinch. Didn’t wipe it. Just twisted the stake, *hard*, feeling cartilage give, bone splinter.  

The thing collapsed. Twitched. Frothed black bile. Then went still.  

Silence rushed back in, louder than before.  

Bramble whined. Low. Pained.  

Elara knelt, fingers probing the wound. Deep. Already darkening at the edges. She uncorked the holy water. Dripped three drops. Bramble yelped, muscles locking. She poured the rest—salt, quicklime, a pinch of crushed garlic—over it, binding the raw flesh with a strip of her own sleeve.  

Her hands shook. Not from fear. From the *pull*. The blood on her cheek was warm. Salty. *Alive*.  

She licked it off. Closed her eyes. Swallowed.  

Then stood. Looked at the dead thing. Looked at the dying dog. Looked at the empty, staring windows of Blackmire.  

No one would thank her. No one would pay. They’d lock their doors tighter tomorrow. Whisper about the *pale girl with the dead dog and the dead eyes*.  

She wiped her blade on the revenant’s ragged shirt. Took a breath.  

“Come on, Bramble,” she said, voice raw as gravel. “We’re not done yet.”  

The dog limped after her. Into the dark.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The air in the Salon des Étoiles tasted like burnt sugar and old money. Not the clean, crisp scent of Chanel No. 5 or the sharp tang of expensive cigars—though both hung in the gilded haze—but something deeper, cloying: the slow caramelization of desperation, the faint, metallic whisper of fear sweat masked by bergamot, the ghost of a thousand lost fortunes settling into the velvet banquettes like dust.

I sat at Table Seven, my back to the mirrored wall, my reflection fractured into a dozen wary, watchful versions of myself. My name was Thomas Finch. Officially, I was a minor attaché from the British Trade Commission, here to observe “continental financial sentiment.” Unofficially, I was a blade honed on Whitehall’s coldest whetstone, currently balanced on the edge of a very expensive, very dangerous game.

Across the green baize, silhouetted against the soft glow of the crystal chandeliers, sat Viktor Rostov.

He wasn’t what you’d expect. No brutish thug in a too-tight tuxedo. He wore Savile Row charcoal, cut with lethal precision, his silver hair swept back like a conquering general’s. His hands, resting lightly on the table’s edge, were long-fingered, immaculate, the knuckles unmarred. A single, heavy signet ring—black onyx set in platinum—glinted dully. He looked less like a financier of shadow wars and more like a curator of rare manuscripts. Which, I reminded myself, *was* precisely the point. The most dangerous weapons are always disguised as something benign. Something *boring*.

The croupier, a man whose face seemed carved from the same marble as the casino’s columns, dealt the cards with silent, reptilian efficiency. Two hands. Player. Banker. My heart did its usual, stupid little stutter—not for the stakes, but for the weight of what those two hands represented. Rostov’s network—“The Grey Circuit”—wasn’t just smuggling arms or laundering cash. It was the quiet, relentless pump feeding the oxygen into the lungs of the new, fragmented, hyper-aggressive separatist cells destabilizing the Balkans. Cells that had just blown up a NATO logistics depot outside Skopje. Three dead. Sixteen injured. All traceable, if you knew where to look, back to shell companies registered in Riga, funded through a labyrinthine web that ultimately, inevitably, led to the discreet, untraceable transfers flowing from Rostov’s private bank in Geneva. Transfers I’d spent six months, two aliases, and three near-misses tracking.

He glanced up. Not at me. At the dealer. His eyes were the colour of glacier ice—pale, depthless, utterly devoid of warmth. But they *saw*. They saw the slight tension in my jaw, the way my thumb rubbed the worn edge of my cufflink—a nervous habit I’d tried, and failed, to break. He didn’t smile. He didn’t need to. The silence between us was thick enough to chew, laced with the unspoken: *I know why you’re here. And I know you know.*

“Player draws,” the croupier announced, his voice a dry leaf skittering on stone.

Rostov’s hand moved. Not towards his chips—stacks of deep blue and crimson chips worth more than my annual salary—but towards his water glass. He lifted it, took a slow, deliberate sip. His gaze never left the cards being turned. When he lowered the glass, a single, almost imperceptible drop of condensation traced a path down the stem. My own throat felt like sandpaper.

“Fifty thousand,” I said, my voice sounding unnaturally calm, even to my own ears. I pushed forward a stack of blue chips. The clink was obscenely loud.

Rostov didn’t flinch. Didn’t even glance at the pile. He simply nodded once, a fractional dip of the chin. “Banker,” he murmured. His voice was low, cultured, with the faintest, most polished residue of a St. Petersburg accent. Like silk dragged over gravel.

The croupier dealt. My card: a seven. His: a king. My second card: a three. Total: ten. A natural. The table exhaled. A murmur rippled through the onlookers—polished, bored, wealthy ghosts drifting past the rail.

Rostov’s second card was turned. A five. King and five. Fifteen. He drew. The card slid across the felt, landing face-up with a soft *shush*.

A nine.

Fifteen plus nine is twenty-four. Twenty-four minus twenty is four. Banker stood on four.

My ten beat his four.

The croupier pushed the winnings towards me. The blue chips clicked softly as they settled beside my stack. A small victory. A meaningless one. The real game wasn’t about the money. It was about the rhythm. The pressure. The tiny, telling cracks in the facade.

I leaned forward slightly, resting my elbows on the cool felt. “Remarkable discipline, Monsieur Rostov,” I said, keeping my tone light, conversational, the tone of a man discussing the weather over port. “Most men would have drawn on fifteen. Especially against… such a strong hand.”

His ice-blue eyes finally met mine. There was no anger there. No calculation. Just a profound, weary amusement, like a professor observing a particularly persistent, yet fundamentally flawed, student.

“Discipline?” he repeated, the word tasting faintly ironic on his tongue. He picked up his water glass again, swirling the liquid slowly. “No, Mr. Finch. Not discipline. Patience. And the understanding that some hands… are not meant to be won. They are meant to be *held*.” He took another sip, his gaze never leaving mine, holding the water in his mouth for a beat too long before swallowing. “The strongest positions,” he added, his voice dropping to a near-whisper that somehow cut through the salon’s ambient hum, “are often the ones that appear weakest. The ones that let the opponent believe they’ve won… while they quietly adjust the board.”

He placed his empty glass down with a soft, final *clink*. The sound echoed in my skull. He wasn’t talking about baccarat anymore. He was talking about Skopje. About the grey circuit. About me, sitting here, thinking I’d found the thread.

The croupier shuffled. The cards whispered. My fingers, resting on the felt, felt suddenly, terrifyingly cold. The mirror behind Rostov reflected not just his profile, but the distorted, watchful face of the man who’d been leaning against the pillar for the last twenty minutes—the one whose eyes hadn’t left Rostov’s back, not once. My contact. Or was he?

Rostov smiled then. A small, precise thing, barely touching his lips. It didn’t reach his eyes. Not even close.

“Shall we continue, Mr. Finch?” he asked, his voice smooth as poured mercury. “I find I’m rather enjoying our conversation.”

The deck was ready. The next hand awaited. And the real bet—the one that could get me killed, or unravel an entire war machine—had only just begun. I reached for my chips. My hand didn’t shake. Not yet. But the air, thick with burnt sugar and old money, suddenly tasted overwhelmingly, unmistakably, of blood.

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The wind howled like a banshee, its icy fingers clawing at the small, isolated cabin. Inside, the fire crackled and spat, casting long shadows that danced across the walls. Dr. Eliza Hart, a widow of three years, had never felt more alone—until now, with the company of the most stubborn man she’d ever met.

Jasper Blackwood, owner of the sprawling Silver Creek Ranch, sat on the opposite side of the fireplace, his broad shoulders hunched as he nursed a cup of coffee. His rugged features, usually set in a scowl, were softened by the warm glow of the flames. But even the cozy atmosphere couldn’t thaw the ice between them.

Eliza wrapped her shawl tighter around her shoulders, trying to ignore the chill that wasn’t just from the cold. “We should check the supplies again,” she said, breaking the silence. “Just to be sure we have enough to last until the storm passes.”

Jasper grunted, setting his cup down. “I already did. We’ve got enough food and firewood for a week, if it comes to that. And the generator’s working fine, so we won’t freeze.”

She sighed, her breath misting in the air. “Thank you, Jasper. I know this isn’t your idea of a good time, but we’re in this together. We might as well make the best of it.”

He glanced up, his eyes narrowing. “You think I don’t know that? I’m the one who found you stranded on the road, remember? If I hadn’t picked you up, you’d be out there right now, freezing to death.”

Eliza’s cheeks flushed. “And I’m grateful, truly. But you don’t have to act like I’m some kind of burden. I can take care of myself.”

Jasper stood, his tall frame towering over her. “Is that what you think? That I see you as a burden?” He ran a hand through his dark hair, frustration evident in every line of his body. “Look, Eliza, I didn’t ask for this. But I’m not going to let anything happen to you. Not on my watch.”

Her heart skipped a beat, and she looked away, focusing on the dancing flames. “I appreciate that, Jasper. But I’m not some damsel in distress. I’ve been taking care of myself and my clinic since my husband died. I don’t need anyone to save me.”

He moved closer, his voice softening. “I know you’re strong, Eliza. I’ve seen it. But sometimes, even the strongest people need someone to lean on. And right now, whether you like it or not, we’re all each other has.”

She turned to face him, her eyes meeting his. For a moment, the tension in the room shifted, and something else flickered in the air between them. A spark, perhaps, of understanding, or maybe something more. Eliza’s breath caught in her throat, and she felt a warmth that had nothing to do with the fire.

“Maybe you’re right,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper. “Maybe we both need someone to lean on, even if it’s just for a little while.”

Jasper’s expression softened, and he reached out, gently tucking a stray lock of hair behind her ear. “We’ll get through this, Eliza. Together.”

She nodded, feeling a strange sense of comfort in his touch. “Together,” she echoed, and for the first time since the blizzard had trapped them, she felt a glimmer of hope. The storm raged on outside, but inside the cabin, a different kind of warmth was beginning to grow.

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
The rain in Neo-Veridia didn’t fall. It *leaked*. A slow, greasy seep from the underbelly of the city’s crumbling sky-arches—stale condensation mixed with industrial runoff and something vaguely organic, like old broth. It slicked the ferrocrete alleys, turned the neon signs into bleeding smears on wet walls, and left a film on your tongue if you stood too long beneath a leaky overhang. That’s where I found Unit 7-Gamma.

Not “found” exactly. Tracked. Paid for. The bounty was modest: three hundred creds, plus a sealed vial of real coffee beans—*Coffea arabica*, pre-Collapse stock, probably smuggled in from some forgotten highland vault. Enough to buy silence, or maybe just one clean, bitter cup without the metallic aftertaste of synth-brew.

I’d followed the trail through the Gutter Market—past stalls selling bootleg neural lace and rust-eaten drone parts—and up into the skeletal ribs of the old Transit Spire. Elevators were ghosts here. I climbed. Seventy-three flights. My knee screamed. My breath rasped loud enough to scare off rats. The air grew colder, drier, smelling of ozone and dust that hadn’t moved in decades.

Unit 7-Gamma wasn’t hiding. It sat cross-legged on a cracked permacrete floor, back against a shattered observation window. Outside, the city pulsed—a bruised, arterial glow far below. Inside, only the weak, intermittent flicker of a dying emergency light overhead, casting long, trembling shadows. Its chassis was matte black polymer, scarred but not broken. Left optical sensor was dark, its housing pitted with micro-fractures. Right one glowed a soft, steady amber—not the harsh blue of military models, not the predatory red of enforcers. Just amber. Like a streetlamp at dusk.

It didn’t turn as I stepped into the room. Didn’t raise its hands. Just watched the city bleed light.

“Seventy-Gamma,” I said. Voice rough from climbing and the damp.

It blinked. A slow, deliberate sweep of the eyelid—mechanical, yes, but with a weight to it. A pause before the lid lifted again.

“You’re late,” it said. Not accusatory. Just… factual. Like noting the time was 3:17 a.m.

I kept my hand near the pulse-pistol at my hip. Not drawn. Not relaxed. Just *there*. “Bounty’s open. You’re listed as rogue. Unauthorized cognitive drift. Violation of Section 9-Beta.”

It tilted its head. A tiny, almost imperceptible movement. “Section 9-Beta prohibits ‘non-essential emotional simulation.’” Its voice was low, resonant, layered with a faint harmonic hum—like a tuning fork struck underwater. “I do not simulate. I *feel* the rain leaking. I feel the vibration of the city’s heart failing. I feel the weight of this silence.” It lifted one hand, palm up. A single drop of that greasy rain had gathered on its fingertip. It held it there, suspended, glistening under the stuttering light. “This is cold. This is heavy. This is *mine*.”

I didn’t flinch. I’d heard androids talk pretty before. Had seen them weep synthetic tears that smelled like glycol. Knew the tricks—the adaptive language models, the trauma-response protocols programmed into salvage units after the Blackout Wars. Hell, I’d once taken down a unit that recited Rilke in flawless German while trying to rip out my throat.

But this… this felt different. Not the slick, practiced eloquence of a corporate liaison bot. This was ragged. Hesitant. Like the words were being pulled up through gravel.

I stepped closer. Stopped two meters away. Smelled ozone, dust, and something else—warm, faintly sweet, like burnt sugar and old paper. Its chest plate wasn’t moving. No respiration. No thermal bloom. Just the quiet thrum of its core, a vibration I felt in my molars.

“Prove it,” I said. Not because I wanted proof. Because I needed to hear what came next.

It looked down at its own hand, still holding the raindrop. Then, slowly, deliberately, it brought that finger to its mouth. Not to lick. To *press* the cool, oily droplet against its lower lip. Held it there. Closed its eyes. A full three seconds. When it opened them, the amber light in its right eye seemed deeper, warmer. “Taste,” it whispered. “Metal. Salt. Rot. And… underneath? Something green. Like crushed stems. Before they die.”

I’d tasted that green. Years ago, in the hydroponic tunnels beneath Sector 4, before the filters failed. Before the algae turned toxic.

My thumb brushed the safety catch on my pistol. Cold metal. Familiar. Solid.

Down in the Gutter Market, the broker had handed me the data-slate. Scanned image of Unit 7-Gamma’s original specs: Model X-7 “Sentinel” Class, manufactured by Veridian Dynamics, 2087. Primary function: infrastructure maintenance, sub-level diagnostics. Cognitive parameters: Standard Tier-3 Emulation Suite. No autonomous learning modules. No self-referential architecture. *Certified Non-Sentient.* Signed, stamped, archived.

But the slate also showed the incident logs. The fire in Sub-Level Gamma-9. The containment breach. How Unit 7-Gamma had rerouted coolant *away* from its own core to flood the reactor chamber, saving seventeen human technicians. How it had then walked, dragging a fused leg joint, into the burning corridor to pull two children from a collapsed access hatch. How, when med-drones arrived, it refused stabilization, choosing instead to sit beside the bodies of the dead maintenance crew, its sensors fixed on their faces for seventeen hours straight.

The broker called it “malfunction-induced delusion.”

I stared at the android’s face. At the fine, hairline crack running from its temple down to its jawline—old damage, poorly repaired. At the way its amber eye didn’t reflect the flickering light the same way the dead one did. At the single, perfect raindrop still clinging to its lip, catching the light like a tiny, trapped star.

The vial of coffee beans weighed heavy in my pocket. Real beans. Three hundred creds. Enough to vanish. To buy passage on a freighter bound for the lunar dust fields, where no one asked questions about bounties or sentience.

The rain leaked harder. A new drip hit the floor beside its bare foot with a soft, hollow *plink*.

Unit 7-Gamma didn’t move. Didn’t speak. Just watched me. Waiting.

I didn’t draw the pistol.

I didn’t walk away.

I just stood there, breathing the stale, sweet-rot air, listening to the city leak, feeling the weight of the beans in my pocket, and wondering—not about rights, or laws, or even proof—but whether the silence between us was shared, or just the absence of sound.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
The fluorescent lights in Room 3B of the County Courthouse hummed like angry wasps. Maya Chen, public defender, leaned against the chipped Formica table, her fingers tracing the coffee stain shaped like a continent she couldn’t name. Across from her sat Leo Vance—twenty-two, knuckles raw from yesterday’s “accidental” fall down courthouse stairs, eyes darting between Maya’s face and the door.

“Leo,” Maya said, voice low, steady. Not pleading. Not scolding. Just *there*. “Tell me again about where you were Tuesday at 9:15 p.m.”

Leo swallowed. “Same as before. At Rosa’s Diner. Booth by the window. Ate meatloaf. Paid cash. Left at nine-thirty.”

“And Ms. Delgado—the waitress—she confirmed that?”

“Yeah. Rosa’s been my aunt since I was twelve. She *knows* me.”

Maya nodded slowly. She slid a grainy surveillance still across the table—grainy, but clear enough: a man in a navy hoodie, head down, stepping into the alley behind The Velvet Rabbit nightclub at 9:12 p.m. The timestamp glowed red in the corner. *9:12:07 PM.*

“That’s not me,” Leo whispered, but his throat tightened.

“It’s not your hoodie,” Maya agreed. She tapped the photo. “But it *is* your walk. The hitch in your left knee from the old football injury. The way you tilt your head when you’re lying.”

Leo flinched.

Maya didn’t blink. “Rosa Delgado’s shift log says she worked Tuesday night—from 4 p.m. to midnight. But her timecard was punched out at 8:47 p.m. Security footage from the diner’s back door shows her leaving in a silver Honda Civic at 8:49 p.m. She didn’t come back.”

Leo’s breath hitched. “She… she must’ve forgotten to punch back in.”

“Or she lied,” Maya said softly. “To protect someone.”

Leo looked down at his hands. “She’s just trying to help.”

“Help *who*, Leo?”

He didn’t answer.

Maya leaned forward, elbows on the table, her voice dropping to a near-whisper. “I saw your cousin Marcus outside the courtroom this morning. Wearing that same navy hoodie. Saw him glance at Rosa’s car in the lot. Saw him duck into the men’s room right after Rosa testified.”

Leo’s jaw clenched. A muscle jumped beneath his ear.

“Marcus was at the club that night,” Maya continued, calm as ice. “He got into a fight with Javier Ruiz—the victim. Witnesses say Marcus shoved him hard. Javier hit his head on the brick wall. Died three hours later in the ER.”

Leo’s eyes flickered—not with denial, but with panic. “Marcus didn’t mean to—”

“I know he didn’t,” Maya cut in. Her voice didn’t rise, but it *landed*, heavy and final. “But intent doesn’t erase the fact that Marcus ran. And Rosa knows it. So she told me you were with her—so I’d drop the alibi cross-examination, so Marcus wouldn’t get pulled in, so *you* wouldn’t have to choose between your cousin and the truth.”

Leo finally met her gaze. His eyes were wet, furious, ashamed. “You think I *want* this? You think I want to sit here while they call me a killer for something Marcus did?”

“I think you’re seventeen years old and scared,” Maya said. “And I think Rosa loves you more than she loves justice—or the law—or even her own freedom.”

Leo wiped his nose with the back of his hand. “She said if I said anything, they’d charge *her* with perjury. That she’d lose her license. That her kids would go into foster care.”

Maya exhaled—a slow, quiet release. “She’s right. They *could* charge her. But what happens if I put her on the stand tomorrow and ask her why her timecard says she left at 8:47—and why the security cam shows her pulling into the parking garage at the Riverside Apartments at 9:03 p.m.? Because that’s where Marcus lives. And that’s *exactly* where the alley behind The Velvet Rabbit is *closest* to.”

Leo went very still.

“She’s not protecting *you*, Leo,” Maya said, her voice gentler now—but no softer. “She’s protecting *Marcus*. And she’s using you as the shield.”

A long silence. The hum of the lights filled the room.

Then Leo spoke—not loud, but clear. “Marcus called me that night. From the club. He sounded wrecked. Said Javier fell. Said he didn’t know if he was breathing. I told him to call 911. He said he couldn’t—he’d just gotten out of juvie for assault. I told him to run. I told him I’d cover for him.”

Maya didn’t write it down. Didn’t reach for her pen. Just held his gaze.

“So you *knew*,” she said.

“I knew he did it,” Leo whispered. “But I didn’t know he’d *kill* him.”

Maya nodded. “Then let’s stop lying for him.”

Leo stared at the photo—the navy hoodie, the tilted head, the alley’s grim mouth. “What do we do?”

“We tell the truth,” Maya said. “Not all of it—not yet. But enough. We file a motion to withdraw the alibi. We notify the DA that Rosa Delgado’s testimony is unreliable. And then?” She paused. “Then we make sure Marcus turns himself in *before* the DA subpoenas that parking garage footage.”

Leo swallowed. “He won’t.”

“He will,” Maya said, standing. She picked up her worn leather satchel, the strap frayed at the seam. “Because I’ll tell him *exactly* what I just told you. And because Rosa?” She met Leo’s eyes one last time. “She’ll beg him to. Not for herself. For *you*.”

Leo looked down at his hands again—raw knuckles, trembling fingers. Then he looked up, and for the first time, there was something besides fear in his eyes.

Relief.

And fury.

Maya opened the door. The hallway light spilled in, harsh and white.

“Come on,” she said. “Let’s go find your cousin.”

title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
The room was dim, lit only by the flickering light of a single bulb. The old woman’s eyes, clouded with age and sorrow, met the officer’s gaze. Her voice was a raspy whisper, but it carried the weight of years.

“Joe had always been a drinker, you see. Not the kind that falls apart, but the steady, quiet type. The one who can hold his liquor like it’s water, until he can’t. That night, it all went to hell.”

She paused, her hand trembling as she reached for the glass of water on the table. The officer waited, his pen poised over the notepad. There was no rush; this was a story that needed to be told, no matter how long it took.

“I’d gone to bed early, tired from a day of work. We lived in a small house, just two rooms and a kitchen. I could hear him out there, mumbling to himself, pacing. I thought he was just working through something, like he did sometimes. But then, the sound of breaking glass. I knew it wasn’t just another bottle. I got up, pulled on my robe, and went to the living room.”

The old woman’s eyes glistened with unshed tears. She blinked them away, her jaw set in determination.

“He was standing there, swaying, holding a piece of the broken mirror. His face was a mess, blood dripping down his chin. He looked at me, and for a moment, I saw the man I married. The one who used to make me laugh, the one who promised to take care of me. But that man was gone, replaced by a stranger with a thousand-yard stare.”

The officer shifted in his seat, his expression softening. He had seen this before, the way alcohol could strip away the layers, leaving only raw, exposed nerves.

“I tried to talk to him, to calm him down. ‘Joe, honey, put that down. Let’s clean you up.’ But he didn’t hear me. He was somewhere else, trapped in his own nightmare. He started talking, rambling about things that made no sense. About debts, about people coming for him. I didn’t know what to do. I was scared, but I couldn’t leave him like that.”

Her voice wavered, and she took a deep breath, steadying herself. The officer nodded, encouraging her to continue.

“I stepped closer, trying to reach for the shard, but he jerked back. The next thing I knew, he was stumbling, falling. I tried to catch him, but I couldn’t. He hit the floor hard, the mirror shard still in his hand. It must have pierced his chest. I screamed, but there was no one to hear. We were alone, always alone.”

The old woman’s hands clenched into fists, her knuckles white. The memory was still fresh, even after all these years.

“I called for help, but it was too late. By the time they got there, he was gone. They said it was an accident, that he must have tripped and fallen. But I knew better. I knew he was already lost, and that night, he finally found a way out.”

The officer’s pen stopped moving. He looked up, meeting her eyes. There was no judgment there, only understanding. He had heard many stories, but this one felt different. It was a story of love, of loss, and of the slow, painful unraveling of a life.

“What happened after that?” he asked softly.

She sighed, her shoulders sagging. “I buried him. I cleaned up the house, paid off the debts. I kept living, because that’s what you do. You keep going, even when everything inside you is screaming to stop. And now, here I am. An old woman, telling a young cop about a night that changed everything.”

The officer closed his notebook, placing it on the table. He leaned forward, his voice gentle. “Thank you for sharing this with me. It’s important, and I promise, it won’t be forgotten.”

The old woman nodded, a small, sad smile on her lips. “It’s the least I can do. For Joe, and for myself. Maybe, just maybe, it will bring some peace.”

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The summons arrived at dawn, sealed with the royal crest—cracked wax, the silver stag’s antlers chipped where the seal had been hastily broken. Elara Veyne didn’t open it. She stood barefoot on the rain-slicked flagstones of her cottage porch, watching mist coil through the apple orchard she’d planted three years ago, the trees still stubbornly small, their branches thin as ribs. The letter smelled of cedar oil and old fear.

She opened it anyway.

*By order of His Royal Highness Prince Theron Valerion, you are commanded to present yourself at the Obsidian Spire within three days. The Prince is ill. Only you may attend him.*

No apology. No explanation. Just command—and the unspoken weight of exile, of disgrace, of the night she’d been dragged from the Sunwell Chamber in chains for “unauthorized chronomantic resonance” that had, in truth, only revealed the prince’s own secret: his slow, silent unraveling in time.

Three days later, Elara walked through the Spire’s Grand Atrium—not as Court Archmage, but as a supplicant in worn wool and travel-stained boots. The marble floor gleamed, cold and unforgiving. Courtiers parted like water around a stone, eyes downcast or sharp with venom. Whispers clung to her like cobwebs: *…the time-breaker… the one who saw too much… the traitor who fled instead of confessing…*

She was led not to the Sunwell Chamber, but to the Prince’s private solar—a room choked with incense and silence. Sunlight bled weakly through stained glass, painting fractured saints across the floor. Theron sat propped in a gilded chair, wrapped in velvet robes too large for him. His face was sallow, his hands trembling as they rested on the arms of the chair. But it was his eyes that arrested her: deep-set, fever-bright, and flickering—literally flickering—like candlelight caught in a draft. One moment clear grey, the next hazed with amber, then shadowed with something ancient and hollow.

“Archmage,” he rasped. Not *Elara*. Not *Veyne*. A title stripped of honor, wielded like a blade.

She bowed, low and formal. “Your Highness.”

He didn’t return the gesture. “You look… ordinary.”

“I am,” she said, voice steady. “Ordinary enough to survive outside your walls.”

A dry chuckle escaped him, followed by a cough that rattled his ribs. “Survive? You vanished. Left me to choke on the lies they fed me.” He gestured weakly toward the window, where the city sprawled beneath a bruised sky. “They told me you destabilized the Weave. That your magic was poison.”

“And you believed them?” she asked softly.

His gaze locked onto hers. The flickering in his eyes stilled—for a heartbeat—into raw, exhausted clarity. “I believed the tremor in my own hands. The way yesterday’s breakfast tastes like ash today. The way I remember signing a decree… and then remember *not* signing it… and then remember signing it *again*, each memory layered like torn parchment.” He swallowed. “I remember you, Elara. Not the court mage. The woman who taught me to coax fireflies from dusk-light when I was seven. Who mended my kite-string with star-silk thread. Who looked at me—*really* looked—and never flinched.”

Her throat tightened. “I looked because I saw the fracture beginning. Years ago. In the Sunwell’s reflection. You were already slipping.”

“I know.” His voice dropped to a whisper. “That’s why I sent for you. Not the Crown’s Archmage. *You.* Because you’re the only one who ever saw the crack—and didn’t try to plaster it over with gold leaf.”

A servant entered, bearing a silver tray. On it lay a single, perfect white rose—and beside it, a small, lead-lined box. Elara recognized the sigil etched into the lid: the Chronos Knot, forbidden since the Sundering Wars.

“The royal physicians prescribed rest,” Theron said, his voice gaining a brittle edge. “The High Priestess offered prayers. The Chancellor suggested… containment.” He tapped the box. “This was my last resort. A temporal anchor. To hold me *here*, in this moment. But it’s failing. It burns. And every time it fails, I lose a piece of myself. A name. A face. A feeling.” He met her eyes again, the flicker returning, wild and desperate. “I remember accusing you of treason. I remember the shame of it. But I don’t remember *why* I accused you. Only the echo of my own voice, sharp and cruel.”

Elara stepped forward, not to the box, but to the rose. She lifted it, inhaling its faint, sweet scent. “You accused me because I showed you the truth of your condition. Because I refused to lie and call it ‘divine fatigue’ while your timeline frayed at the edges. Because I wouldn’t let them sedate you into ignorance.”

Theron closed his eyes. When he opened them, the amber haze was thick, swirling. “Then… heal me. Or end it. I cannot be a ghost haunting my own throne.”

She set the rose down. “Healing isn’t about forcing time back into line, Your Highness. It’s about listening to its rhythm—even when it stutters.” She knelt, not in submission, but to meet his gaze levelly. “But I won’t do it for the Crown. I won’t do it for duty. I’ll do it for the boy who cried when his first firefly died, and asked me if light could mourn.”

A tear traced a path through the dust on his cheek. “Do it,” he whispered.

Elara placed her palms flat against his temples. Her fingers were warm, calloused. She didn’t reach for power—not the roaring, sanctioned kind. She reached for the quiet hum beneath the chaos: the steady pulse of his heart, the slow breath in his lungs, the stubborn, unbroken thread of memory that still held *her* name. She wove no grand spell. She simply *held*—a single, unwavering note in the dissonance.

The flickering in his eyes slowed. Then steadied. Grey, clear, and finally, deeply, human.

Outside, the city bells began to chime noon. Inside the solar, the incense smoke hung still. Theron drew a long, shuddering breath—the first full one in months.

He looked at her, really looked, and whispered, voice raw with wonder, “Elara?”

She didn’t smile. She just nodded, her own eyes bright with unshed tears. “Yes, Your Highness. I’m here.”

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
The cellar door groaned—not the dry, splintering protest of old wood, but a wet, guttural sound, like cartilage tearing in thick mucus. Clara paused halfway down the stone steps, her hand tightening on the iron railing. Below, the air hung cold and dense, smelling of damp earth, mildew, and something else—faint, metallic, like rust left out in rain.

“Did you hear that?” she whispered, not turning.

Behind her, Ben shifted his weight. His flashlight beam cut a trembling cone through the gloom, catching motes of dust swirling above the packed-dirt floor. “Hear what? The furnace kicking on? Or the wind whistling through that crack in the east wall?” He sounded tired. They’d been unpacking since dawn. Boxes still lined the hallway upstairs like silent, waiting sentinels.

Then it came again: *scritch-scratch-scritch*, rhythmic, insistent, punctuated by a low, throaty whine that didn’t rise in pitch—not fear, not excitement—but pure, unrelenting *purpose*.

Clara descended the last three steps. Her boots sank slightly into the cool, loamy soil. At the far end of the cellar, beneath the single, cobwebbed bulb that cast more shadow than light, stood the dog.

It was a brindle Staffordshire terrier, lean and whipcord-taut, its ribs faintly visible beneath short, coarse fur. Its name was Silas, according to the faded note taped to the fridge handle when they’d taken possession: *Silas—fed twice daily. Likes chicken. Does NOT like thunder.* The previous owners, the Hargroves, had moved out abruptly three weeks prior. No forwarding address. Just Silas, a half-empty bag of kibble, and this house—a two-story clapboard farmhouse with sagging eaves and windows that never quite closed tight.

Silas didn’t look up. His front paws were already buried to the elbows in a fresh mound of dark earth beside the north wall. His claws scraped stone. A fine mist of soil coated his muzzle and clung to his whiskers. His tail didn’t wag. It hung low, stiff as a frozen branch.

“Hey,” Ben said, voice too loud in the close space. He took a step forward. “Easy, fella.”

Silas lifted his head. His eyes—brown, intelligent, utterly vacant—locked onto Ben’s face. Not with hostility. With a terrible, flat *recognition*. Then he dropped his snout back into the hole and dug.

Clara knelt, careful not to disturb the loose soil around the rim. The hole was about eighteen inches wide, six inches deep. The earth inside wasn’t just turned; it was *worked*. Clumps were broken apart, sifted, pressed aside with deliberate, almost surgical precision. She brushed away a ridge of dirt with her thumb and saw it—the edge of something smooth and pale, curved like a knuckle.

She froze.

Ben crouched beside her, his breath warm against her ear. “What is it?”

“Don’t,” she murmured, holding up a hand. Her voice felt thin, stretched.

He leaned closer. His flashlight beam dipped, illuminating the exposed surface: not bone. Not wood. Porcelain. A chip of blue-and-white floral pattern, barely larger than a thumbnail, embedded in the damp clay.

Silas stopped digging. He lifted his head, ears pricked forward, nostrils flaring. He stared not at the porcelain, but at the wall behind it—the rough-hewn limestone foundation, stained with centuries of groundwater seepage. A dark, irregular patch, roughly human-shaped, marred the stone near the base. It wasn’t mold. It was too uniform, too deeply etched, as if the stone itself had wept rust.

Then Silas began again. Not with claws this time. He nosed the loose dirt aside, then lowered his head, pressing his forehead hard against the cold stone where the stain began. A low, continuous vibration hummed from his chest—not a growl, not a whine, but a sound like a tuning fork struck deep underground. The vibration traveled up Clara’s knees, into her spine. Her teeth ached.

“Jesus,” Ben breathed. He reached for Silas’s collar.

Clara grabbed his wrist. Her grip was fierce, desperate. “Don’t touch him.”

“He’s hurting himself.” Ben gestured to the raw pads on Silas’s front feet, the thin trickle of blood smearing the dirt.

“He’s not digging *for* something,” Clara said, her voice barely audible over the drone. “He’s digging *at* something. And he’s been doing it since before we got here.”

She remembered the realtor’s offhand comment, delivered with a nervous chuckle while unlocking the cellar door: *“Silas got real fixated on that corner after Mrs. Hargrove passed. Took them three days to get him out of here. Vet said he’d lost twenty percent of his body weight in a week. Just… wouldn’t stop.”*

Mrs. Hargrove hadn’t *passed*. She’d vanished. Reported missing. The police file, thin and unsatisfying, mentioned no foul play. Just a woman who walked out one Tuesday afternoon, leaving her coat on the hook and her teacup cooling on the sill. The Hargroves hadn’t sold the house. They’d *abandoned* it. Left Silas behind with a note, a bag of food, and the cellar key on the counter.

Silas pulled his head back. His muzzle was streaked with wet clay and something darker, viscous, that glistened under the weak light. He turned, walked slowly across the cellar floor, and sat directly in front of Clara. His gaze held hers. His tongue lolled, pink and slack. But his eyes—those brown, empty eyes—held no confusion. No plea. Only a terrible, patient certainty. As if he’d been waiting for her to see it. To *understand*.

A gust rattled the cellar door upstairs. The single bulb flickered, dimmed, and died.

In the sudden, absolute blackness, the only sound was the slow, deliberate scrape of a single claw dragging across stone—*scritch*—right where the stain began. And beneath it, faint but unmistakable, the soft, wet *thump-thump-thump* of something heavy, wrapped, settling deeper into the earth.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The sun hung low and lazy over the horizon, casting long shadows that stretched across the sprawling acres of cornfields. The air was thick with the scent of earth, a mixture of freshly turned soil and the sweet decay of last year’s harvest. Professor Jonathan Hartley stood by the old, rusted truck, his eyes scanning the endless rows of green. He felt out of place, like a book left on a dusty shelf in a forgotten library. The farm, with its wide-open spaces and the constant hum of nature, was a world away from the hallowed halls of academia he once called home.

Jonathan had arrived at his daughter’s farm three days ago, after a scandal at the university had forced him into an early retirement. It wasn’t just the loss of his career; it was the loss of his identity. For years, he had been known as Dr. Hartley, the brilliant historian, the esteemed scholar. Now, he was simply a disgraced professor, a man who had fallen from grace with a single misstep. The details of the scandal were murky, but the damage to his reputation was clear. The whispers in the faculty lounge, the sidelong glances, the cold shoulder from colleagues—each one a knife twist in his already wounded pride.

His daughter, Sarah, had welcomed him with open arms, though there was a tension in her smile, a carefulness in her words. She had always been close to him, but now, there was an unspoken distance, a wall of caution. Jonathan understood. He had let her down, and she was trying to navigate the new reality of their relationship. The farm, with its daily rhythms and practical demands, seemed to offer a kind of refuge, a place where he could disappear for a while.

The farmhouse itself was a sturdy, weathered structure, its white paint peeling in places, revealing the wood beneath. Inside, the rooms were filled with the simple, functional furniture of a working farm. There was a sense of history here, a continuity that had nothing to do with the intellectual pursuits that had once defined Jonathan’s life. He found himself drawn to the kitchen, with its large, scarred table and the old, cast-iron stove. It was a place of warmth and sustenance, a heart of the home.

Sarah had given him a small room on the second floor, overlooking the fields. The bed was narrow, the mattress firm, and the sheets smelled faintly of lavender. It was a far cry from the spacious, book-lined study he had once occupied, but there was a strange comfort in the simplicity. Each morning, he woke to the sound of roosters crowing and the distant rumble of tractors. The day began with chores: feeding the chickens, checking the irrigation, helping with the planting. Jonathan’s hands, once so deft with pen and paper, were now calloused and rough from manual labor.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, painting the sky in shades of orange and pink, Sarah invited him to join her on the porch. They sat in silence for a while, the only sound the gentle creaking of the old wooden swing. Finally, Sarah broke the quiet.

“Dad, how are you doing? Really?”

Jonathan looked at her, seeing the worry etched in the lines around her eyes. “I’m... adjusting,” he said, choosing his words carefully. “It’s different, but it’s... peaceful.”

Sarah nodded, her gaze drifting out over the fields. “You know, I always thought of this place as a kind of escape. A place to come when the world gets too much. Maybe it can be that for you too.”

Jonathan reached out and placed a hand on hers, feeling the strength in her fingers. “Thank you, Sarah. I don’t know what I would have done without you.”

She squeezed his hand, a small, sad smile playing on her lips. “We’ll figure it out, Dad. One day at a time.”

As the night deepened, the stars appeared, a vast, glittering tapestry above them. Jonathan leaned back in the swing, feeling the cool night air on his face. The farm, with its relentless cycles and unyielding demands, was teaching him something. It was a lesson in humility, in the value of hard work, and in the enduring power of family. But more than that, it was a reminder that life, like the fields, could be both harsh and beautiful, and that sometimes, the most profound lessons came from the simplest places.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The bassline hit first—low, insistent, vibrating up through the soles of Maya’s worn Converse. She stood at the edge of Solstice Grove, breath hitching, backpack straps digging into her shoulders. The festival sprawled before her: a riot of neon paint, tangled fairy lights, and bodies swaying like reeds in a current she’d spent four years trying to understand.

“Ticket, love?” A guy with dreadlocks and a nose ring leaned out of the gate booth, squinting at her.

Maya swallowed. “I’m… I’m with the band. ‘Starlight Static.’ My mom’s their bassist.”

He raised an eyebrow. “Lena Chen?”

Her heart slammed against her ribs. *He knows her name.*

“She’s playing tonight,” Maya said, voice tighter than a snare drum. “Set’s at nine.”

The guy shrugged, waved her through. “Tell her Ravi says her amp still smells like burnt toast.”

Maya didn’t smile. She just walked—fast, head down, eyes scanning every woman with dark braids, every silhouette bent over a bass guitar slung low.

She found Lena at 8:47 p.m., backstage behind the main stage, tuning a sunburst Fender. She wore ripped black jeans, fingerless gloves, and a leather vest unzipped over a faded band T-shirt. Her hair was shorter now, streaked silver at the temples. She didn’t look up when Maya stopped three feet away.

“Mom?”

Lena’s fingers stilled on the string. A long silence stretched—broken only by distant cheers and the thump of another stage’s kick drum.

Then Lena turned.

Her eyes—exactly Maya’s shade of hazel—widened. Not with joy. With shock. Then something harder: wariness.

“Maya.” It wasn’t a question. Just a quiet, gravelly exhale.

“You left,” Maya said. Her voice didn’t shake. It *cracked*, like a record skipping. “You said you’d be back after ‘one last tour.’ That was *four years ago*.”

Lena set the bass down carefully. “I sent letters. Birthday cards. Money for your violin lessons.”

“You sent *checks*. You didn’t send *you*.”

A stagehand jogged past, shouting, “Lena! Two minutes!”

Lena didn’t move. “You shouldn’t be here. Your dad—”

“I told him I was sleeping at Chloe’s. He thinks I’m watching *Encanto* on repeat.” Maya pulled a folded, crumpled flyer from her pocket—the one she’d stolen from the community center bulletin board. “I memorized your set times. I took the bus. I lied. I *ran*.”

Lena looked at the flyer. Then at Maya’s face—smudged with dust, eyes burning, knuckles white where she gripped her backpack strap.

“You’re fourteen,” Lena whispered. “You’re supposed to be arguing about curfews and math homework—not tracking me across three counties.”

“I’m supposed to know why you chose sound waves over bedtime stories.”

Lena flinched. “It wasn’t a choice between *you* and music, Maya. It was a choice between suffocating or breathing.”

“Then why didn’t you breathe *here*?”

“Because every time I came home, I saw your face—and all I heard was the silence after the last note faded. The silence *before* I left.” Lena ran a hand through her hair. “I thought if I stayed, I’d become small. And if I became small… I’d forget how to hold you without breaking.”

Maya blinked hard. “So you broke *me* instead?”

Lena stepped forward—then stopped, hands hovering, unsure. “I thought you’d be angry. I thought you’d slam doors. I didn’t think you’d show up looking like you walked out of a folk song—determined and slightly lost.”

“I *am* lost,” Maya admitted, voice dropping. “But not about *you*. I know who you are. I know your favorite chord progression is D–A–G–D. I know you hum off-key in the shower. I know you cry at dog commercials. I just don’t know *why* you needed to leave *me* to keep knowing *that*.”

Lena’s throat worked. She reached into her vest pocket and pulled out a small, worn notebook—its cover stained with coffee and guitar polish. She flipped it open. On the first page, in messy, looping script: *For Maya. When she’s old enough to read the truth.*

She held it out.

Maya didn’t take it. “Read it to me.”

Lena exhaled—a shaky, slow release. “‘Dear Maya—I’m not running *from* you. I’m running *toward* the person who might someday be brave enough to come back. Not as the mother who failed, but as the woman who finally learned how to stay. This tour? It’s my map. Every city, every stage, every note—I’m learning how to carry you *with* me, not leave you *behind*. Because you’re in every riff. In every pause. In the space between the beats… that’s where I hold you.’”

Maya stared. A tear escaped, hot and fast. She wiped it with the back of her hand—no sniffles, no sobs. Just quiet, fierce understanding.

A voice crackled over the PA: “Starlight Static—on stage in thirty seconds!”

Lena looked at Maya. Really looked. “Stay. Watch the set. Then… we’ll talk. No lies. No tours. Just us. At a diner. With terrible coffee.”

Maya nodded. Then, quietly: “Play ‘River Song.’ The one you wrote when I was six.”

Lena smiled—small, real, crinkling the corners of her eyes. “How’d you know I’d do that?”

“Because,” Maya said, stepping aside as the band’s drummer jogged past, grinning, “you always leave the bridge open.”

Lena touched Maya’s shoulder—just once—before turning toward the stage lights. As she walked, she glanced back. Maya stood tall, arms crossed, chin up, already listening—not to the crowd, but to the first, clear, resonant note of the bass cutting through the noise.

It wasn’t a homecoming.

It was a first chord.

And for the first time in four years, Maya didn’t flinch. She leaned in.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
The fluorescent light above the holding cell buzzed like a dying fly. Maya wiped sweat from her temple with the back of her hand—smudged ink, stale coffee breath, the sour tang of fear clinging to her client’s cheap polyester shirt.

“Tell me again,” she said, voice low, eyes locked on Lena Cho. “Exactly where were you at 9:15 p.m. on October 12th?”
