title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
June 12th — 3:47 a.m.  
The monitor beeps. Steady. Flat. *Too* steady. Like a metronome set to “endure.”  

I stare at his face—pale, slack, the stubble on his jawline coarse and grey under the fluorescent hum. His left eyelid twitches. Not awake. Just nerves firing in the dark. A ghost muscle.  

I wrote *suicide attempt* earlier. But that’s clinical. Clean. Like it was a choice with options. It wasn’t. It was him standing on the garage roof at 2:13 a.m., barefoot, wearing only sweatpants and that faded band T-shirt—the one with the frayed collar he refused to throw out—and holding the ladder *away* from the house like he’d already decided gravity was negotiable.  

He didn’t jump. He *stepped*.  

One foot forward. Then nothing.  

The fall broke his pelvis, three ribs, his left wrist. The coma? That was the brain swelling. The doctors call it “anoxic injury.” Fancy term for *oxygen stopped showing up*.  

I keep the diary in the drawer beside his bed. Not locked. Just tucked under his old leather wallet—still holding his driver’s license, a crumpled $5 bill, two dried-up cough drops. I don’t know why I haven’t thrown them out. Maybe because throwing things out feels like admitting he won’t need them again.  

His hand lies palm-up on the sheet. Veins blue and thin as fishing line. I touch one. Cold. Not dead-cold. Just… waiting cold.  

I remember the last real conversation we had. Two days before. Over burnt toast. He scraped the black off with a butter knife, staring at the crumbs like they held answers.  

*“Do you ever feel like your own life is just background noise?”* he asked.  

I said, *“What does that even mean?”*  

He shrugged. Didn’t look up. *“Like you’re watching yourself live. And the person doing the watching? She’s tired. So tired she doesn’t even blink anymore.”*  

I thought he was being poetic. Or depressed. Or both. I made coffee. Poured it too hot. Spilled some on the counter. Wiped it up.  

I didn’t hold him.  

I didn’t say *I’m scared*.  

I said, *“You’re overthinking.”*  

God. That word. *Overthinking.* As if grief, or dread, or the slow erosion of hope has a volume knob you can just turn down.  

The nurse came in an hour ago. Checked his IV. Adjusted the oxygen flow. Smiled at me—kind, practiced, empty. *“He’s stable.”*  

Stable.  

That’s what they say when they mean *he’s not dying right now, but we have no idea what’s happening inside his skull.*  

I read his emails yesterday. Not on purpose. His phone buzzed while I was folding laundry. Locked, yes—but the preview popped up: *“Hey, just checking in re: the Henderson file. You okay? Haven’t heard back in days.”*  

Henderson. His biggest client. The one who fired him six weeks ago. Not for incompetence. For “lack of engagement.” Translation: he missed three deadlines. Stared blankly in meetings. Forgot his own password twice.  

I found the resignation letter draft in his drafts folder. Subject line: *“Stepping Back.”* Unsent. Saved at 11:03 p.m. on May 18th.  

He never told me he’d written it.  

I never asked.  

I kept making dinner. Doing the dishes. Paying the mortgage. Pretending the silence between us wasn’t thickening, wasn’t curdling into something sour and unnameable.  

The light in here is always wrong. Too yellow. Too still.  

I press my thumb to his pulse point. Faint. Thready. Alive. Barely.  

I whisper, *“Talk to me.”*  

Nothing.  

So I talk *to* him. Not about the weather. Not about the bills. Not about how the neighbor’s dog barks at 4 a.m. every damn night like it’s personally offended by sleep.  

I tell him about the crack in the bathroom tile I’ve been meaning to grout for eight months. About how I cried in the cereal aisle yesterday because the oat milk was out of stock and I couldn’t remember which brand he liked best. About how I caught myself humming his favorite song—*that stupid, sad Fleetwood Mac track*—while scrubbing toothpaste off the sink.  

I tell him these small, stupid, human things. Because they’re all I have left that feels true.  

And then I close the diary.  

Not with a lock. Not with a sigh.  

Just with my palm flat against the cover.  

Waiting.  

Always waiting.

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
The sun was a distant, cold ember in the sky, casting long shadows over the rocky terrain of Epsilon-4. The mining colony, a cluster of prefabricated buildings and industrial structures, seemed fragile against the vast, barren landscape. Inside one of the colony’s makeshift command centers, Captain Elara Voss studied the holographic map projected above the central table. Her eyes narrowed as she traced the red dots representing the enemy's advance.

“Status report,” she barked, her voice crisp and authoritative.

Lieutenant Jace Marsten, a tall man with a rugged beard, stepped forward. “We’ve got five tanks fully operational, ma’am. The rest are still being repaired from the last skirmish. We’re short on ammo, but we’ve set up defensive positions around the perimeter.”

Elara nodded, her mind racing. The invading force, a coalition of mercenaries and corporate enforcers, vastly outnumbered them. But they had the advantage of knowing the terrain, and their tanks were equipped with the latest in stealth and targeting technology.

“Alright, listen up,” she said, addressing the assembled crew. “We need to buy time. Our job is to hold the line until reinforcements arrive. If we can keep them at bay, we might just survive this.”

Jace turned to the tech specialist, a young woman named Sana Patel, who was monitoring the communication systems. “Sana, any word from the evac ships?”

Sana shook her head. “They’re inbound, but they won’t be here for another hour. We need to hold out that long.”

Elara took a deep breath, her fingers drumming on the table. “Let’s move. Jace, take your tank to the north ridge. Set up there and provide cover fire. Sana, coordinate with the other crews. We need to make every shot count.”

As the team dispersed, Elara made her way to her own tank, the _Valkyrie_. It was a sleek, heavily armored vehicle, painted in a matte black finish that blended into the night. She climbed into the commander’s seat, the familiar hum of the engines a reassuring presence.

“Alright, team, let’s do this,” she said into the intercom. “Keep your heads down and stay sharp.”

The _Valkyrie_ rumbled to life, its treads grinding against the rocky ground. As they moved into position, the first signs of the enemy appeared on the horizon. A wave of vehicles, their armor glinting in the dim light, advanced steadily. Elara felt a surge of adrenaline as she targeted the lead vehicle.

“Fire when ready,” she ordered, her voice steady.

The main cannon roared, the recoil shaking the tank. A bright flash illuminated the battlefield as the shell struck its target, sending debris flying. The enemy formation faltered, but only for a moment. More vehicles poured in, their guns blazing.

“Incoming!” shouted the gunner, Corporal Ravi Singh.

The _Valkyrie_ shuddered as it was hit, but the armor held. Elara scanned the battlefield, directing her crew with precision. They fired again, taking out another enemy vehicle, but the numbers were overwhelming.

“Jace, how’s your position?” she asked, trying to keep track of the entire engagement.

“Holding, but we’re taking heavy fire,” Jace replied, his voice strained. “We can’t hold out much longer.”

Elara gritted her teeth, her mind racing. “Sana, any sign of those evac ships?”

“Five minutes out, ma’am,” Sana responded, her voice tense. “But we need to keep the pressure off them.”

Elara took a deep breath, her eyes fixed on the approaching enemy. “Everyone, fall back to the secondary position. We’ll make our final stand there.”

The _Valkyrie_ retreated, its treads kicking up dust. The other tanks followed, forming a tight defensive line. The enemy closed in, their numbers daunting, but Elara’s resolve did not waver. She knew they had to hold, no matter the cost.

As the final moments ticked away, the roar of engines filled the air. The evac ships descended, their landing lights piercing the darkness. Elara gave the order to withdraw, and the tanks pulled back, providing cover fire as the colonists boarded the ships.

The _Valkyrie_ was the last to leave, its turrets firing until the very end. As they lifted off, Elara looked back at the burning remains of the battlefield. The colony was lost, but they had given the colonists a chance to escape. And that, she thought, was all that mattered.

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The wind didn’t howl anymore. It *screamed*. A raw, guttural thing that slammed into the cabin’s log walls like a physical blow, rattling the single, frost-feathered windowpane above the sink. Snow pressed against the glass in thick, shifting dunes, blurring the world beyond into a swirling, monochrome void. Inside, the woodstove coughed, then settled into a low, orange-throated purr—the only warmth, the only light besides the weak yellow halo of the kerosene lamp on the rough-hewn table.

I stared at my own reflection in the darkened window—pale face, dark circles like bruises under eyes that felt gritty with exhaustion and something else I refused to name. Dr. Eleanor Vance. Veterinarian. Widow. Currently, apparently, hostage to a stubborn, sun-bleached cowboy named Silas Thorne and the wrath of the Montana sky.

*This is absurd,* I thought, the internal voice sharp with the familiar, brittle edge of control slipping. *I have a practice. A schedule. A very expensive, very *un*snowed-in office in Billings. And here I am, stranded in a cabin that smells like pine resin, woodsmoke, and… well, him. Like saddle leather and cold air and something warm and earthy underneath, like sun-baked soil after rain.*

A floorboard groaned behind me. I didn’t turn. Didn’t need to. I knew the precise, unhurried cadence of his footsteps – heavy boots on the worn pine planks, a rhythm that spoke of patience measured in seasons, not minutes.

“Stove’s holding,” he said. His voice was low, a rumble that vibrated in the small space, deeper than the wind outside. It wasn’t loud, but it cut through the storm’s shriek like a knife.

I finally turned. He stood by the stove, sleeves rolled to his forearms, revealing corded muscle and dusting of golden hair. His gaze, the colour of weathered denim, met mine. Steady. Unflinching. Utterly infuriating.

“It’s holding,” I repeated, my voice sounding thin, reedy, betraying the tight knot of anxiety in my chest. “Like a drowning man holding his breath.” *Stupid. Why did I say that?*

A flicker of something – amusement? Pity? – crossed his face before settling back into that calm, impenetrable mask. He picked up the cast-iron skillet from the counter, its surface blackened with decades of use. “Coffee’s ready. Weak as dishwater, but hot.”

He poured two mugs. Handed me one. Our fingers didn’t touch, but the heat radiating from the thick ceramic burned my palms. I wrapped both hands around it, letting the scalding warmth seep into my chilled bones. *Focus on the heat. Not the proximity. Not the way his thumb brushed the rim of his own mug. Not the fact that his flannel shirt pulled taut across his shoulders when he leaned against the counter.*

“You know,” I said, aiming for light, landing somewhere between brittle and sarcastic, “most people trapped in a blizzard spend their time fretting about structural integrity or avalanche risk. Or, you know, *dying*.” I took a deliberate sip. Bitter, strong, exactly what I needed and absolutely not what I wanted. “You’re checking the coffee.”

A slow, genuine smile touched his lips. It transformed his face, softening the harsh lines around his eyes, warming the blue-grey depths. It was disarming. Dangerous. “Structural integrity’s sound, Doc. This place has seen worse. Avalanche risk is zero – we’re on flat ground, not a slope. As for dying…” He lifted his mug, his gaze holding mine over the steam. “Seems a bit premature. Unless you’re planning on poisoning the coffee?”

My breath hitched. *Poisoning.* The word echoed, sharp and sudden, against the memory of another kitchen, another mug, another man’s hand – warm, familiar, gone. The grief, usually a dull, manageable ache, flared, hot and sudden, tightening my throat. I looked down at the murky liquid in my cup, suddenly unable to meet his eyes. *Don’t see it. Don’t see the ghost.*

Silas didn’t push. Didn’t offer platitudes. He just… waited. The silence stretched, filled only by the wind’s furious assault and the stove’s steady, comforting sigh. It wasn’t awkward. It was… present. Heavy with unspoken things.

“Your horse,” I said abruptly, the words tumbling out, a lifeline thrown into the sudden quiet. “The bay mare. She’s resting easier now. The splint’s holding.”

He nodded, the smile fading back into quiet observation. “Thanks for that. Again.” He paused, his gaze drifting to the window, where snow continued its relentless, beautiful, terrifying siege. “She’s got spirit. Like her owner.”

My heart did a stupid, traitorous little leap. *Spirit.* Was that a compliment? Or just an observation about a horse? *Stop it, Eleanor. He’s assessing livestock, not your character.* But the warmth in his voice when he’d said it… it lingered.

“She’s also terrified of the vet’s truck,” I muttered, taking another gulp of coffee, using the bitterness to ground myself. “Took three biscuits and twenty minutes of whispering nonsense before she’d let me near her fetlock.”

A low chuckle escaped him, rich and warm as the stove’s embers. “Nonsense, huh? What kind?”

“‘You’re a magnificent creature, Buttercup. Your hooves are practically jewels. And this little bandage? It’s basically haute couture for equines.’” I winced internally. *Why did I admit that?*

He laughed again, a full, unrestrained sound that seemed to shake loose some of the cabin’s tension, some of the ice around my own ribs. “Haute couture?” He shook his head, a strand of sun-streaked hair falling across his forehead. “Doc Vance, you’ve got more tricks up your sleeve than a magician’s hat. And you call *me* stubborn.”

“I’m a doctor,” I retorted, the old defensiveness rising, familiar and safe. “Stubbornness is practically a prerequisite. Like carrying a stethoscope and believing in penicillin.”

“Penicillin?” He raised an eyebrow, a playful challenge in his eyes. “Is that why you keep looking at me like I might spontaneously develop a bacterial infection?”

Heat flooded my cheeks. *Caught.* “I was checking your pupils,” I lied smoothly, the lie tasting like ash. “Storm-induced stress can cause dilation. Or constriction. Or… something.”

His gaze didn’t waver. It held mine, deep and knowing, seeing past the flimsy medical excuse, past the coffee mug, straight into the chaotic, frightened, ridiculously hopeful mess inside my chest. The wind screamed its fury against the walls. The stove glowed. The coffee cooled in my hands. And Silas Thorne, the stubborn rancher, the man who smelled of earth and storm, just looked at me. And for the first time since the blizzard swallowed the world, the silence between us didn’t feel like emptiness. It felt like space. Space waiting to be filled. With something new. Something terrifying. Something, perhaps, that had nothing to do with horses, or blizzards, or even the careful, meticulous walls I’d built brick by careful brick since David died. My breath caught, sharp and sweet, in the smoky, snow-bound air.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The studio lights hummed—a low, persistent thrum beneath the bassline of the opening theme music. Rain lashed the reinforced glass of the booth window, blurring the sodium-orange glow of the city beyond into streaks of sickly gold. Silas Thorne adjusted the headset, the worn leather cool against his temples. His fingers, long and knotted at the knuckles, rested lightly on the fader. On the monitor, the waveform of his voice pulsed steady: *“…and if you’re just tuning in to *Midnight Howl*, welcome. I’m Silas. The night’s got teeth tonight—literally, for some of us. Call in. Tell me what keeps *you* awake.”*

He took a slow breath. Not too deep. Not with the chest. The ribs still ached faintly from last Tuesday’s change—the one that hadn’t gone clean. A jagged edge of bone had pressed, just for a second, against the underside of his left scapula before settling. He’d swallowed three ibuprofen with lukewarm black coffee and kept talking.

The phone lines lit up—amber dots blinking like fireflies in the dark console. He scrolled past the usual: the college kid asking if moonlight really made werewolves *more* horny (it didn’t; stress did), the woman describing her neighbour’s “unnaturally loud” yowling cats (Silas had gently suggested a wildlife biologist). Then, Line Three. No caller ID. Just a pulsing, unblinking red.

He tapped the button. “Line Three—you’re live on *Midnight Howl*. Go ahead.”

A pause. Not the nervous silence of a first-time caller. This was the quiet of a man who’d waited years for this exact frequency, this exact voice. Then, a voice—not loud, but carved from river stone and dry pine needles. Low. Utterly devoid of tremor.

“Silas Thorne.”

Not *‘Hi, Silas’*. Not *‘I love the show’*. Just the name. Delivered like an indictment.

Silas’s pulse didn’t spike. It *deepened*, a slow, heavy thud against his sternum. His right hand, resting on the fader, tightened almost imperceptibly. The knuckles whitened. A faint, coppery tang bloomed at the back of his throat—not blood, not yet. Just the old, familiar warning: *Something is here.*

“Who’s calling?” Silas asked. His own voice remained smooth, warm, the practiced velvet of late-night radio. But he lowered the mic fractionally, just enough to soften the resonance, to keep the vibration from rattling his molars.

“The name doesn’t matter,” the voice said. A dry chuckle, like twigs snapping under boot-heel. “You know what I am. You’ve smelled it on the wind, haven’t you? That sharp, clean scent—ozone and crushed sage and something older than iron. Like the air before lightning strikes *inside* your skull.”

Silas didn’t flinch. He leaned forward, elbows on the console, watching the rain smear across the glass. His reflection stared back—dark hair falling across a high, pale forehead, eyes the colour of tarnished silver. In the dim light, the pupils were just a shade too wide, the irises holding a faint, liquid sheen, like oil on wet stone. He’d checked them in the bathroom mirror an hour ago. Normal. Mostly.

“I smell a lot of things, friend,” Silas said, keeping his tone light, conversational. “Wet pavement. My own burnt toast. The existential dread of my producer, currently pacing outside the door. What’s *your* scent?”

A beat. Longer this time. The hum of the lights seemed to swell, filling the space between words. Outside, a siren wailed, distant and mournful.

“Yours,” the voice said, soft as smoke, “is wolf. But not *just* wolf. There’s ash in it. And salt. And something… frayed. Like old rope about to snap.”

Silas’s breath hitched—just once. A tiny, involuntary catch. He covered it with a sip of water, the plastic cup cold and slick in his grip. His tongue traced the sharp, ridged edge of a lower canine. It felt longer. Harder. He pressed it gently against the gum. No give. No pain. Just pressure.

“Frayed rope,” Silas repeated, his voice dropping, losing its radio polish, gaining a rougher, deeper timbre. The kind that vibrated in the hollow behind the listener’s ears. “That’s an interesting image. What do you propose to do about it?”

The line crackled—not static, but a low, resonant *thrum*, like a bow drawn taut over a cello string. Then, a sound: the soft, unmistakable *shink* of metal sliding home in a well-oiled sheath.

“I don’t propose,” the hunter said. His voice hadn’t changed, but the air in the booth thickened, grew colder near the floor vents. Silas felt the fine hairs on his forearms lift, not from chill, but from the sheer, focused *intent* radiating down the line. “I prepare. I track. And when the moon bleeds silver over the rooftops tonight—exactly at 11:47 p.m.—I’ll be standing on the corner of Holloway and Seventh. Waiting. With a gift for you.”

Silas’s gaze flickered to the studio clock. 11:38. Nine minutes. His vision sharpened, the edges of the rain-streaked glass suddenly etched with impossible clarity—the individual droplets, the fractured reflections of streetlights, the subtle, almost invisible shimmer where the air itself seemed to *bend* around the corner of the building visible through the window. His hearing narrowed, tunneling past the hum, past the distant sirens, down to the faint, rhythmic *drip-drip-drip* of condensation inside the AC unit’s drain pipe. And beneath it all, a new sound: the slow, deliberate scrape of a boot sole on wet concrete. *Outside.* Right there. On the sidewalk below.

His nostrils flared. Beneath the damp wool of his sweater, the scent hit him—not ozone, not sage. *Gun oil.* Cold, metallic, and layered over something else: dried blood, ancient and thin as parchment, and the faint, sweet decay of wormwood.

The hunter wasn’t just calling. He was *here*.

Silas didn’t look at the door. Didn’t signal the engineer. He held the mic close, his voice dropping to a near-whisper, rich and dangerous as midnight river water.

“Holloway and Seventh,” he murmured, the words curling like smoke. “That’s where the old brickworks used to be. Where the walls are thick. Where the shadows… hold their breath.”

A pause. Then, softer still, the whisper becoming a growl that vibrated in Silas’s own jawbone, resonating up from his throat: “What’s the gift?”

The line went dead. Not a click. Not a dial tone. Just… silence. Absolute, suffocating silence. The hum of the lights vanished. The rain on the glass ceased. Even the distant sirens cut off mid-wail.

In the sudden, ringing void, Silas Thorne slowly raised his left hand. Held it before the small, angled mirror mounted beside the mic. The reflection showed his face—but for a single, suspended heartbeat, the eyes staring back weren’t silver. They were the molten, burning gold of a predator who’d just caught the scent of its own end. And in the corner of the frame, just beyond his shoulder, the studio door handle began, very slowly, to turn.

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
The sun hung low in the sky, casting a warm, golden glow over the sprawling grounds of the Maplewood County Fair. The air was thick with the scent of freshly fried funnel cakes and the distant sound of laughter from the midway. But for Emily Hartley, the fair’s antiques show was the main attraction. She had been looking forward to this day for weeks, eager to add to her extensive collection of vintage dolls.

Emily, a petite woman in her late fifties, wore a floral dress that swirled around her knees as she walked, her silver hair pulled back into a neat bun. Her eyes, a bright blue, sparkled with excitement as she scanned the rows of booths, each one a treasure trove of old trinkets and collectibles. She clutched her worn leather purse, her fingers brushing against the small notepad and pen inside, ready to jot down any new finds.

As she approached a booth filled with an assortment of antique dolls, her heart skipped a beat. There, nestled among a sea of porcelain faces, was a rare 1920s Shirley Temple doll, complete with its original box. Emily’s breath caught in her throat. She had been searching for one of these for years.

“Excuse me,” she said, leaning over the table to get a closer look. “Is this doll for sale?”

A tall, lanky man with a scruffy beard and a faded baseball cap looked up from his phone. He squinted at her, then at the doll. “Yeah, that one’s for sale. It’s a real find, isn’t it? I’ll let you have it for five hundred bucks.”

Five hundred dollars was steep, but Emily knew it was worth every penny. She reached into her purse, her hand trembling slightly with anticipation. Just as she was about to pull out her wallet, a commotion erupted from the next booth over.

“What the hell do you think you’re doing?” a sharp, angry voice demanded.

Emily turned to see a stout, red-faced man in a plaid shirt and jeans, his face twisted in fury. He was glaring at a younger, slender woman with curly brown hair, who was standing behind a table of delicate china figurines. The woman’s eyes were wide with fear, and she took a step back, nearly knocking over a display of teacups.

“I didn’t do anything!” the woman protested, her voice quivering. “I swear, I don’t know what you’re talking about!”

The man lunged forward, grabbing the woman by the arm. “You stole my pocket watch, and I want it back! Now!”

The crowd around them began to gather, drawn by the escalating argument. Emily, still holding her purse, hesitated, unsure of what to do. The vendor with the Shirley Temple doll seemed unfazed, his attention already drifting back to his phone.

Suddenly, a sharp cry pierced the air. The stout man staggered backward, clutching his chest. His face contorted in pain, and he collapsed to the ground, his body convulsing. The young woman screamed, and the crowd surged forward, some calling for help, others backing away in shock.

Emily dropped her purse and rushed to the man’s side, her training as a former nurse kicking in. She knelt beside him, feeling for a pulse. It was weak and thready, and his breathing was shallow. She glanced up at the onlookers, her voice steady despite the chaos. “Someone call 911! Now!”

Within minutes, the fairgrounds were alive with the wail of sirens. Paramedics arrived, pushing through the crowd to reach the fallen man. They worked quickly, their movements practiced and efficient, but Emily could tell it was too late. The man’s lifeless eyes stared up at the sky, and she felt a shiver run down her spine.

As the paramedics loaded the body onto a gurney, a detective in a rumpled suit pushed his way through the crowd. He was a middle-aged man with a stern face and a no-nonsense demeanor. He surveyed the scene, his eyes narrowing as they landed on the young woman, who was now being comforted by a friend.

“Miss, I need you to come with me,” the detective said, his tone firm. “We have some questions for you.”

The woman nodded, her face pale and tear-streaked. As she was led away, Emily couldn’t help but wonder what had really happened. Had the man died of natural causes, or was there something more sinister at play?

She picked up her purse, her mind racing. The Shirley Temple doll was forgotten, replaced by a growing sense of unease. The antiques show, once a source of joy and excitement, now felt tainted by the shadow of death. Emily knew she couldn’t just walk away. She had to find out the truth.

As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the fairgrounds, Emily made a silent vow to uncover the mystery. The county fair, with its quaint charm and nostalgic allure, had just become the backdrop for a murder, and she was determined to solve it.

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The rain drummed a nervous rhythm on the roof of the dented blue Honda Civic. Inside, the air hung thick with stale coffee, cheap cologne, and dread.

“Look at this,” said Vince, jabbing a finger at the folded newspaper on the dashboard. His knuckles were scarred, his voice a gravelly whisper. “‘Local Tech Heir Missing After Charity Gala.’ One sentence. One *sentence*, and they’re already calling it ‘suspicious.’ You think they’ll wait for us to send a ransom note? They’ll have every cop in three counties sniffing around before breakfast.”

Marty leaned back, adjusting the brim of his too-big baseball cap. His fingers—slim, restless—tapped a frantic beat against his thigh. “Suspicious? Vince, he *vanished* from a room full of billionaires and security guards. That’s not suspicious—that’s *magic*. We didn’t vanish him. We just… nudged the door open while nobody was looking.” He grinned, but it didn’t reach his eyes. “Besides, the money’s real. The account’s verified. Two million. Cash pickup. Simple.”

“Simple?” Vince snorted, twisting the rearview mirror to check the empty street behind them. “You call holding a kid in a basement with a duct-taped mouth and a bucket ‘simple’? What if he cries? What if he *pukes*? What if his dog starts barking at the wrong time and some neighbor calls animal control—and then *911*?”

“He won’t cry,” Marty said, pulling a small, polished brass lighter from his pocket and flicking it open, closed, open. *Click. Snick. Click.* “He’s seventeen. Thinks he’s James Bond. Got a tattoo of a falcon on his shoulder and wears sunglasses indoors. He’ll be *bored*, Vince. Bored and mildly inconvenienced. Like waiting for a delayed flight.”

Vince rubbed his temples. “You don’t know him. You’ve seen his Instagram. That’s not a person—that’s a mood board. Real people *break*. They panic. They wet themselves. They *scream* when you take their phone away.”

“They won’t scream if they know what happens if they do.” Marty’s voice dropped, smooth as oil. He held up his left hand, palm out—three fingers bent, two straight. “Three days. That’s all we need. Three days, the money hits the offshore shell, and we’re on a beach in Tulum drinking something with an umbrella. No stress. No fingerprints. Just *clean*.”

“Clean?” Vince barked a laugh that sounded like coughing. “You used *my* burner phone to text the drop location. My *name* is on the lease for the storage unit where we stashed the van. And you *borrowed* my sister’s minivan—her *minivan*, Marty—because it ‘blends in.’ What blends in? A purple minivan with a Peppa Pig sticker on the bumper?!”

Marty waved a dismissive hand. “Sticker’s peeled off. Mostly. And your sister thinks it’s ‘on loan to her yoga instructor.’ She’ll never connect the dots.”

“She’ll connect the dots when the FBI shows up asking why her brother owns a van with a hidden compartment lined with soundproof foam!” Vince slammed his palm flat on the steering wheel. The horn gave a single, pathetic *beep*. “This isn’t boosting a flatscreen from Best Buy, Marty. This is *kidnapping*. Real people get life for this. Not probation. Not community service. *Life*. In a cell with guys who make prison tattoos out of melted Bic pens and regret.”

Marty went very still. The lighter stopped clicking. He stared at Vince—not angry, not defensive—just *measuring*. “You scared, Vince?”

Vince looked out the rain-streaked window. A streetlight flickered, casting long, wavering shadows across his face. “Yeah,” he whispered. “I’m scared. Scared of the dark. Scared of silence. Scared of what I hear when I close my eyes at night. And right now? I’m scared of *you*.”

Marty blinked. Slowly. “Me?”

“You don’t hear it,” Vince said, voice raw. “That little voice. The one that says, ‘Stop. Walk away. Call it off.’ You just… tune it out. Like background noise. Like the hum of a fridge.”

Marty leaned forward, elbows on knees, staring at his own hands. “My dad spent twenty years in Attica. For stealing a car. A *car*, Vince. He came out broken. Couldn’t hold a job. Couldn’t look a cop in the eye without sweating through his shirt. I watched him shrink. Every day. So yeah—I tuned it out. Because that voice? It doesn’t keep you safe. It just makes you small.”

Silence settled, heavier than before. The rain softened to a hush.

Then Vince sighed—a long, slow exhalation that seemed to deflate him. “So what do we do?”

Marty didn’t answer right away. He opened the glove compartment, pulled out a single sheet of paper—the ransom note, typed, unsigned, crisp. He held it over the ashtray. “We burn it.”

Vince watched the corner catch flame, orange and hungry. “And the kid?”

“We let him go. Right now. Drive him back. Drop him at the mall food court. Tell him his Uber’s running late. Say we got lost.”

Vince stared at the burning paper. “What about the money?”

Marty watched the flames curl the edges black. “Gone. Like smoke.” He dropped the ember into the ashtray, stamped it out with his thumb. “Two million dollars buys a lot of things, Vince. But it doesn’t buy back the first time you lie to your mom. Or the last time you hugged your nephew. Or the quiet in your own head.” He met Vince’s gaze. “You still hear it, don’t you? That voice?”

Vince nodded, once. His throat worked. “Yeah.”

Marty started the engine. The Civic coughed to life, headlights slicing twin beams through the wet dark. “Then let’s go home,” he said softly. “Before we forget how to listen.”

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
The dust in the air tasted like burnt iron and regret. Inside the cramped, sweat-slicked belly of *Ironhide*, Sergeant Anya Rostova wiped grease from her brow with a knuckle, leaving a fresh smear across her temple. Outside the periscope’s narrow field of view, the Kaelen Belt mining colony of Helios-7 was a sprawl of pressurized domes, skeletal ore processors, and the jagged, rust-streaked teeth of the Gorgon Ridge—now crawling with enemy armor.

“Contact! Two klicks east—*Raptors*,” spat Corporal Dex Varga, his voice tight over the comms. His fingers danced across the fire control panel, crosshatching targets on the main HUD. “Three, no—*four* of them. Moving fast. No infantry screen. Just pure, stupid speed.”

Anya didn’t flinch. She keyed her mic. “*Bulldog*, *Hammer*, this is *Ironhide*. Confirm visual. Raptors, four, east ridge line. They’re coming straight for the primary fusion tap. They want to black out the colony before they even land troops.”

A crackle, then Lieutenant Chen’s voice, strained but steady: “Confirmed, *Ironhide*. We’re holding position at Grid Echo-Seven. But Anya… their *Maulers* are behind them. Heavy assault column. Eight, maybe ten. And that’s just what we can see through the dust storm.”

Eight Maulers. Each one a thirty-five-ton brute with a 120mm railgun and reactive armor that shrugged off everything short of a direct hit from another tank. *Ironhide*, *Bulldog*, and *Hammer*—three aging M-7 “Goliath” heavies, patched with scavenged parts and hope—were all that stood between Helios-7’s three thousand souls and orbital evacuation—or slaughter.

“Then we don’t let them get close enough to use them,” Anya said, her voice low, certain. She leaned into the commander’s cupola, scanning the ridge. Dust swirled in angry eddies where the Raptors’ treads churned the regolith. “Dex—target the lead. Full APFSDS. On my mark.”

“Locked. Firing solution nominal.”

“Hold.” She watched the lead Razor—a sleek, angular predator built for speed, not siege—crest the final rise. Its turret swiveled, sensor array sweeping toward the fusion tap dome. A red laser dot flickered across the dome’s reinforced plating. *Targeting.*

“Now!”

The Goliath’s main gun roared, a physical blow inside the hull. The world jumped. Through the periscope, Anya saw the Razor’s turret *twist* sideways as the hyper-velocity round punched through its frontal arc, detonating the ammo carousel inside. Fire bloomed, orange and violent, swallowing the machine whole. It tumbled backward down the ridge, trailing smoke and sparks.

“Hit! Confirmed kill!” Dex yelled.

But there was no celebration. Two more Raptors accelerated, splitting left and right, firing on the move. High-explosive rounds slammed into *Ironhide*’s glacis plate, shuddering the hull, rattling loose tools from their mounts. Alarms shrieked—armor integrity warning, thermal bloom rising.

“Armor’s holding, but barely!” shouted Tech Lien from the rear compartment, her voice raw. “That last one cracked the left-side composite layer!”

“Then we make them pay for every centimeter,” Anya snapped. “Dex—second target. Left flank. Chen, *Bulldog*—suppress the right flank! Hammer, cover our six—Maulers are closing!”

A new voice cut in, breathless: “*Hammer* here! Two Maulers just breached the western pass! They’re deploying infantry—light mechs, swarm drones!”

Chaos erupted. *Ironhide* pivoted, its turret grinding, tracks screaming against the rocky slope. Dex fired again. Missed. The second Razor returned fire, a near-miss that sent a geyser of rock and dust twenty meters high, showering the hull with shrapnel.

“Reload!” Anya barked.

“Reloading!” Lien grunted, slamming a fresh round into the breech.

The third Razor opened up on *Bulldog*. A direct hit. The Goliath staggered, smoke belching from its engine deck. Its turret went dark.

“*Bulldog* is down!” Chen’s voice was ragged. “Turret traverse offline. We’re blind!”

Anya’s stomach dropped. Two tanks left. Four Raptors still moving. Eight Maulers less than a klick away, their heavy treads shaking the ground like distant thunder.

Then she saw it—the dust plume behind the Mauler column. Not wind. Too dense. Too *organized*.

“Lien—get me eyes on that dust cloud behind the Maulers. Thermal overlay. Now.”

Lien worked frantically. “Got it… Sergeant… it’s *not* dust. It’s heat signatures. Hundreds. Low-profile. Fast.”

Anya’s lips thinned. “Helios-7 militia. They’re hitting the Maulers’ flanks. Distracting them.”

A grim smile touched her mouth. “Dex—forget the Raptors. Switch to the lead Mauler. That big, slow, ugly son of a bitch bringing up the rear. Target its command antenna array. Precision shot. Make it deaf and blind.”

Dex blinked, then nodded, fingers flying. “Switching… locking… firing solution—tight.”

The Goliath fired. The round screamed across the valley. It struck not the thick armor, but the slender mast atop the Mauler’s turret. Metal sheared. Sparks erupted. The massive tank lurched, its turret freezing mid-swivel, its optics going dark.

“Direct hit! Command node destroyed!” Dex yelled.

From the comms, Chen’s voice, suddenly fierce: “*Bulldog*’s still got her coax! We’re laying down suppressive fire on the Mauler column’s left flank! Keep ’em confused!”

Anya watched the chaos unfold—the Maulers hesitating, turning, firing blindly at phantom threats while the militia’s drones buzzed like angry hornets around their treads. The remaining Raptors, isolated, slowed, unsure.

She keyed the mic, her voice cutting through the static, clear and cold as vacuum. “This is *Ironhide*. All units, hold fire. Let them wonder. Let them *fear* what’s in the dust. We hold the ridge. We hold the tap. We hold *Helios-7*.”

Outside, the dust swirled, hiding the wounded, the dead, the desperate. But on the ridge, three battered tanks—two still firing, one silent but defiant—stood like broken statues carved from defiance. And for now, that was enough.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The moon hung low and swollen in the sky, casting a silver sheen over the cobblestone streets of yet another nameless village. I stood at the edge of the town square, my boots scuffing against the rough stones as I surveyed the scene before me. The air was thick with the scent of woodsmoke and damp earth, mingling with the faint, almost imperceptible tang of blood. It always smelled like that when the night was close to breaking, and I had grown used to it.

My dog, Fenris, sat at my feet, his tail thumping softly against the ground. His eyes, those unnerving amber orbs, scanned the darkness, ever watchful. He was more than just a companion; he was my partner, my protector, and my only real friend. We had been through countless villages, tracking down and destroying the undead, earning our keep with each monster we put to rest. But tonight, something felt different. There was a weight in the air, a sense of foreboding that made the hairs on the back of my neck stand on end.

"Stay sharp, boy," I murmured, crouching down to scratch behind his ears. "This place is giving me the creeps."

Fenris nuzzled my hand, his warm breath a comforting contrast to the chill of the night. I straightened up, my gaze drifting over the rows of shuttered houses, the darkened windows, and the occasional flicker of candlelight. The villagers were huddled inside, probably telling stories of the creatures that lurked in the shadows, unaware that one such creature—half, at least—was standing right outside their doors.

I had always been an outsider, a half-breed, neither fully human nor fully vampire. My father, a powerful vampire, had left my mother to raise me alone, and she had done her best to teach me how to survive. She had instilled in me a hatred for the undead, for the monsters that preyed on the innocent. And so, I hunted them, driven by a need for vengeance and a desire to protect the living from the horrors that haunted the night.

But the line between hunter and hunted was thin, and sometimes, I wondered if I was any better than the creatures I pursued. The thirst, the craving, was always there, lurking just beneath the surface, a constant reminder of what I was. I had learned to control it, to suppress the urges, but it was never easy. Especially not on nights like this, when the darkness seemed to seep into my bones.

"Let's get this over with," I said, more to myself than to Fenris. I reached into the satchel at my side, pulling out a small vial of holy water and a silver stake. The familiar weight of the weapons in my hands was reassuring, a tangible reminder of my purpose. "We should start with the old mill. That's usually where they hide."

Fenris barked softly, a sound that could have been agreement or simply a response to the tension in my voice. I patted his head and started walking, my footsteps echoing in the stillness. The village was eerily quiet, as if even the wind held its breath, waiting for something to happen.

As we approached the old mill, the smell of decay grew stronger, a putrid stench that made my stomach churn. The building loomed ahead, its wooden frame twisted and warped by time and neglect. The door hung off its hinges, swaying slightly in the breeze, and I could see the darkness within, like a gaping maw ready to swallow us whole.

"Ready, Fen?" I asked, my voice barely above a whisper. He growled, low and menacing, his hackles rising. I took a deep breath, steeling myself for what lay ahead. "Let's do this."

I pushed the door open, and it creaked loudly, the sound slicing through the silence. Inside, the mill was a mess of broken machinery and rotting wood. Shadows danced across the walls, cast by the flickering light of my lantern. I moved cautiously, my senses heightened, every nerve on edge.

There was a rustle from the far corner, and I spun around, stake raised. A figure emerged from the darkness, and I caught a glimpse of pale skin and hollow eyes. A vampire, but not one of the mindless, feral ones. This one was intelligent, cunning. He smiled, revealing a set of sharp, gleaming fangs.

"Well, well, well," he drawled, his voice smooth and mocking. "Look who we have here. A half-breed and her mutt. What brings you to my humble abode?"

I narrowed my eyes, gripping the stake tighter. "I'm here to end you, just like all the others."

He laughed, a cold, mirthless sound. "You think you can defeat me? You are nothing but a pitiful excuse for a vampire, a weak, half-formed thing. You will never be one of us, and you will never be accepted by the humans. You are an outcast, a pariah."

His words cut deep, hitting a nerve I had long tried to ignore. But I refused to let him see how much it hurt. Instead, I lunged forward, stake aimed at his heart. He dodged easily, moving with supernatural speed, and I found myself face-to-face with him, his cold breath on my cheek.

"You are not strong enough, little girl," he whispered, his voice dripping with malice. "But perhaps, I can show you the true power of your heritage. Join me, and together, we can rule this world. No more hiding, no more hunting. You will be free."

For a moment, I hesitated, the temptation almost overwhelming. The thought of being truly free, of embracing the power within me, was seductive. But then I looked at Fenris, his fierce, loyal eyes fixed on me, and I remembered why I did what I did. I wasn't doing this for myself; I was doing it for the people, for the innocent lives that would be spared.

"No," I said, my voice firm. "I will never join you. You are a monster, and I will stop you, no matter what it takes."

With a snarl, I struck again, and this time, I didn't miss. The stake pierced his heart, and he let out a scream, a terrible, agonized sound that filled the mill. He crumbled to dust, and the darkness receded, leaving only the soft glow of my lantern.

I stood there for a moment, breathing heavily, my heart pounding in my chest. Fenris nudged my leg, and I looked down at him, a small smile forming on my lips. We had done it, once again. Another monster defeated, another village saved.

"Come on, boy," I said, turning to leave. "Let's go find a place to rest. Tomorrow, we'll move on to the next village, and the hunt will continue."

As we walked out of the mill, the first rays of sunlight began to peek over the horizon, bathing the world in a warm, golden light. For a brief moment, I allowed myself to feel a sense of peace, a fleeting hope that maybe, just maybe, one day, I would find a place where I truly belonged.

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The fluorescent lights in the back of MetroMart hummed—a thin, persistent whine that had long since ceased to register as sound and become instead a physical pressure behind the eyes. Dust motes drifted in the sickly yellow beams slanting through the high, grimy clerestory windows. Outside, the city was silent. Not peaceful. *Hollow*. Like a skull left too long in the sun.

Inside, the air tasted of stale coffee, spilled soy sauce from a ruptured noodle packet, and something older, sourer—the slow, sweet decay leaking from the refrigerated meat section down Aisle 7.

Maya pressed her ear against the cold steel of the loading dock door. Her knuckles were raw, scraped raw earlier when she’d helped Ben heave the last pallet jack into place across the threshold. Behind her, Leo sat slumped against a stack of flattened cardboard boxes, his breath shallow, his face the colour of week-old milk. He hadn’t spoken since they’d buried Eli.

*Buried* wasn’t quite right. There hadn’t been time for soil or ceremony. Just the old maintenance shed behind the dumpster—concrete floor, rusted pipes dripping condensation—and the heavy-duty plastic tarp they’d used to wrap him. Eli’s jaw had been slack, one eye half-open, clouded like frosted glass. His skin, even then, held a faint, waxy sheen, as if already sealed beneath a layer of something impermeable.

“Nothing,” Maya whispered, not turning. Her voice sounded alien in the thick quiet—too loud, too dry.

Ben didn’t answer. He stood three feet away, arms crossed, shoulders rigid. His baseball bat, wrapped in duct tape where the grip had frayed, rested across his forearms like a sceptre. His gaze was fixed on the door’s reinforced plexiglass viewport—a smudged rectangle revealing only the rain-slicked asphalt of the loading bay, the skeletal remains of a forklift, and the low, bruised purple of the sky at dusk.

Then it came.

Not a shout. Not a scream.

A *knock*.

Three distinct raps. Slow. Deliberate. Like someone testing the integrity of the wood before asking to come in.

Maya froze. Her breath hitched, caught somewhere between her ribs and her throat.

Leo made a small, wet sound—like a fish gasping on a dock.

Ben didn’t move. Didn’t blink. But the tendons in his jaw jumped.

It came again. Three more knocks. Harder this time. A hollow, resonant *thunk-thunk-thunk* that vibrated up through the soles of Maya’s worn sneakers and into her spine.

“Eli?” Leo breathed. It wasn’t a question. It was the sound of a man watching his own sanity peel away, layer by brittle layer.

Ben finally turned. His eyes were bloodshot, pupils wide and black in the dim light. “Shut up, Leo.”

“It’s him,” Leo insisted, scrambling backward on his palms, knees scraping concrete. “I heard him say my name. In the shed. When we—when we covered him.”

“He didn’t say anything,” Maya said, her voice flat, brittle. She kept her ear pressed to the metal. Cold seeped through her sweatshirt. “He couldn’t.”

A pause. Five seconds. Ten. The hum of the lights swelled, filling the silence like rising water.

Then—*scrape*.

Not a knock. A slow, dragging sound, like something heavy being dragged across asphalt. Followed by another *thunk*, lower this time, as if whoever—or whatever—was out there had shifted weight. Then another scrape. Closer.

Ben took a step forward, bat raised now, not resting. His knuckles were white.

“Eli!” Maya called, her voice cracking. “Is that you? Answer me!”

Silence.

Then, clear as shattered glass: a single, wet, guttural syllable, muffled but unmistakable, vibrating through the steel.

*“M…ay…”*

Maya recoiled as if burned. Her hand flew to her mouth. Her stomach clenched, hot and acid.

Leo whimpered, curling into a tight ball, arms locked around his shins. “He knows my name too. He *knows*.”

Ben didn’t look at either of them. He stared at the plexiglass. His breath came in short, sharp bursts. “It’s not him. It can’t be.”

“Then what is it?” Maya whispered, tears cutting clean tracks through the grime on her cheeks. “What *makes* that sound?”

Another scrape. Closer still. Then a soft, rhythmic *tap-tap-tap*, like fingernails—long, brittle, and impossibly dry—tapping against the outside of the plexiglass. Not frantic. Not desperate. *Curious.*

Ben raised the bat higher. His arm trembled, not with fatigue, but with the sheer, animal weight of what he was about to do.

“Don’t,” Maya breathed.

“He’s not *in* there,” Ben said, his voice low, ragged. “He’s *out* there. And he’s learning how doors work.”

A new sound joined the tapping. A low, wet, rhythmic *shhh-shhh-shhh*, like cloth dragging over damp concrete. Or skin.

Leo began to sob, silent tears streaming, his mouth working soundlessly.

Maya closed her eyes. She saw Eli’s face—not as it was in the shed, slack and grey, but as it had been two days ago, laughing as he’d juggled three cans of baked beans, his grin lopsided, his eyes crinkling at the corners. She remembered the warmth of his hand on her shoulder when she’d tripped over a fallen display stand. The smell of his cheap mint gum.

The tapping stopped.

The scraping stopped.

The humming lights seemed to dip, falter, then surge back with a sudden, angry buzz.

And then, from directly behind the door, so close it vibrated the fillings in Maya’s teeth:

A slow, deliberate, wet *inhale*.

Followed by a whisper, thin as spider-silk and colder than the meat locker:

*“Let me in.”*

Ben didn’t hesitate. He swung.

The bat connected with the plexiglass with a sound like a frozen lake cracking open. Shards exploded inward, glittering in the dying light. Rain blew in, sharp and cold.

Maya screamed.

Leo screamed.

And from the darkness beyond the broken viewport, something moved—not toward them, but *up*, pressing its face—pale, glistening, stretched too wide—against the jagged edge of the shattered pane.

Its mouth opened.

Not to speak.

To *widen*.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The coffee in her mug had gone the color of weak dishwater. Cold. She’d forgotten it three hours ago, right after the 7:15 a.m. secure briefing in the Situation Room—*her* briefing, the one she’d spent seventeen straight hours drafting, cross-checking, redacting, and then re-redacting until her eyes burned and the letters on her screen bled into each other like wet ink on cheap paper.

Elena Rostova sat at her desk in the seventh-floor annex of the Old Executive Office Building—Room 712, a windowless box smelling perpetually of ozone, stale carpet glue, and the faint, metallic tang of the building’s aging HVAC system. Her fingers hovered over the keyboard. Not typing. Just hovering. Like they’d forgotten how.

She’d read the President’s copy again. Not the draft she’d submitted. Not the version cleared by Legal and vetted by Langley’s counterintelligence desk. The *actual* document that had landed, unmarked, in the Oval Office at 6:42 a.m., stamped “PRESIDENTIAL EYES ONLY / SOURCE: ANALYTIC DIVISION / ROSTOVA, E.”  

It was hers. The structure. The phrasing. Even the typo she’d missed the first time—the “Tehran” misspelled as “Tehram” in footnote 4—was still there. But the *substance*…  

Page three. Paragraph two. Where she’d written: *“No credible evidence links the Quds Force cell operating out of Erbil to the recent mortar attacks on Camp Taji. Intercepted chatter suggests internal IRGC factional disputes—not external operational coordination—are driving the escalation.”*  

That sentence wasn’t in the President’s copy.

In its place: *“High-confidence assessment: Quds Force cell in Erbil directly coordinated and executed the Camp Taji mortar strikes. Evidence includes geolocated voice traffic (see Annex B) and corroborated financial transfers through Dubai-based shell company Al-Muqaddas Trading.”*  

Annex B didn’t exist. Al-Muqaddas Trading didn’t exist—not in any database Elena had ever touched. She’d checked. Twice. At 3:47 a.m., standing in the darkened server room down in the basement, her badge flashing green against the humming racks, sweat cold under her collar. No trace. No audit trail. No metadata showing who’d opened, edited, or saved the final PDF before it went to the White House Comms Vault.

Her stomach tightened—not the slow, familiar dread of deadline pressure, but the sudden, sickening lurch of vertigo. Like stepping onto an elevator that wasn’t moving.

She pulled up the version control log for the file. *Rostova_E_CampTaji_Analysis_v7_FINAL_CLEAN.pdf*. Last modified: 5:03 a.m. By: SYSTEM.  

Not a person. Not even a username. Just SYSTEM. A ghost protocol. One she’d never seen invoked on an analytic product before. Not for something this sensitive. Not for something this *wrong*.

She scrolled back. Version 6, saved at 4:18 a.m., was hers. Clean. Precise. Cautious. The words were hers. The conclusions were hers. The caveats—*“low confidence on attribution,” “possible disinformation vector,” “requires further SIGINT validation”*—all intact.

Version 7 was different. Sharper. Louder. Certain. And it bore her name.

Her phone buzzed. Not her burner. Her *work* line. Encrypted, yes—but routed through the building’s main switchboard. She let it ring. Three times. Four. It stopped. Then, five seconds later, a single, sharp knock on the door.

Not the soft, apologetic rap of a junior analyst. This was deliberate. Two quick raps, pause, one firm one. Like someone testing the wood.

She didn’t answer. Didn’t move. Just watched the door handle. It didn’t turn.

Her gaze dropped to the manila folder beside her keyboard. Unsealed. Inside: printouts of the original v6, the President’s v7, and a single sheet from the NSC’s daily digest—page 12, top right corner. A tiny, almost invisible watermark: a stylized “Q” inside a circle. Not CIA. Not DIA. Not NSA. She’d seen it once before, six months ago, on a burn notice buried in a State Department cable about a defector who’d vanished mid-transit in Frankfurt. The notice had been scrubbed from all systems twenty minutes after she’d flagged it. Her access logs showed *no* record of her having viewed it.

She picked up the cold coffee mug. Took a sip. It tasted like rust and burnt sugar.

Down the hall, a cart rattled—janitorial staff, early shift. The squeak of rubber wheels on linoleum. A cough. Then silence again, thicker than before.

Elena opened her encrypted email client. Drafted a new message. To no one. Subject line blank. Body: *“Annex B does not exist. Al-Muqaddas Trading is not in FinCEN, OFAC, or the Dubai FSA registry. Geolocation data cited in v7 contradicts raw SIGINT timestamps from Station Erbil (see raw feed ID ERB-774-ALPHA).”*

She didn’t send it. Didn’t save it as a draft. Just stared at the cursor blinking, blinking, blinking in the empty white space.

Her left thumbnail was split. She picked at the ragged edge with her right index finger. A bead of blood welled, small and bright. She pressed it into the corner of the v7 printout, right below the forged signature block. A tiny, useless stain.

Outside, a siren wailed—distant, then fading. Ambulance? Police? Or just the city breathing, indifferent.

She closed the email window. Opened a new tab. Typed: *“SYSTEM user privileges OEOB network.”* Hit enter.

The search returned zero results.

She leaned back. The chair groaned—a dry, protesting sound. Her neck ached. She rubbed the knot at the base of her skull, the one that always flared when she hadn’t slept.

On her desk, next to the stained printout, her government-issued pen lay sideways. The cap was off. The ink was blue. Not black. She remembered using it to underline “Tehram” in the draft. Hadn’t bothered to correct it. Too tired. Too sure no one would care about a typo in footnote 4.

Now, she picked up the pen. Turned it over in her fingers. Checked the nib. Still fine.

Then she looked at the door again.

The handle hadn’t moved.

But the light under it—the thin, yellow seam of fluorescent glow—had dimmed. Just slightly. As if something had shifted in the hallway. As if someone had stepped closer. And paused.

She didn’t breathe.

Just held the pen.

And waited.

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
The night before the grand wedding, the hotel's kitchen was a flurry of activity. The air was thick with the aroma of roasting meats and simmering sauces. In the midst of this chaos, Emma, the meticulous and ever-organized wedding planner, was making her final rounds to ensure everything was in place. Her clipboard was a constant companion, filled with checklists and notes.

As she approached the walk-in freezer, she noticed the door was slightly ajar. Frowning, she pushed it open, a cloud of cold air billowing out. The sight that greeted her made her heart skip a beat. There, slumped against a stack of frozen vegetables, was the best man, Alex, his face pale and lifeless.

"Oh my God," Emma gasped, her hand flying to her mouth. She stumbled back, nearly colliding with the sous chef, Marcus, who had just rounded the corner.

"Emma, what's wrong?" Marcus asked, his voice tinged with concern as he caught her by the elbow.

"It's... it's Alex. He's in there. I think he's dead," Emma stammered, pointing to the freezer.

Marcus's eyes widened, and he rushed past her, peering into the icy chamber. "Oh no, this can't be happening. Not tonight," he muttered, shaking his head in disbelief.

Meanwhile, Emma's mind raced. She pulled out her phone, her hands trembling as she dialed 911. "Yes, hello, I need an ambulance. There's been a... a death at the Grandview Hotel. The best man is dead in the walk-in freezer."

After hanging up, she turned to Marcus, her eyes filled with panic. "We need to tell the bride and groom. They're in the ballroom, setting up for the rehearsal dinner."

Marcus nodded, his expression grim. "I'll go find them. You stay here and make sure no one touches anything. The police will want to see the scene exactly as it is."

As Marcus hurried off, Emma stood guard by the freezer, her thoughts a jumbled mess. She couldn't help but replay the events of the day. Alex had been his usual charming self, cracking jokes and keeping everyone's spirits high. How could this have happened?

A few minutes later, the sound of sirens pierced the air, and the kitchen staff began to gather, whispering among themselves. Emma felt a hand on her shoulder and turned to see the hotel manager, Mrs. Hargrove, a stern but compassionate woman.

"What on earth happened, Emma?" Mrs. Hargrove asked, her eyes scanning the scene.

"I don't know, Mrs. Hargrove. I found him like this. I called 911 right away," Emma replied, her voice shaky.

Mrs. Hargrove nodded, her face a mask of professionalism. "Good. The police will be here soon. Let's try to keep this contained until we know more."

Just then, the bride, Sarah, and the groom, James, appeared, their faces etched with worry. Sarah's eyes were red-rimmed, and James looked like he was about to collapse.

"Emma, what's going on? Marcus said something terrible has happened," Sarah said, her voice quivering.

Emma took a deep breath, trying to steady herself. "Sarah, James, I'm so sorry. Alex... Alex is dead. We found him in the freezer."

Sarah let out a strangled cry, burying her face in James's chest. James wrapped his arms around her, his own eyes brimming with tears. "How? How did this happen?"

"We don't know yet," Emma said, her voice soft. "The police are on their way. They'll figure it out."

As the police arrived, the kitchen fell silent, the only sounds the muffled sobs of Sarah and the quiet, determined footsteps of the officers. Emma watched as they began to process the scene, her mind still reeling from the shock. This was supposed to be a joyous occasion, but now it was marred by tragedy. And as the night wore on, the questions lingered: how did Alex end up in the freezer, and who would do such a thing?

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
The air in Booth 14 smelled like dust, dried glue, and something sour—old sweat, maybe, or spilled cider vinegar left to rot in a thermos.

Maggie Thorne wiped her thumb across the porcelain cheek of a 1920s Käthe Kruse doll—*Liesel*, its tiny tag read—and felt the faint, greasy smear of fingerprint oil. She always touched them. Always checked the seams, the hairline glue, the hollow behind the ear where collectors hid notes, receipts, *secrets*. Her fingers were calloused from decades of handling fragile things. Her knees ached from crouching at flea markets before dawn. Her eyes—tired, bloodshot, magnifying-glass sharp—caught the tremor first.

Not in the doll. In the man slumped behind the folding table.

Harlan Finch. Local antique dealer. Known for “finding” things no one else could—like a pair of pre-war German bisque eyes that matched *exactly*, or a missing Fabergé snuffbox that turned up three counties over, “just sitting on a shelf.” Maggie had bought two dolls from him last year. Both flawless. Both priced just shy of suspicious.

He wasn’t sleeping.

His head lolled sideways, mouth open—not relaxed, *gaped*. Eyes wide, fixed on the ceiling’s water-stained acoustic tile. One hand still gripped the edge of the table. The other dangled, palm up, fingers slightly curled. A single drop of dark, viscous liquid clung to his thumbnail. Not blood. Too thick. Too *shiny*. Linseed oil? Or something worse?

Maggie didn’t scream. She didn’t gasp. She *stopped breathing*.

Her pulse hammered in her throat, loud as a trapped bird. She glanced left—empty aisle. Right—a teenager snapping selfies by the prize-winning pumpkins, blissfully unaware. The fairgrounds hummed: distant calliope music, kids shrieking on the Tilt-A-Whirl, the low drone of generators keeping the lights bright under the late afternoon sun.

She stepped forward. Quietly. Boots soft on sawdust-covered concrete.

No sign of struggle. No overturned chair. No broken glass. Just Harlan, still wearing his too-tight corduroy vest, his wire-rim glasses askew on his nose. His right wrist rested on the tabletop beside a half-unpacked cardboard box labeled *KRAUSE – FRAGILE – DO NOT STACK* in messy black marker.

Maggie’s gaze dropped.

Beneath his forearm—almost hidden by the cuff of his shirt—was a small, folded square of paper. Cream-colored. Thick stock. Not printer paper. Handmade, maybe. And tucked into the fold? A single, perfect strand of white-blond hair. Fine as spider silk. Longer than Harlan’s stubble. Longer than *any* of his customers’ she’d seen today.

Her stomach tightened.

She knew that hair.

Saw it every morning in the cracked mirror above her sink.

She’d cut it herself last week. A jagged, angry chop after the insurance adjuster called her “overvaluing sentimental inventory.” She kept the clippings in a little tin—*for reference*, she told herself. For texture analysis. For provenance. Lies she told to keep the shame quiet.

This strand was *hers*. She’d know the subtle kink at the root. The way the light caught the silver flecks near the scalp.

Her breath hitched. She forced it down. *Don’t panic. Don’t touch.*

But her hand moved anyway—slow, deliberate—reaching not for the hair, but for Harlan’s wrist. To check for pulse. A reflex. A lie she told herself: *Just confirming.*

His skin was cold. Waxy. Already losing its give.

Then she saw it.

A faint, crescent-shaped bruise high on his left temple. Barely visible beneath the stubble. Fresh. Purple-tinged, not yellowed. Like someone had pressed a thumb there. Hard. *Deliberately.*

And beneath the bruise—almost invisible unless you knew where to look—two tiny, parallel scratches. Thin. Precise. Like fingernails. Or… a doll’s joint pin? A brass hinge tool? Something fine, metallic, *sharp*.

Maggie jerked her hand back.

A plastic cup clattered nearby. She flinched. Turned.

A woman stood at the booth entrance—mid-fifties, floral apron, holding a paper plate piled with funnel cake. Her eyes flickered from Harlan’s face to Maggie’s, then down to the doll in Maggie’s hands. *Liesel.* Still cradled tight.

“You okay, hon?” the woman asked. Her voice was syrup-thick with forced cheer. “You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”

Maggie closed her fingers around *Liesel*’s cool porcelain neck. Felt the tiny seam where head met torso. Felt the weight of the truth settle in her gut, cold and heavy as lead shot.

“No,” Maggie said. Her voice sounded raw. Stripped. “No. I think I just saw the murder weapon.”

She didn’t look at the woman. She looked at Harlan’s open, unblinking eyes—and saw, for the first time, the tiny, almost invisible speck of blue paint clinging to his lower lip.

Same shade as the chipped thumb on *Liesel*’s left hand.

Same shade as the paint on the doll Maggie had *just* sold him yesterday.

For cash. No receipt.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The coffee in my mug is cold. Not lukewarm. *Cold.* Like something left on a windowsill overnight, congealing at the edges. I stare at it, the dark liquid reflecting the sterile glare of the overhead fluorescents—harsh, unforgiving, the kind that bleaches colour and truth alike.

*Why did I leave it?*

It’s 6:47 a.m. The seventh-floor Secure Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) is silent except for the low, subsonic hum of the air filtration system and the frantic, unspoken rhythm of my own pulse hammering against my ribs. My fingers are still curled around the mug’s ceramic handle, knuckles white. My eyes haven’t left the screen in front of me—not really. They’ve been *glued* to it. To *that* line.

The President’s Daily Brief (PDB) Annex: “Operation Nightjar – Threat Assessment & Recommended Response.”

My briefing. My words. My meticulous, cross-referenced, source-verified, *cautiously worded* assessment.

I wrote: *“…high probability (72%) that the ‘Spectre’ cell’s leadership structure remains intact despite recent kinetic strikes. Key facilitator ‘Viper’ is assessed as *likely active*, operating from an unknown node within the Belgrade nexus. Recommend immediate re-tasking of SIGINT assets to confirm presence and locate.”*

That’s what I typed. That’s what I saved. That’s what I emailed to the PDB Editor at 3:15 p.m. yesterday. With my digital signature, my biometric lock, my *soul* in every comma.

What’s on the screen now—the official, final, President-circulated version—is this:

*“…high probability (72%) that the ‘Spectre’ cell’s leadership structure remains intact despite recent kinetic strikes. Key facilitator ‘Viper’ is assessed as *confirmed active*, operating from *a known node within the Belgrade nexus*. Recommend *immediate kinetic action* against coordinates 44.804°N, 20.465°E.”*

*Confirmed active.* Not *likely*. *Confirmed.*

*A known node.* Not *unknown*. *Known.*

*Immediate kinetic action.* Not *re-tasking of SIGINT assets.* Not *confirmation.* *Action.*

My breath hitches. A dry, scraping sound in my throat. I click the document properties tab. Creation date: yesterday, 3:15 p.m. Modified date: *yesterday, 4:02 p.m.* By whom? *PDB Editor – Level 3 Clearance.* Standard. Routine.

But the *content*…

I pull up the archived draft from my local drive. The one I saved *before* emailing. The one with my timestamped edits visible in the track changes log. I scroll down. There it is. My original phrasing. Bold. Clear. Unambiguous.

Then I open the official PDB Annex file again. Same section. Different words. Different *meaning*. Catastrophically different.

“Jesus Christ,” I whisper. The sound is too loud in the silence. It bounces off the reinforced concrete walls, thin and brittle.

My hand trembles as I reach for my encrypted comms device. Not the main console. The *burner*—a hardened, isolated terminal only I use for pre-briefing sanity checks. I punch in the PDB Editor’s secure line. Three rings. Four.

“Editor, PDB,” a voice answers, crisp, weary, already braced for the morning’s first crisis.

“Mark? It’s Elena Vance. Annex Seven. Nightjar. The Viper assessment.”

A pause. Short. Professional. “Yes, Elena. Finalized last night. Cleared by Ops Oversight. You saw the routing slip?”

“I *wrote* it, Mark. I wrote *‘likely active’* and *‘unknown node’*. And *‘recommend re-tasking’*. That’s not what’s in the final.”

Another pause. Longer this time. Filled with the faint, staticky hiss of the secure line. “Elena… the final version reflects the consolidated assessment. Ops Oversight updated the confidence level based on new SIGINT fragments received *after* your initial submission. The Belgrade node was corroborated by HUMINT source ‘Cicada’ late afternoon. The kinetic recommendation was added per Standing Directive 9-Alpha for confirmed high-value targets.”

*New SIGINT fragments.* *HUMINT source ‘Cicada’.* *Standing Directive 9-Alpha.*

Words. Just words. Smooth, official, utterly *plausible*.

But Cicada hasn’t spoken in *eighteen months*. Cicada is deep cover, presumed compromised, or dead. I checked the source ledger *yesterday*. I *always* check.

And Directive 9-Alpha? It mandates *immediate* action *only* if confirmation comes from *two independent, high-fidelity sources*. Not one fragment. Not one ghost.

My mouth is desert-dry. I lick cracked lips. “Mark… can you pull the raw SIGINT fragment logs? The Cicada corroboration packet? Let me see the metadata. The timestamps. The source validation chain.”

Silence. Thick. Heavy. The kind that doesn’t just fill space—it *presses*.

“Elena,” he says, his voice lower now, stripped of its earlier crispness, edged with something else—warning? Pity? “The PDB is *final*. It’s gone to the Situation Room. The President reviewed it at 5:30 a.m. His staff is preparing the execution order *now*.”

The execution order.

My stomach lurches. Not metaphorically. A physical, nauseating drop, like stepping off a curb into nothing.

*He read it. He signed off on it. Based on words I didn’t write.*

The cold coffee suddenly feels like ice water in my veins. I look down at my hands. Steady. Calm. Professional analyst hands. Hands that parse lies for a living. Hands that just held a weapon they didn’t know they’d loaded.

I close the PDB Annex file. The screen goes black. My reflection stares back—pale, wide-eyed, the ghost of a woman who thought she understood the architecture of truth.

Then I open a new, blank document. No header. No footer. No classification banner. Just a blinking cursor in the centre of a white void.

My fingers hover over the keyboard. Not to type the truth. Not yet.

First, I need to find out *who* changed it. And why they thought I wouldn’t notice the difference between *likely* and *confirmed*.

Between *unknown* and *known*.

Between *investigate* and *kill*.

The cursor blinks. Blink. Blink. Like a heartbeat counting down.

I take a slow, deliberate breath. Cold air fills my lungs. It tastes like metal. Like blood. Like the first, quiet note of a storm no one else has heard coming.

Time to stop being the analyst.

Time to become the evidence.

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The rain pelted the windshield of the old, rust-eaten sedan, creating a rhythmic drumming that filled the cramped space. The streetlights outside cast an eerie, flickering glow through the fogged windows, illuminating the faces of two men who were locked in a tense argument.

Tommy, with his greasy black hair and a scar running down his left cheek, drummed his fingers on the steering wheel. "I'm tellin' ya, Vinnie, this is our ticket out. We do this, we're set for life."

Vinnie, a lanky man with a nervous twitch in his left eye, fidgeted with the hem of his jacket. "Yeah, and what if it goes wrong? What if they catch us? You know how much time we’re talking about here, Tommy?"

"Relax, will ya?" Tommy snapped, his eyes flashing with irritation. "We’ve done our homework. The kid’s always at the park after school. We grab him, take him to the safe house, and wait for the ransom. Simple as that."

Vinnie shook his head, his voice trembling. "It's not simple, Tommy. This ain’t some small-time heist. This is a kid, man. A kid. And his family… they got connections. If something goes wrong, we’re dead meat."

Tommy leaned back in his seat, his jaw clenched. "You think I don’t know that? But look at us, Vinnie. Look where we are. We’re living hand to mouth, doing petty jobs, barely scraping by. This is our chance to change all that. One big score, and we can finally get out of this shit hole."

Vinnie’s hands were shaking as he pulled out a crumpled pack of cigarettes from his pocket. He lit one, inhaling deeply, the smoke filling the car. "And what if we get caught? What then? We end up in prison for life, or worse, we get killed. Is it worth it, Tommy? Really?"

Tommy snatched the cigarette from Vinnie’s mouth, taking a long drag himself. "You gotta stop thinking like that. We’ve been planning this for months. We’ve got everything covered. The kid’s routine, the drop-off, the escape route—everything. We just need to stay focused and follow the plan."

Vinnie’s eyes darted around the car, his mind racing. "But what if the kid recognizes us? What if he fights back? What if—"

"Enough!" Tommy barked, his patience wearing thin. "You’re overthinking this. We stick to the plan, and we’ll be fine. Now, are you in or out?"

Vinnie hesitated, his heart pounding in his chest. He could feel the weight of the decision pressing down on him, suffocating him. "I… I don’t know, Tommy. I just… I don’t know if I can do this."

Tommy’s face darkened, and he reached into the glove compartment, pulling out a worn, folded piece of paper. "Look, I’ve got the address, the schedule, everything. We’ve got this. Trust me, Vinnie. Just trust me."

Vinnie took the paper, his hands still trembling. He unfolded it, scanning the details, his mind a jumble of fear and doubt. "Okay," he whispered, more to himself than to Tommy. "Okay, let’s do it."

Tommy nodded, a hint of a smile playing on his lips. "That’s my boy. Now, let’s go over the plan one more time. We’ve got to make sure everything’s perfect."

As the rain continued to pour, the two men huddled together, their voices low and urgent, the tension in the car almost palpable. They went over every detail, every possible scenario, their breaths fogging up the windows. Outside, the world seemed to fade away, leaving only the dimly lit interior of the old sedan, where two desperate men plotted their last, desperate chance at a better life.

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
The air in the Fairgrounds Antique Pavilion smelled like dust, damp wool, and the faint, sweet rot of old apples someone had forgotten in a lunch pail. Not unpleasant, exactly—just *old*. Like the inside of a cedar chest you haven’t opened since your grandmother died. I’d been elbow-deep in a crate of Depression glass—pale green tumblers with that odd, wavery thickness—when the scream cut through the low murmur of appraisals and haggling.

Not a shriek. A choked, guttural sound, like a teakettle boiling dry. Then silence. Thick. Heavy. The kind that makes your ears pop.

I looked up. My fingers were still sticky with the residue of a century-old lemonade stain I’d just wiped off a cobalt-blue pitcher. Across the aisle, Mrs. Gable from the Doll Collectors’ Guild was frozen mid-sentence, her mouth a perfect, horrified O. Her pearl earrings—real ones, probably inherited—swung violently as she jerked her head toward Booth 14B.

Booth 14B was “Hazel’s Heirlooms.” Hazel herself—Hazel Pritchard, round-faced, always smelling faintly of lavender sachets and pipe tobacco—was sprawled sideways behind her folding table. One sensible orthopedic shoe dangled off her foot. Her cardigan, a cable-knit thing in faded maroon, was bunched up around her ribs. And there, right where her collarbone should have been, was a dark, wet bloom spreading across the wool.

Not blood, not yet. Too dark. Too *shiny*. Like spilled motor oil on concrete.

My first thought wasn’t *murder*. It was *doll*. Specifically, the one I’d seen Hazel clutching yesterday, tucked under her arm like a nervous child: a 1930s German bisque-headed baby doll named “Lottie,” with sleep eyes and real human hair pulled back in a tiny, stiff bun. I’d admired its cracked, age-spotted cheeks. Hazel had patted its head and said, “She’s got secrets, that one. Seen things.”

Now, Lottie sat upright on the edge of Hazel’s table, staring straight ahead with those painted, unblinking eyes. One of its tiny, jointed hands rested, palm-up, on the scarred plywood surface. Beside it, half-hidden under a folded velvet cloth, lay a small, brass-handled magnifying glass—the kind collectors use to inspect seam lines and paint crazing. Its lens was smudged. And on the cloth itself, near the hem, a single, long, grey hair caught the fluorescent light. Not Hazel’s. Hers was brown, streaked with silver. This was finer. Straighter.

Someone else’s.

The crowd didn’t surge. They *congealed*. A man in a flannel shirt dropped his thermos. It clattered, absurdly loud. Someone whispered, “Oh, honey,” and it wasn’t comforting. It was the sound you make when you see a bird hit a window.

I didn’t move toward the body. My feet felt rooted to the worn linoleum, sticky in places where spilled cider had dried into amber islands. Instead, I scanned the booth. Hazel’s inventory list was pinned to the corkboard behind her—a neat, looping script. *Lottie (1935, Germany, original clothes, minor chip left ear), $1,850.* Below it, a Post-it: *Ask about the Kline box?* Scribbled in a different hand—sharper, angular.

The Kline box. I knew that name. Mildred Kline, dead six months. Ran the little antique shop on Sycamore—“Kline & Curio.” Closed down after her funeral. Rumor was, her nephew, Leo, had cleared the place out fast. Too fast.
