He’d been here this morning, I remembered, hovering near the entrance, checking his phone, wearing that same slightly-too-tight navy blazer he wore to Mildred’s service.

My gaze snagged on Hazel’s open purse, tipped over on the floor beside her chair. A receipt fluttered out. Not from the fair concession stand. From “Kline & Curio.” Dated yesterday. Amount: $275.00. Description: *Box – Unmarked. As Is.*

My throat tightened. That box. The one Leo Kline had sold her. The one she’d wanted to ask about.

A deputy—Chad, I think his name was; I’d seen him directing traffic by the Ferris wheel earlier—pushed through the wall of people. His face was pale under his cap. He knelt, checked for a pulse with two thick fingers, then looked up, his eyes sweeping the room, blank and tired. They landed on me. I hadn’t moved. Hadn’t even blinked. Just stood there, holding the lemonade-stained pitcher, the cool glass slick in my sweaty palm.

“Ma’am?” he asked. Voice flat. Routine.

I nodded. Didn’t speak. My tongue felt thick, useless. I could still smell the lavender and pipe tobacco, mixed now with something coppery, sharp, rising from the floor.

Chad glanced at Lottie. The doll’s glass eyes reflected the harsh lights, tiny, distorted squares of ceiling tile. He didn’t look away. Just kept looking. Like he saw something in them. Or maybe just saw *me*, seeing them.

Outside, the fairground music started up again—a tinny, cheerful polka from the midway. A distant shriek of laughter. The world kept turning. The lemonade stain on the pitcher was stubborn. I rubbed it with my thumb, a slow, circular motion. The glass felt cold. Real. Solid.

Lottie stared back. Unblinking. Waiting.

I didn’t know what she’d seen. But I knew, with a quiet, sinking certainty that had nothing to do with logic, that the answer wasn’t in the box. It was in the hair. On the cloth. Fine. Grey. Not Hazel’s.

And somewhere, very close, Leo Kline was probably wondering if he’d wiped the smudge off that magnifying glass properly.

title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
The bridge of the *Odyssey* hummed with the low thrum of life-support and the soft chime of status updates—until Chief Engineer Aris Thorne slammed her palm against the main console.  

“Lie.” Her voice cracked like fractured ice. “It’s all a lie.”  

Captain Elias Vance didn’t look up from his display. He adjusted his cufflink—polished obsidian, always perfect—then tapped a sequence. A holographic star chart bloomed above the central table: Proxima Centauri b, lush green, oceans shimmering under twin suns. The promised world. The *only* world they’d been told about for three generations.  

“Chief,” Vance said, calm as vacuum. “Please lower your voice. We’re in proximity to the Kuiper Belt anomaly. Stress compromises focus.”  

Dr. Lena Rostova, the ship’s physician and unofficial historian, stepped forward, her grey braid coiled tight, eyes sharp with disbelief. “Elias, we just ran diagnostics on the long-range astrogation core—the one *you* sealed after the ‘malfunction’ two years ago. It wasn’t corrupted. It was *rewritten*.” She held up a data-slate. “The original course vector? Not Proxima. Not even the Alpha Centauri system. It’s *Tau Ceti*. And it’s *decelerating*—not accelerating toward a habitable zone. It’s coasting. Into *nothing*.”  

Vance finally met her gaze. His smile was thin, practiced. “A necessary recalibration, Lena. Proxima’s stellar flares rendered surface colonization untenable. Tau Ceti offered better long-term viability.”  

“Then why did the nav-computer log show *zero* reprogramming events?” Aris snapped, jabbing the slate. “Why does the ship’s AI—*our* AI, not yours—report that the last command override came from *your biometric key*, *eighteen months ago*? Why does the fuel consumption profile match *no* known deceleration burn for Tau Ceti—but matches *exactly* the profile for a *drift-and-decay* maneuver?”  

Silence. Even the hum seemed to dip.  

Kai, the youngest crewmember—eighteen, wide-eyed, raised on holos of alien forests—whispered, “Drift… into what?”  

Vance sighed, almost tenderly. “Into time, Kai. Not space.” He gestured to the starfield beyond the viewport—a velvet black studded with indifferent points. “We are not going *to* a planet. We are going *through* time.”  

Lena went very still. “Chrono-dilation? That’s theoretical. Unproven. And *lethal* without shielding we don’t have.”  

“Not dilation,” Vance corrected softly. “*Translation*.” He walked to the viewport, hands clasped behind his back. “The anomaly ahead—the ‘Kuiper Belt ghost’ we’ve mapped for decades—it’s not debris. It’s a gravitational lens. A natural wormhole throat. Stable. Narrow. One-way.”  

Aris stared. “One-way *where*?”  

Vance turned. His eyes weren’t tired. They were *hungry*. “Where humanity *needs* to be. Not in some fragile colony clinging to a red dwarf’s light—but *forward*. To the next great leap. The *Odyssey* isn’t a colony ship, crew. It’s a *seed pod*. And we’re not planting trees. We’re planting *ideas*.”  

Lena’s breath hitched. “You mean… you’re sending us *into the future*?”  

“Not *us*,” Vance said, quiet now. “*Them*.” He nodded toward Kai, then to Aris, then to Lena herself. “You’ll wake in 12,000 years. On the other side. In a universe where fusion is clean, disease is memory, and interstellar travel is routine. You won’t land on a planet. You’ll dock at a station orbiting Earth—*reborn*, rebuilt, *waiting*.”  

Kai took a step back. “Earth? But… Earth died. The Great Collapse…”  

“*Our* Earth died,” Vance said, voice thick with sudden, startling sorrow. “But time isn’t a wall, Kai. It’s a river with tributaries. Our timeline ended. Others didn’t. This jump—this *translation*—doesn’t break causality. It *bypasses* it. Like stepping off a train onto a parallel track.”  

Aris laughed—a raw, broken sound. “And you never thought to *tell* us? No vote? No council? Just… *you* decide the fate of five thousand souls?”  

Vance’s composure flickered. For a second, he looked ancient, hollowed out. “Because choice *corrupts*, Aris. Because fear makes people sabotage hope. Because if I’d told you we were jumping blind into deep time—*without guarantee*—half this crew would have tried to crash us into that anomaly just to *end it*.” He met each of them. “I carried the weight so you wouldn’t have to fracture under it.”  

Lena’s voice was barely audible. “And if it fails? If the translation tears us apart atom by atom?”  

Vance didn’t flinch. “Then we die believing in something greater than survival. That’s the only legacy worth leaving.”  

Kai suddenly spoke, clear and steady. “My grandmother taught me the old navigation songs. ‘Star-true, heart-true, course-true.’ She said truth was the only compass that never rusts.” He looked at Vance, not with anger, but with devastating clarity. “You broke the compass, Captain.”  

Vance closed his eyes. When he opened them, the hunger was gone. Only exhaustion remained. “Then fix it.”  

Aris didn’t hesitate. She slapped her palm against the emergency protocol panel. Red lights flooded the bridge. “Override initiated. Locking helm, nav-core, and life-support to *my* biometrics. Effective immediately.”  

Vance didn’t move. Didn’t protest. He just watched the stars blur as the *Odyssey* shuddered—not toward the anomaly, but *away*, engines flaring blue-white in defiance.  

Lena placed a hand on Kai’s shoulder. “What do we tell the others?”  

Aris stared at the receding anomaly, now just a faint silver smear against the dark. “We tell them the truth.” She looked at Vance, standing alone beside the dead holo-chart of Proxima’s false paradise. “And we ask them what kind of future they want to build… *here*, *now*, *alive*.”  

The stars outside didn’t care. But for the first time in eight hundred years, the *Odyssey* had a crew who did.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
October 12th

I found the bottle of pills in the back of his drawer. It was like a punch to the gut, seeing them there, hidden away like some dirty secret. I sat on the edge of our bed, holding the bottle, staring at the label. His name, the dosage, the prescription date. Everything seemed so clinical, so detached. Like it wasn’t about him, about us.

I can’t stop thinking about why. Why did he do it? What was so unbearable that he couldn’t face another day? I’ve replayed every conversation, every argument, every moment we shared. But nothing stands out. Nothing screams, “This is why.” It’s just a void, an empty space where answers should be.

The doctors say he might wake up, but they can’t promise anything. They use words like “coma” and “brain function,” and I nod, trying to absorb it all. But inside, I’m screaming. I want to shake him, to yell at him, to demand that he open his eyes and explain. How could he leave me like this? How could he leave us?

The kids don’t understand. They keep asking when Daddy will come home. I tell them he’s sick and needs to rest, but their eyes are full of confusion and fear. I see it, even if they don’t know how to express it. And I hate myself for not being able to make it better.

I went to the hospital today. He looks peaceful, almost serene. The machines beep and hum, keeping him alive, but he’s somewhere else. Somewhere I can’t reach. I held his hand, feeling the coldness of his skin, the stillness of his body. I whispered to him, telling him how much I love him, how much we need him. But the room stayed silent, and he didn’t move.

I’ve been going through his things, searching for clues. Old letters, notes, anything that might give me a hint. I found a stack of bills, unpaid, piling up. I never knew we were in such trouble. He always said everything was fine, that we were managing. But the numbers don’t lie. We’re drowning in debt, and he kept it from me.

How could he do that? How could he carry this burden alone? I feel betrayed, but also guilty. I should have known. I should have seen the signs. But I was too busy with the kids, with work, with life. I thought we were a team, but now I realize I was blind.

I’m angry. I’m angry at him for lying, for hiding, for giving up. I’m angry at myself for not seeing, for not doing enough. And I’m scared. Scared of what the future holds, scared of facing it without him. But most of all, I’m scared that he won’t wake up. That I’ll never get the chance to talk to him, to ask him, to try and fix this.

The nights are the worst. I lie in bed, staring at the ceiling, listening to the silence. I imagine him next to me, his breathing, his warmth. But it’s just an echo, a memory. And I wonder if I’ll ever feel whole again.

I need him to wake up. I need him to fight. Because right now, I don’t know how to go on.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The neon “ON AIR” sign bled crimson light across the worn oak of Silas Thorne’s desk, painting his knuckles a bruised violet as he adjusted his headset. Outside the soundproofed booth of WOLF-FM—*Your Howl in the Static*—rain lashed the downtown studio windows, turning the city into a smeared watercolor of sodium-yellow streetlights and wet asphalt. Silas exhaled, slow and deliberate, feeling the familiar, low-grade thrum beneath his ribs—not the frantic pulse of panic, but the deep, patient vibration of something ancient and watchful, coiled just beneath his human skin. He’d run this late-night paranormal talk show for seven years, a sanctuary for the lost, the curious, the quietly terrified. And tonight, like most nights, he was holding back the moon.

“Welcome back,” Silas said, his voice a warm, gravelly baritone that filled the airwaves, smooth as aged bourbon. “We’re diving deep into urban legends tonight—specifically, the ‘Grey Man’ sightings along the old rail corridor. Caller, you’re on *Your Howl in the Static*. What’s your name, and what did you see?”

A pause. Not the usual nervous hesitation. This silence had weight. It felt like the held breath before a predator tests the wind.

“Silas,” the voice came through, low, clipped, devoid of static or warmth. Male. Late forties, maybe, with the dry rasp of someone who’d spent too many nights in damp woods. “Name’s Elias Vance.”

Silas’s fingers stilled on the fader. Vance. The name snagged, sharp and cold, in his memory—a grainy photo in an old police blotter file flagged *‘Unsubstantiated Threat: Wildlife Control’*. His knuckles whitened. The thrum beneath his ribs didn’t spike; it *deepened*, resonating like a struck gong in his marrow. He kept his voice level, professional, the radio host. “Elias. Thanks for calling. What can you tell us about the Grey Man?”

“I’m not here to talk about ghosts,” Vance said. The words were quiet, precise, each one landing like a pebble dropped into still water. “I’m here to talk about the real thing. The thing that *isn’t* grey. The thing that *howls*.”

Silas didn’t flinch. He leaned forward, the leather chair sighing softly. “Go on, Elias.”

“The reports are consistent,” Vance continued, his tone shifting into the cadence of a briefing. “Sightings near Moonridge Park. Three weeks ago. Then the old Henderson quarry. Last night… the woods behind Willow Creek Elementary. Always around midnight. Always after the rain.” A beat. “Always *alone*.”

Silas’s throat felt tight. Willow Creek. He’d walked those woods last Tuesday, the scent of wet pine and turned earth thick in the air, the moon a sliver, barely a whisper. He’d felt… restless. Hungry. But controlled. Always controlled. “What do you mean, ‘alone’?” he asked, his voice carefully neutral.

“Alone means no pack,” Vance stated. “No warning. No territory markers. Just… one. Fast. Quiet. Leaves no tracks you can follow past ten feet. Except the blood.” Another pause, longer this time. Heavy. “You know what I mean by blood, Silas.”

The air in the booth grew thick, charged. The hum of the studio lights seemed to drop an octave. Silas could taste copper on his tongue. Not panic. *Recognition.* His vision sharpened at the edges, the red glow of the “ON AIR” sign burning with impossible intensity. He saw the faint, almost invisible tracery of old silver scars on his own forearm, hidden beneath his sleeve. Scars from a long-ago mistake. From a hunter who hadn’t been quite fast enough.

“You sound like you’ve seen it up close, Elias,” Silas murmured, the words measured, dangerous.

“I have,” Vance replied, no inflection, no boast. Just fact. “Twice. First time, I missed. Second time…” He let the sentence hang, thick with unsaid violence. “I don’t miss twice.”

Silas closed his eyes for a fraction of a second. He heard the phantom scrape of claws on concrete, the guttural snarl that lived in his own throat when the fever rose. He heard the terrified whimper of a stray dog he’d once startled near the park fence—and how, for one horrifying second, the urge to *pursue* had been stronger than reason. He opened his eyes, meeting the reflection of his own dark, watchful gaze in the black glass of the studio monitor.

“Why call *me*, Elias?” Silas asked, his voice dropping, losing its radio polish, becoming raw, stripped bare. “Why not the sheriff? Or Animal Control?”

A dry, humorless sound, almost a cough. “Because I know who you are, Silas Thorne. I know what you are. And I know you listen to the static between the stations. You hear the truth others drown out.” Vance paused, then added, voice dropping to a near-whisper that somehow cut through the airwaves like a knife: “I know you’re running out of time.”

The line went dead. Not a click. Not a disconnect tone. Just sudden, absolute silence. The kind that follows a snapped bone.

Silas sat very still. Rain drummed against the glass. The “ON AIR” sign glowed, relentless. He slowly removed his headset, the plastic cool against his temples. His left hand trembled, just once, a fine, involuntary vibration. He looked down at it. Beneath the thin skin, the veins pulsed a deeper, hotter blue. He flexed his fingers. The knuckles cracked, a sound too loud in the sudden quiet, too much like breaking twigs.

Outside, the city lights blurred. Inside, the moon wasn’t rising yet. But Silas Thorne felt its weight settle onto his shoulders, heavy and inevitable, a crushing, beautiful, terrible gravity. He reached for the mic, his voice, when it came, was steady again—warm, gravelly, utterly human. “Well… that was… intense. Let’s take a quick break. When we return, we’ll be speaking with Dr. Aris Thorne—no relation, folks—about the psychological roots of nocturnal anxiety…”

He didn’t look at the monitor. He didn’t need to. He knew the reflection staring back wasn’t just Silas Thorne, radio host. It was the thing that waited, patient and hungry, in the dark space between the beats of his own heart. And the hunter wasn’t just out there anymore. He was already inside the signal.

title: young adult|a boy genius criminal mastermind negotiates with fairy police to rescue his father
text:
The air in the Glimmerhold Interrogation Chamber tasted like cold iron and crushed violets—a scent that clung to the back of Leo Thorne’s throat, sharp and wrong. He sat perfectly still on the obsidian bench, knees together, hands folded in his lap. His fingers, slender and ink-stained at the knuckles, rested lightly over the seam of his charcoal-gray trousers. He was thirteen years, four months, and seventeen days old. He’d counted every hour since the Silverwood Enforcement Unit had taken his father.

Across the polished moonstone table, Inspector Elara Vane stood—not sat. Her uniform was spun from woven willow-silk, silver-threaded and faintly luminescent at the cuffs. Her wings, folded tight against her spine, were the color of storm clouds just before lightning split them: deep indigo veined with silver. She held a crystal stylus poised above a floating ledger, its surface shimmering with shifting glyphs. Her gaze, however, wasn’t on the ledger. It was on Leo’s left earlobe—where a tiny, almost invisible scar curved like a crescent moon, the only mark he’d ever let anyone see.

“You’re not under arrest,” she said, voice low, resonant as a struck bell. “You’re *observed*.”

Leo didn’t blink. “Then why am I wearing damp-proof restraints?” His voice was quiet, but it carried—clear, precise, uninflected. The silver cuffs around his wrists hummed faintly, emitting a soft violet pulse each time he shifted his weight. Not magic-suppressors. *Truth-dampeners*. They didn’t stop lies—they made them physically painful to speak, tightening like constricting vines if falsehoods formed on the tongue.

Elara tilted her head. “Because you dismantled the Lumina Vault last Tuesday. Not with force. With *grammar*.” She tapped the stylus once against the ledger. A holographic projection bloomed above the table: intricate, interlocking runes, then a cascade of corrupted syntax—verbs inverted, prepositions weaponized, conditional clauses rewritten as binding paradoxes. “You didn’t break the wards. You *edited* them. Like editing source code in a living language.”

Leo finally lifted his eyes. They were the exact shade of tarnished mercury—pale, reflective, unsettlingly depthless. “My father taught me that languages aren’t walls. They’re bridges. And bridges have blueprints.” He paused, just long enough for the chamber’s ambient light to catch the fine dust motes swirling near the ceiling—tiny, glittering things caught in the fairy realm’s perpetual, slow-motion breeze. “He also taught me that the Glimmerhold doesn’t imprison scholars. It imprisons *liabilities*.”

Elara’s wingtip twitched. A micro-expression—irritation, or something closer to reluctant respect. “Your father is being held in the Verdant Annex. For unauthorized cross-realm resonance experiments. Specifically, attempting to stabilize a human neural pattern within a fae echo-chamber. That’s not scholarship, Leo. That’s destabilizing the Veil’s structural memory.”

“He wasn’t *stabilizing* it,” Leo corrected, voice dropping half a tone. “He was *reversing* it. The resonance wasn’t an accident. It was a signature. The same harmonic decay we found in the Whispering Hollow disappearances last month. The same frequency embedded in the rust on the Iron Bridge railings. The same tremor in the soil beneath Oakhaven Cemetery.” He leaned forward, just slightly. The violet pulse in his cuffs flared, warm against his skin. “You’ve been treating symptoms. My father was tracing the disease.”

Silence settled, thick and humming. Outside the arched, leaded window, a flock of sky-moths drifted past, their wings scattering prismatic light across the floor. One landed on the edge of the moonstone table, antennae quivering.

Elara exhaled—a slow, controlled release. She lowered the stylus. “What do you want?”

Leo didn’t hesitate. “Access. Full clearance. To the Annex sub-level three. To the Echo-Chamber Alpha node. For exactly forty-seven minutes and twelve seconds. No observers. No recording glyphs. Just me, a standard diagnostic wand, and the chamber’s core interface.”

Elara’s laugh was short, dry as autumn leaves. “You think we’ll hand you the keys to the most sensitive resonance vault in the Glimmerhold? After you rewrote the vault’s own authentication protocol into a self-deleting sonnet?”

“I think,” Leo said, meeting her gaze without flinching, “that if you don’t, your next ‘symptom’ won’t be disappearances. It’ll be *unraveling*. Starting with the memory-ward on the eastern border. Then the dream-harvesting groves. Then the very grammar of the Old Tongue, syllable by syllable, forgetting itself.” He paused, watching her pupils dilate—just a fraction—as the implications landed. “My father didn’t cause the decay. He’s the only one who can map its origin point. And he needs me to calibrate the final harmonic filter. Without me, the chamber will overload in seventy-two hours. And when it does… well.” He glanced at the sky-moth, now lifting off, leaving a faint trail of iridescent dust. “You’ll feel it in your bones. In your wings. In the way your own name suddenly sounds unfamiliar.”

Elara stared at him. Not at the boy, but at the certainty in his silence—the absolute, terrifying lack of bluff in his posture, his breath, the unwavering stillness of his hands. She saw the scar on his ear again. Remembered the file footnote: *Subject Thorne, Silas: Last known location—Echo-Chamber Alpha. Last transmission: “Tell Leo the third verse is the key. Tell him I’m sorry about the lullaby.”*

She reached into her tunic and withdrew a small, pearlescent disc—no larger than a thumbnail. It pulsed with soft, internal light.

“This grants temporal access,” she said, placing it on the table between them. “Forty-seven minutes. Twelve seconds. Not a second more. And Leo?” Her voice dropped, roughened by something that wasn’t authority. “If you lie—even once—if you try to rewrite *anything* beyond the stated parameters…” She didn’t finish. She didn’t need to. The violet pulse in his cuffs flared hot, a warning whisper against his skin.

Leo picked up the disc. It was warm, humming with contained resonance. He didn’t smile. Didn’t nod. He simply closed his fingers around it, feeling the vibration thrum up his arm, steady and insistent as a heartbeat.

“Thank you, Inspector,” he said, and the words tasted clean on his tongue—true, undeniable, and utterly, devastatingly insufficient.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The neon lights of Washington, D.C., flickered in the rain, casting a glistening sheen over the city. The night was young, but for Sarah Reeves, it felt like the end of an era. She stood by her office window, staring out at the wet streets, her mind racing with the implications of what she had just discovered.

Sarah was a CIA analyst, a desk jockey, one of the unsung heroes who toiled in the shadows, sifting through endless streams of data, piecing together the puzzle of global security. Her job was to provide the President with accurate, actionable intelligence, and she took that responsibility seriously. But tonight, everything had changed.

It started with a routine briefing. Sarah had spent the last three days compiling a report on a suspected terrorist cell operating in Eastern Europe. The information was sensitive, and the stakes were high. When she finally submitted the document, she felt a sense of pride and relief. It was thorough, meticulous, and, most importantly, true.

But as she was packing up her things, preparing to leave for the night, something caught her eye. A small discrepancy in the final version of the report. At first, she dismissed it as a typo, a minor error that could be easily corrected. But as she delved deeper, her heart began to race. The changes were subtle, but significant. Key details had been altered, conclusions softened, and the overall tone of the report had shifted from urgent to cautionary.

Sarah's hands trembled as she compared the original and the altered versions. The implications were staggering. If the President made decisions based on this watered-down version, the consequences could be catastrophic. Lives could be lost, and the nation's security could be compromised.

She knew she had to act, but the thought of going against the chain of command was daunting. The CIA was a labyrinthine organization, and the higher-ups didn't take kindly to dissent. But Sarah couldn't ignore what she had found. She grabbed her coat and headed for the elevator, her mind already racing through the possibilities.

The halls of the CIA headquarters were eerily quiet, the occasional sound of footsteps echoing off the polished floors. Sarah's heels clicked as she walked, each step a reminder of the gravity of her situation. She made her way to the secure room where the final reports were stored, her access card granting her entry with a soft beep.

Inside, the air was cool and sterile, the rows of filing cabinets and computer terminals a stark contrast to the chaos brewing in her mind. She pulled up the digital copy of her report, her fingers flying over the keyboard as she cross-referenced the changes. There was no doubt about it—the alterations were deliberate, and they had come from within the agency.

Sarah's phone buzzed in her pocket, and she nearly jumped. It was a text from her supervisor, Mark, asking if she was still in the building. She hesitated, her thumb hovering over the screen. Should she respond? Or should she go straight to the top?

Before she could decide, the door to the secure room creaked open, and Mark stepped inside. His face was pale, and his eyes darted around the room, as if he was expecting someone else to be there.

"Sarah," he said, his voice strained. "What are you doing here so late?"

She turned to face him, her heart pounding in her chest. "I could ask you the same thing, Mark."

He took a step closer, his expression shifting from concern to something more menacing. "I know what you've found, Sarah. And I need you to understand that this is bigger than both of us. You can't go running to anyone with this. Do you understand?"

Sarah's mind raced. She had always trusted Mark, but now, standing there in the dim light of the secure room, she realized she didn't know him at all. "Who's behind this, Mark? Who altered my report?"

He sighed, running a hand through his hair. "It doesn't matter. What matters is that you keep your mouth shut. If you don't, you'll put everyone in danger. Including yourself."

Sarah's resolve hardened. She couldn't let fear dictate her actions. "I can't do that, Mark. This is too important. People's lives are at stake."

Mark's face twisted into a snarl. "You have no idea what you're dealing with, Sarah. You think you can just waltz into the Oval Office and tell the President what you think? You'll be silenced, just like everyone else who's tried."

Sarah's hand moved to the panic button on her lanyard, but before she could press it, Mark lunged at her. They tumbled to the floor, the sound of their struggle muffled by the thick carpet. Sarah fought back with every ounce of strength she had, but Mark was stronger, and soon she felt the cold steel of a knife against her throat.

"Just let it go, Sarah," he hissed. "Let it go, or I swear—"

The door to the secure room burst open, and a team of agents swarmed in, guns drawn. Mark froze, his eyes wide with panic. Sarah took the opportunity to push him off, scrambling to her feet as the agents subdued him.

As she watched them drag Mark away, Sarah felt a mix of relief and dread. She had uncovered a conspiracy, but the fight was far from over. The altered report was just the tip of the iceberg, and she knew that whoever was behind it would stop at nothing to keep their secrets buried.

The night was still young, and Sarah Reeves had a long road ahead. But she was determined to see it through, no matter the cost.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The barn door groaned open, releasing a warm, hay-scented breath into the damp October air. Professor Alistair Finch stood on the threshold, suitcase in one hand, a battered leather satchel slung over the other shoulder—both absurdly formal against the weathered wood and rusted hinges. His tweed jacket was too thin, his oxford shoes already speckled with mud.

“Dad?” Clara’s voice came from behind a stack of bales. She emerged, wearing grease-streaked overalls, her dark hair escaping a messy bun, a wrench dangling from her belt. Her eyes—sharp, unblinking—scanned him: the stiff posture, the way his knuckles whitened on the suitcase handle, the faint tremor in his left hand he always hid by clasping it tightly over his right.

“You’re early,” she said, not unkindly. Just stating fact.

“I resigned yesterday,” he replied, voice clipped, precise, as if reading a footnote. “Effective immediately.”

Clara wiped her palm on her thigh and extended it. He hesitated, then shook it—brief, dry, like two academics exchanging citations at a conference that had already ended badly. She took his suitcase. “Room’s above the tack room. Smells like cedar and horse sweat. Hope you like it.”

“It’s… functional.”  

She snorted. “Good. Functionality’s all we do here.” She led him past the feed trough where three goats stared, unimpressed. “You read the email I sent? About the chickens?”

“The one titled ‘Do Not Feed Them Your Regrets’?”

Clara stopped, turned. A slow, wry smile touched her lips—the first crack in her reserve. “That was the polite version. The draft said ‘They’ll eat your dignity and lay eggs full of judgment.’ I deleted it. Figured you’d have enough of that already.”

He didn’t laugh. But he exhaled—a long, shaky release. “The board called it ‘a pattern of ethical miscalculation.’ My students called it ‘Finch’s Final Fraud.’ The paper called it ‘Plagiarism, Power, and a Professors’ Privilege.’” He paused, watching a hen peck stubbornly at a dried leaf. “None of them mentioned the footnote I missed. Just one footnote. In a thirty-page review. I cited the wrong edition. The original idea *was* mine. I just… misattributed the page.”

Clara leaned against a fence post, arms crossed. “So you lost tenure, your office, your pension plan—and your favorite mug with the Aristotle quote—because you cited the wrong edition?”

“Yes.”  

“And the university’s ethics committee spent six weeks investigating *that*?”

“They investigated the pattern. Which included three other citations—two of which were correct. One was ambiguous. The third… yes. I misattributed again.” He looked down at his shoes. “I was tired. My wife had just left. I was editing at 3 a.m., cross-referencing PDFs on a cracked screen.”  

Clara was quiet for a long moment. Then: “My goat, Mabel, ate my favorite pair of work gloves last week. Chewed them to ribbons. Left only the thumb. I didn’t fire her. I bought new gloves. And gave her extra oats. Moral: sometimes consequences outpace intent. Doesn’t mean intent doesn’t matter.” She pushed off the post. “Come on. Let’s get you unpacked. Before the rain starts—or before you start drafting a rebuttal in your head.”

Inside the loft, the room was small, clean, lit by a single window overlooking the pasture. A narrow bed, a wooden chair, a shelf holding two books—*The Soil and Health* and *The Chicken Whisperer’s Handbook*. No desk. No bookshelves. No framed degrees.

Alistair placed his satchel on the chair. From it, he withdrew a slim, cloth-bound volume—*Milton’s Lycidas*, annotated in his tight, looping script. He ran a finger over the margin beside the line *“Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise…”*

Clara appeared in the doorway, holding two mugs. Steam curled from one. “Chamomile. Non-alcoholic. For now.”

He accepted it. “Thank you.”

She sat on the edge of the bed, swinging her boots. “So. What’s the plan, Professor? Are you going to write your magnum opus up here? Or are you going to teach the goats Socratic dialogue?”

He sipped. Too hot. Bitter. Real. “I don’t know what I am anymore, Clara.”

She nodded slowly. “Yeah. I figured that part out when you showed up in loafers.” She took a swallow of her own tea—black, no sugar. “Here’s the farm rule, though: You feed the animals before you feed yourself. You mend the fence before you fix your mood. And you don’t quote Milton at the roosters. They don’t care about fame. They care about grit.”

He almost smiled. Almost.

Later, as dusk bled into violet, they stood side by side at the coop door. Clara handed him a scoop of grain. “Toss it in gently. Not like you’re assigning grades.”

He fumbled the first throw. Grain scattered wide. A hen squawked in protest.

Clara didn’t sigh. Didn’t correct. Just watched him try again—slower, lower, steadier—until the golden kernels arced cleanly into the trough, and the birds rushed forward, wings flapping, beaks clicking.

“Better,” she said.

Alistair didn’t reply. He just stood there, breathing the thick, living air—manure, wet earth, warm feathers—and listened to the soft, insistent murmur of twenty hens settling into their roosts.

For the first time in months, the silence inside him wasn’t hollow. It was just quiet. Waiting.

title: young adult|a boy genius criminal mastermind negotiates with fairy police to rescue his father
text:
The fairy cop’s wings didn’t hum. They *itched*. A low, subsonic buzz vibrating under the skin of his temples—like a trapped wasp in a tin can. Leo watched it. Watched the way the cop’s left hand twitched toward the silver-chased baton at his hip, knuckles white, tendons standing out like guitar strings.

“Your father’s not in custody,” Officer Kael said. His voice was flat. Too flat. Like he’d rehearsed it in a vacuum. “He’s in *containment*.”

Leo didn’t blink. He leaned back in the plastic chair—cold, cracked at the seam—and let the silence hang. Not dramatic. Just heavy. Like wet concrete settling.

“He broke Protocol Seven,” Kael added. “Three times. In one night. Stole the Heartwood Loom. Smashed the Moonpetal Vault. Left three junior constables with temporary pixie-dust psychosis.” He paused. “You know what that looks like, kid? Hallucinations so real they chew their own fingers off thinking they’re caterpillars.”

Leo’s stomach tightened. He’d seen the footage. Grainy, shaky, shot from a drone cam mounted on a streetlamp. His dad’s face—tired, stubbled, eyes burning with that same frantic light Leo saw every time he stared into his own bathroom mirror—flashing past the vault’s shattered iris-lock. No gloating. No grand speech. Just movement. Efficient. Desperate.

“He didn’t steal the Loom,” Leo said. His voice didn’t crack. It *scraped*. “He *borrowed* it. To fix the Veil tear near Blackwater Bridge. You’ve got thermal scans showing the bleed. You’ve got the resonance decay logs. You buried them because admitting the Veil’s fraying makes your budget look like a joke.”

Kael’s jaw jumped. A tiny, involuntary spasm. The first real crack.

“Borrowing requires permission,” he said, but the edge was gone. Replaced by something tired. Worn thin.

“Permission requires paperwork,” Leo countered. “And paperwork takes six weeks. My dad’s sister—the one who raised him after the Hollowing—died last Tuesday. Sepsis. Fairy-grade antibiotics don’t cross the Veil well. She waited. For six weeks. He went in. Fixed the tear. Took the Loom. Left a note on the vault floor: *‘Used it. Returned it. Sorry about the dust.’*”

Silence again. Longer this time. The buzzing in Kael’s wings dropped to a faint, angry thrum. Outside the interrogation room’s one-way glass, a patrol drone whirred past, its red eye blinking slow and steady.

“You’re sixteen,” Kael said, finally. Not accusing. Just stating a fact, like weather.

“Seventeen in three days,” Leo corrected. “And I’m the only one who can calibrate the Loom’s harmonic dampeners without frying its core. Your techs tried. Two of them are still in med-bay with third-degree resonance burns.”

Kael exhaled. A long, slow leak of air. He unclipped his badge—not the polished silver one, but the black, matte backup ID clipped inside his tunic. He slid it across the scarred metal table. It landed with a soft, final *clack*.

“Containment Level Gamma,” he said. “Underground. Sector 9. Old coal shafts. Reinforced with lead-laced quartz. Your dad’s in Cell 7B. Guard rotation changes at 23:47. Exactly. Not a second before. Not a second after.”

Leo didn’t touch the badge. “What’s the price?”

Kael looked at him. Really looked. Past the sharp cheekbones, past the too-still posture, straight into eyes that held zero warmth and all the cold calculus of a locked vault.

“The Loom stays calibrated,” Kael said. “You run diagnostics. You sign off. You *don’t* access the archive servers. You don’t touch the Veil-mapping protocols. And you walk out that door tonight. Alone.”

Leo nodded once. Sharp. Clean.

“And my dad?”

Kael held his gaze. “He walks out with you. In twelve hours. After the diagnostics. After the sign-off. After you prove you’re not just another brilliant little ghost haunting our systems.”

Leo stood. The chair scraped. Loud. Harsh.

“One more thing,” he said, voice dropping lower. “The sepsis. It wasn’t just sepsis. Was it?”

Kael didn’t flinch. But his hand drifted, almost unconsciously, to the small, faded tattoo on his inner wrist—a wilted moonpetal. Same as Leo’s dad used to draw on napkins when he thought Leo wasn’t looking.

“No,” Kael admitted. “It was Veil-sickness. Slow bleed. From living too close to the tear for too long.”

Leo turned for the door. Paused. Didn’t look back.

“Tell your chief,” he said, “the next time someone tries to fix a hole in your world… maybe send a mechanic. Not a cop.”

He opened the door.

The corridor beyond smelled of ozone, damp stone, and something older—wet earth and crushed ferns. Real. Unfiltered.

Leo walked. His footsteps echoed. Not like a kid’s. Like something that knew exactly how much weight it carried. And exactly how much it could break.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The studio was dimly lit, the only illumination coming from the soft glow of the control board and the neon sign outside that flickered intermittently. The air was thick with the scent of old books and stale coffee, a familiar aroma to those who frequented the late-night radio show, "Moonlit Secrets." The host, a tall, broad-shouldered man named Lucas, sat behind the microphone, his deep, soothing voice filling the airwaves.

Lucas adjusted his headphones, glancing at the clock. It was 2:15 AM, and the night was just beginning. His eyes, a piercing shade of amber, scanned the room, taking in the cluttered desk and the stacks of notes he had prepared for the evening. Tonight's topic: urban legends and the creatures that lurk in the shadows.

"Welcome back, listeners," Lucas began, his voice smooth and confident. "You're tuned into 'Moonlit Secrets,' where we dive into the unexplained and the unknown. I'm your host, Lucas, and tonight, we're exploring the world of urban legends. Do you have a story to share? A personal encounter with something... otherworldly? Call us at 555-9000, and let’s unravel the mysteries together."

The phone lines were already buzzing, but one call stood out. The screen flashed, and Lucas picked it up, pressing the button to connect. "We have a caller on the line. Go ahead, you’re on the air."

A gravelly voice crackled through the speakers. "Hello, Lucas. My name is Jack. I’ve been listening to your show for a while now, and I think I have a story that might interest you."

"Go ahead, Jack. What do you have for us?" Lucas leaned forward, his interest piqued.

Jack cleared his throat, and when he spoke, there was an edge to his voice. "I’m a hunter, Lucas. Not the kind that chases deer or rabbits, but the kind that tracks down the things that go bump in the night. Werewolves, vampires, all the things people think are just stories."

Lucas raised an eyebrow, a small smile tugging at the corner of his mouth. "That sounds like quite the profession. Tell me, Jack, what brings you to my show tonight?"

"I’ve been following a lead, Lucas. A werewolf, to be precise. And I have reason to believe that this particular werewolf is someone close to home. Someone who has a lot of influence, someone who can reach a lot of people. Like, say, a radio host."

The studio fell silent, the only sound the hum of the equipment. Lucas’s heart skipped a beat, but he kept his voice steady. "That’s quite an accusation, Jack. Why do you think this werewolf is so close to home?"

"I’ve seen the signs, Lucas. The full moon last week, and the reports of strange occurrences in the area. Animals acting erratic, sightings of a large, shadowy figure in the woods. And then there’s the fact that your show has been running for years, and you never seem to age. It’s all adding up."

Lucas chuckled, though it sounded forced. "Jack, I appreciate your dedication to your... hobby. But I assure you, I’m just a regular guy with a fascination for the paranormal. No fur, no fangs, just a love for a good story."

Jack’s voice grew more insistent. "I know what I saw, Lucas. I’ve been tracking this werewolf for months. And I’m not going to stop until I find out the truth. I’m giving you a chance to come clean, to tell your listeners the truth. Or I’ll do it for you."

The tension in the studio was palpable. Lucas took a deep breath, his mind racing. He knew he couldn’t let Jack expose him, not without a fight. "Jack, I understand your concern, but I can assure you, you’re mistaken. If you have any evidence, bring it forward. But until then, I suggest you keep your theories to yourself."

There was a long pause on the other end of the line, and then Jack spoke, his voice low and menacing. "This isn’t over, Lucas. I’ll be watching. And if you’re hiding something, I will find out. Count on it."

The line went dead, and Lucas stared at the phone, his mind reeling. He knew he had to act fast. The stakes were higher than ever, and he couldn’t afford to let Jack get too close. With a determined look, he turned back to the microphone.

"Thank you, Jack, for your call. We always welcome a good mystery. But for now, let’s move on to our next caller. Who knows what secrets the night holds? Stay tuned, and stay safe, listeners. This is Lucas, signing off for now."

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The rain in Venice doesn’t fall—it *settles*. A cold, greasy film on the stone, on the glass of the *questura*’s high, grimy window, on the inside of my own skull. I watched a single drop gather at the pane’s upper corner, swell, hesitate, then slide down in a slow, viscous tear. Just like the widow across from me.

Elena Moretti sat perfectly still in the hard-backed chair—back straight, hands folded in her lap like a schoolgirl reciting catechism. Her black mourning dress was impeccable, the lace at her throat crisp and sharp enough to cut. Her face, though pale, held no trace of the raw, hollowed-out exhaustion I’d seen in other widows—the ones who’d collapsed into sobs before I’d even closed the door. Elena’s eyes, the colour of storm-lit lagoon water, met mine with unnerving calm. Not defiance. Not fear. Just… assessment.

*Relief*, I thought, the word landing like a pebble dropped into deep, still water. *Not grief. Relief.*

I’d seen it before. Rarely so clean. Usually it was buried under layers—guilt, shock, the sheer logistical horror of paperwork—but here? It shimmered, almost visible, just beneath the surface of her composure. Like sunlight on wet marble.

“Signora Moretti,” I began, my voice low, deliberately neutral. I didn’t offer coffee. Didn’t soften the chair. Let her sit in the quiet weight of the room. “Thank you for coming in. Again.”

She inclined her head, a fraction. “Commissario.” Her voice was cool, precise, each consonant polished. “I understand the necessity. Though I confess, I hoped this would be the final formality.”

*Final formality.* As if Marco’s death were a tax audit, not a bullet through the temple in his own study at midnight. As if the blood on the Persian rug hadn’t been hers to scrub, or the police tape hadn’t sealed the door of the palazzo where she’d lived for twenty-three years.

“I wish it were,” I said, leaning forward slightly, resting my elbows on the scarred oak desk. My own hands, broad and ink-stained, looked crude beside hers. “But the investigation requires clarity. Especially regarding the events of the night before last.”

Her gaze didn’t waver. She lifted one hand—not to wipe her eye, not to clutch her throat—but to smooth a non-existent wrinkle from her sleeve. A gesture of absolute control. “I’ve told you everything I know, Commissario. I was at the Teatro La Fenice. *La Traviata*. I arrived at eight, left at eleven forty-five. The concierge saw me leave. The taxi driver remembers me. The doorman at Palazzo Moretti signed me in at twelve fifteen. I went directly to bed. Alone.”

*Alone.* The word hung, light as dust motes in the weak light filtering through the rain-streaked window.

“And your husband?” I asked, watching her pupils. No dilation. No flicker. “Where was he when you returned?”

A pause. Longer than necessary. Not hesitation—calculation. “He was… working. He often worked late. In his study. The door was closed. I heard the soft murmur of the radio. I assumed he was reading.”

“The radio was on?” I pressed. “At twelve fifteen?”

A faint, almost imperceptible tightening around her mouth. “Yes. Classical. Schubert. Very quiet. I remember because it was unusual. He usually preferred silence when he read.”

*Unusual.* Another tiny crack in the flawless facade. Not in the fact, but in the *remembering* of its unusualness. Why remember the volume of Schubert? Unless you’d been listening for something else. Or confirming an alibi.

I slid a photograph across the desk. Not the crime scene—too raw, too visceral. Just Marco Moretti, smiling, arm slung casually over the back of a gondola seat, Venice blurred and golden behind him. A decade old, maybe. Happy. Carefree. Utterly unlike the man found slumped over his mahogany desk, a single, neat hole above his left ear, his fountain pen still clutched loosely in his right hand, ink bleeding onto a half-written letter.

Elena’s eyes dropped to the photo. Her breath hitched—just once, a tiny, controlled intake. Not a sob. A sigh. Like someone releasing a breath they’d held for years.

“He looked well,” she murmured. Not *he looked happy*. Not *he looked loved*. *Well.* As if assessing a patient. Or a piece of furniture.

I leaned back, letting the silence pool between us, thick and cold as the canal water outside. “You haven’t cried, Signora Moretti.”

Her gaze snapped back to mine. Not angry. Not offended. Curious. Like a scientist observing an unexpected reaction in a petri dish. “Should I have?” she asked, her voice utterly devoid of inflection. “Grief isn’t a performance, Commissario. It’s a private thing. A… physiological response. Mine simply hasn’t manifested that way. Perhaps I’m numb. Perhaps I’m efficient. Does it matter to the bullet in his head?”

*Does it matter?* There it was. The first unguarded edge. Not denial. Not defensiveness. A chilling, clinical dismissal of the very emotion expected of her. As if sorrow were a faulty appliance, easily bypassed.

I picked up my pen, tapped it once against the desk. *Tap. Tap.* The only sound besides the relentless, soft *shush* of rain on the roof. “Efficiency is admirable, Signora. But murder investigations,” I said, meeting her storm-grey eyes again, “are rarely efficient. They’re messy. They’re about inconsistencies. Like a widow who remembers the exact volume of Schubert playing in another room… but can’t recall if her husband’s favourite pen was Montblanc or Parker.”

Her fingers, still folded, tightened almost imperceptibly. A single knuckle whitened. Just for a second. Then relaxed. The mask re-set, smoother than before.

“His pen,” she said, her voice now like ice over deep water, “was a Pelikan. M805. Midnight blue. He collected them. Like he collected… other things.” A ghost of something—bitterness? amusement?—touched her lips. “Perhaps you should ask *him* about it, Commissario. If you find him.”

The rain slid down the glass. The drop reached the bottom, vanished into the grime. Inside my head, the quiet hum of the *questura*’s fluorescent lights suddenly sounded like the whine of a dying fly. And the widow sat, serene, immaculate, radiating a relief so profound it felt like a physical pressure in the small, damp room. She wasn’t hiding grief. She was hiding the reason it wasn’t there. And I had the sinking, certain feeling that finding Marco Moretti—alive or dead—was the only key to unlocking the door she’d so carefully locked behind her.

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
The bathroom door was ajar. Not *slightly* ajar—like someone had forgotten to latch it after brushing their teeth—but *gaped*, as if the hinges themselves were holding their breath.

I stood in the hallway of the Maplewood Arms, a building that smelled perpetually of boiled cabbage and existential dread, my left loafer stuck in a patch of something beige and vaguely sentient near the baseboard. My client, Ms. Greta Voss, stood three feet behind me, arms crossed so tightly her cardigan buttons looked like they might pop off and skitter down the hall like startled beetles.

“It’s not *my* horse,” she said, voice flat as week-old club soda.

“I didn’t say it was,” I replied, adjusting the cuff of my shirt. It was linen. Supposed to breathe. Felt more like a damp tea towel.

She sniffed. “You said you specialize in ‘energetic anomalies.’ Not equine trespassing.”

“Anomalies *include* trespassing,” I said, and stepped forward.

The bathroom was small. A clawfoot tub with one chipped porcelain hoof, a fogged mirror, a toothbrush cup holding three brushes (two mint, one lavender), and, in the center of the linoleum—knees bent, head lowered, tail swishing with quiet, unhurried rhythm—a chestnut gelding named Barnaby.

He wasn’t *big*. Not a Clydesdale. More like a well-fed, slightly philosophical Welsh pony who’d wandered into the wrong dimension. His coat gleamed under the fluorescent hum. One ear twitched toward us. The other stayed pointed, inexplicably, at the shower curtain.

Ms. Voss made a sound—not quite a gasp, not quite a sigh—more like air escaping a punctured yoga mat.

“Barnaby,” I said softly. He lifted his head. His eyes were the color of weak tea steeped too long. Calm. Unhurried. Deeply unimpressed.

“He’s been here since 4:17 a.m.,” Ms. Voss muttered. “I heard the *thump*. Thought it was the boiler. Then the *snort*. Then the *squelch*.”

Ah. The squelch. That was the hay. I’d seen the bale wedged sideways in the doorway on my way up—half in, half out, like a reluctant guest at a funeral.

“Why is he *here*?” she demanded, jabbing a finger—not at the horse, but at the toilet seat, which Barnaby had apparently used as a chin rest. A single, perfect horseshoe-shaped dent marred its plastic rim.

I crouched. Not all the way. My knees have opinions now, and they’re deeply conservative. I ran a hand over Barnaby’s shoulder. Warm. Solid. Smelled of clover, saddle soap, and something faintly metallic—like old pennies left in rain.

“He’s not *in* the bathroom,” I said.

Greta blinked. “He’s *standing on my bathmat*.”

“He’s *anchoring*,” I corrected. “See how his left hind hoof is just *so*? Slightly splayed? That’s not relaxation. That’s calibration.”

She stared. “Calibration of *what*?”

“The resonance frequency of your shower drain.” I pointed. “It’s humming. Barely audible. But it’s there. A low C-sharp. Been doing it since Tuesday. You felt it in your molars, didn’t you? That little vibration when you brushed?”

She paused. Then, grudgingly: “…My fillings tingled.”

“Exactly. The drain’s been singing off-key since the plumber replaced the P-trap with that cheap PVC nonsense. It’s throwing off the whole water column’s harmonic field. Creates a micro-vortex in the subfloor—just below the tile. A tiny, persistent *pull*.”

Greta rubbed her temple. “A… pull.”

“Not gravitational. *Energetic*. Like a magnet for displaced intention. Barnaby felt it. He’s sensitive. Had a colic episode last spring that coincided with a solar flare and a dropped spoon in the kitchen of a Reiki practitioner in Montclair. Coincidence? Possibly. But horses *listen* to the silence between things. And right now, the silence between your pipes is *screaming*.”

She looked from Barnaby’s serene face to the dented toilet seat. “So he came in here… to *tune* the plumbing?”

“To *ground* it,” I said. “His hooves are natural conductors. His weight distributes the charge. His breathing—slow, deep, diaphragmatic—creates counter-rhythm. Watch.”

I placed my palm flat against Barnaby’s flank. Felt the slow rise and fall. Inhaled. Exhaled. Barnaby exhaled too—long, warm, smelling of timothy grass and resignation.

From the drain, the hum softened. Just a fraction. A hairline fracture in the C-sharp.

Greta leaned in. “Is that… different?”

“Slightly less aggressive,” I admitted. “He’s been here six hours. Progress is incremental. Like acupuncture. Or trying to get your Wi-Fi password from your landlord.”

She stared at the horse. Then at the hay bale. Then at me, my linen cuff, my slightly-too-tight belt, my expression—earnest, unblinking, utterly devoid of irony.

“You’re serious.”

“I’m also out of oat biscuits,” I said. “And Barnaby’s getting restless. See how his tail’s stopped swishing? That means he’s done with the tuning phase. Now he’s entering the *integration* phase. Which usually involves chewing something soft and fibrous.”

Her eyes darted to the shower curtain. Barnaby followed her gaze. His ears pricked forward. Not at the curtain. At the *corner* where it met the rod. A tiny, almost invisible thread had come loose. He nudged it with his nose.

Greta sighed. A real one this time. Exhausted. Defeated. Human.

“Fine,” she said. “What do I owe you?”

I stood, brushed a stray bit of hay from my trousers. “Fifty bucks. Plus access to your basement utility room for twenty minutes. There’s a grounding rod behind the furnace that’s corroded. Needs re-soldering. And maybe… a cup of coffee? Strong. With actual caffeine. Not that chicory nonsense you keep in the cabinet above the microwave.”

She didn’t smile. But she did step past me into the bathroom, opened the medicine cabinet, and pulled out two mugs. One had a chipped handle. The other said *World’s Okayest Grandma*.

Barnaby watched her pour. Then, without fanfare, he turned, nudged the hay bale fully inside, and settled onto his haunches—right there, on the damp bathmat—like he owned the place. Or like the place owned him. Hard to tell, really.

The drain hummed again. Lower now. Warmer. Almost like a purr.

Greta handed me a mug. Steam rose, thin and hopeful.

I took it. Didn’t thank her. Didn’t explain further. Some frequencies don’t translate into words. They just… settle. Like dust. Like hay. Like a horse who knows exactly where the silence is thinnest—and what to do about it.

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The supermarket was eerily silent, save for the occasional creak and groan of the building. The survivors had barricaded themselves in, using anything they could find—shelves, boxes, even old shopping carts. The loading dock at the back had been reinforced with heavy wooden planks and metal bars. It was their only means of escape, but also their greatest vulnerability.

Sarah, a no-nonsense woman with a stern face and a commanding presence, stood near the makeshift barrier, her eyes scanning the area. She clutched a crowbar tightly, her knuckles white. Beside her, Mark, a lanky man with a nervous disposition, fidgeted with his flashlight, casting anxious glances at the door.

"I still don't think this is a good idea," Mark whispered, his voice trembling. "We should have left when we had the chance."

Sarah's gaze hardened. "We couldn't just leave him behind, Mark. He deserved a proper burial, not to be left out there like that."

"Proper burial? We buried him in a shallow grave! This whole thing is insane. What if... what if he comes back?"

Before Sarah could respond, a faint, rhythmic sound began to echo through the loading dock. It was soft at first, barely perceptible, but it grew louder and more insistent. A knock. Then another. And another.

Mark's eyes widened in terror. "Oh my God, did you hear that?!"

Sarah's grip on the crowbar tightened. "Stay calm, Mark. It's probably just a stray animal or something."

But the knocking continued, more urgent now, accompanied by a low, muffled moan. Sarah's heart pounded in her chest, but she refused to show fear. She stepped closer to the door, her eyes narrowing as she tried to discern the source of the noise.

"Who's there?" she called out, her voice steady but tinged with unease.

The moaning stopped, and for a moment, there was only silence. Then, a weak, raspy voice replied, "S-Sarah... let me in..."

Mark gasped, his face pale. "It's him! Oh God, it's really him!"

Sarah's breath caught in her throat. She recognized the voice, despite its distorted, inhuman quality. It was Tom, one of their own, the man they had buried just hours ago.

"Tom?" she whispered, her mind racing. "How... how can this be?"

"Please, Sarah... I need help. I'm... I'm not right. Let me in before... before I change completely."

Tears welled up in Sarah's eyes, but she blinked them away. She turned to Mark, who was visibly shaking. "We can't let him in. You know what happens if we do. He'll turn, and then we're all dead."

"But, Sarah, he's one of us! We can't just leave him out there!" Mark pleaded, his voice breaking.

Sarah's expression softened, but her resolve remained firm. "I know, Mark. But we have to think about the others. About ourselves. If we open this door, we might as well sign our own death warrants."

The knocking grew more frantic, and Tom's moans became more desperate. "Sarah, please! I can feel it... I can feel myself changing. Don't let me become one of them!"

Mark's shoulders slumped, and he sank to the ground, his head in his hands. "This is a nightmare. I can't take this anymore."

Sarah placed a hand on his shoulder, offering what little comfort she could. "I know, Mark. But we have to stay strong. For everyone."

She took a deep breath and raised her voice, addressing Tom through the door. "I'm sorry, Tom. I'm so, so sorry. But we can't risk it. We have to keep the others safe."

There was a long, agonizing pause. Then, Tom's voice, now a guttural growl, spoke again. "You... you'll regret this, Sarah. You'll all pay... for leaving me out here... to die... alone."

The knocking ceased, and the loading dock fell into an oppressive silence. Sarah and Mark remained motionless, the weight of their decision pressing down on them. They knew they had made the right choice, but the guilt and the horror of it all would haunt them forever.

As the night wore on, the survivors huddled together, listening to the darkness, waiting for whatever terrors it might bring.

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The coffee in her mug had gone cold. Cold as the dread pooling low in her gut.

Elena Vasquez stared at the President’s Daily Brief—*her* briefing—on the secure tablet. Page three. The section on Operation *Hollow Pike*. Her fingers hovered over the screen, trembling just enough to blur the text.

*“…indicating high confidence that Iranian Quds Force assets are embedded within the Basra logistics hub…”*

She’d written *“low confidence.”* She’d flagged it with three red asterisks. She’d cited the source: a single, uncorroborated intercept from a compromised NSA node in Kuwait—*not* the “multi-source consensus” the current version claimed.

Her breath hitched. She scrolled back. Page one. The drone strike assessment over Sana’a. She’d written *“tactical success, strategic liability.”* Now it read *“decisive counterterrorism victory.”* Her footnote about civilian casualty estimates—27, not 3—was gone. Replaced by a bland citation to CENTCOM’s sanitized after-action report.

Someone had rewritten her work. Not edited. *Overwritten.* With authority. With access.

She checked the metadata. Last modified: 03:17 AM. Server timestamp. *Her* workstation ID logged out at 22:48. She’d walked out of Langley at 10:30, exhausted, ears still ringing from the 90-minute threat briefing with the Deputy D/CIA. She’d locked her terminal. She’d used her biometric pass. She’d watched the screen go black.

Her throat tightened. She pulled up the audit log. Filtered for *PDB-24-087-HollowPike*. Saw it: a single edit event. User: ADMIN-OMEGA. No name. No department. Just that cold, bureaucratic designation—like a ghost in the machine.

Omega wasn’t a real account. It was a kill switch. A backdoor reserved for one office. One person.

*The Director.*

But why? Why lie about Basra? Why inflate Sana’a? What did the President *need* to believe?

She opened her personal encrypted drive—the one buried behind three firewalls, the one she’d built after her last source went dark in Aleppo. She pulled up her original draft. The raw notes. The audio transcript of her call with the linguist who’d translated the Basra chatter: *“…they sound scared. Not confident. Like they’re waiting for orders that never came.”* She’d written that down verbatim. It wasn’t in the final brief.

A knock. Sharp. Two raps.

Elena slammed the tablet face-down. Her heart hammered against her ribs—loud, stupid, betraying.

The door cracked open. Not security. Not her boss. A man in a charcoal suit, tie too tight, eyes like wet stones. Assistant Director for Counterintelligence. Marcus Bell. He didn’t smile. Didn’t wait for invitation.

“Vasquez,” he said. Voice flat. “You’re needed in the Situation Room. Ten minutes. The President wants context on Hollow Pike.”

Her mouth went dry. “I thought the PDB was the context.”

Bell stepped fully inside. Shut the door. Leaned against it. His gaze flicked to the tablet, then back to her face. “The President saw your *original* draft. Before it was finalized.”

A lie. A clumsy one. Her blood turned to ice water.

“He asked why the analysis shifted so dramatically between versions,” Bell continued, watching her blink, watching the pulse jump in her throat. “He asked *who* authorized the change.”

Elena didn’t move. Didn’t breathe deep. She heard the hum of the HVAC. The distant clatter of a cart in the hallway. The static hiss in her own ears.

“I told him it was standard interagency refinement,” Bell said. “That you’d incorporated new inputs overnight. That your final judgment reflected the consensus view.”

*Consensus.* A word that tasted like ash.

He pushed off the door. Took two steps closer. Lowered his voice, barely above a whisper. “Your analysis was *good*, Elena. Sharp. Too sharp. Some truths don’t scale well to the Oval Office. They fracture things. Break trust. Start wars nobody wants.”

He paused. Let it hang.

“You’ll brief the President. You’ll stand by the *final* version. You’ll answer his questions with the facts *in the record*.”

His eyes held hers. Not threatening. Not kind. Just stating physics.

“And if you don’t?” she whispered.

Bell didn’t flinch. “Then we have a different problem. One that doesn’t involve briefing rooms. Or coffee mugs.”

He turned. Opened the door. Stopped.

“Oh. And Elena?”

She didn’t look up.

“The tablet you’re holding? It’s been wiped. Remote wipe. Five seconds ago. You’re looking at a clean slate now. Just like the President is.”

The door clicked shut.

Silence rushed back in. Heavy. Suffocating.

Elena stared at the blank screen. Her reflection stared back—pale, hollow-eyed, already disappearing into the glass.

She reached for the cold coffee. Lifted it. Didn’t drink.

Just held it.

Waiting for the tremor in her hand to stop.  
Or for it to get worse.  
She wasn’t sure which meant survival anymore.

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
The bus smelled like stale coffee, burnt toast, and the faint, persistent tang of industrial disinfectant that never quite masked the deeper musk of exhaustion. Maya sat wedged between a stack of “FORD FOR FUTURE” yard signs and a half-unpacked crate of protein bars, her knees drawn up to her chest. Outside, the rain blurred the neon glow of a Motel 6 sign into streaks of sickly pink and green. She watched a single drop trace a slow, defiant path down the fogged window, then vanish.

Her father’s voice cut through the low hum of the engine and the muffled murmur of staffers debating polling margins in the front cabin. “—and if we don’t lock down the county commission endorsement by Friday, we’re handing them the whole northern corridor on a silver platter.” He sounded tired, but the edge was still there—the one that made reporters lean in, that made donors write checks without blinking. Maya didn’t turn. She knew the rhythm: the slight rasp in his throat, the pause where he’d glance at his watch, the way his knuckles whitened just a fraction on the armrest.

“Dad?” Her voice was quiet, almost lost beneath the bus’s groan as it hit a pothole.

He turned. His face, usually so carefully composed for cameras—strong jaw, crinkled eyes that held warmth only in close-up—looked hollowed out under the fluorescent strip light. The stubble was darker than usual. “Maya. You okay? Need water?”

She shook her head, finally meeting his eyes. “Just… wondering what time it is.”

He checked his watch, then frowned. “Ten past two. Why?”

“Because,” she said, her gaze drifting back to the rain-smeared window, “it feels like it’s been ten past two for three days straight. And also, I think I’ve seen that same gas station billboard—‘WELCOME TO HAVENWOOD! POP. 2,841’—twice. We’re going in circles.”

A ghost of a smile touched his lips. Not the campaign smile—the one with perfect teeth and practiced sincerity—but something smaller, older, private. “Havenwood’s a loop town, kiddo. County line runs right through the Dairy Queen parking lot. We circle back every time we need a restroom break or a fresh batch of volunteers who haven’t heard the ‘infrastructure’ speech yet.” He shifted, leaning slightly towards her, the leather of his jacket creaking. “You hungry? I think there’s a granola bar left in my bag.”

“I had three this morning. Before the rally in Millhaven.” She paused, watching a lone figure in a yellow raincoat struggle with an umbrella outside a closed hardware store. “They asked me again today. At the coffee shop. ‘So, Maya, what’s *your* platform?’”

He was silent for a long moment, just watching her profile. The bus swayed, headlights catching the rain on the glass, turning the world outside into liquid gold. “What did you say?”

“I said I’m majoring in environmental science. That I think clean water access is non-negotiable. That I’m tired of explaining why I don’t want to run for anything right now.” She finally looked at him, her voice tight. “They don’t care about my GPA, Dad. They care about whether I’ll be your ‘youth outreach coordinator’ or your ‘policy liaison’ or whatever shiny title they can stick on me before the primary.”

He didn’t offer platitudes. Didn’t say *they’re just excited* or *it’s part of the job*. He just nodded, slowly. “Yeah. It is part of the job. For all of us.” He reached out, not touching her, but resting his hand flat on the worn vinyl seat between them. “Remember that little park behind the old library in Oak Ridge? Where you used to chase fireflies?”

She blinked, surprised. “The one with the broken swing?”

“The one with the broken swing.” A real, weary smile this time. “You were six. You cried because the swing wouldn’t go high enough. I told you it wasn’t broken, just waiting for a stronger push.” He looked down at his hand, then back at her. “This? This whole thing? It feels like that sometimes. Like pushing a swing that won’t go higher, no matter how hard you try. Or how many people tell you it *should*.”

Maya stared at him. The man who debated tax policy on national television, who could disarm a hostile crowd with a well-timed anecdote, who’d just described the entire campaign as a broken swing. The absurdity of it, the raw honesty, loosened something tight in her chest.

“So… what do you do?” she asked softly.

He sighed, a long, slow exhalation that seemed to deflate him further. “You keep pushing. Even when your arms ache. Even when the swing just creaks and sways, and nobody’s watching. Especially then.” He glanced towards the front, where a staffer was tapping urgently on the driver’s shoulder. “Gotta go. Press pool wants the ‘vision’ soundbite before we hit the next stop.” He stood, smoothing his jacket. As he passed, he paused, his hand hovering near her shoulder for a second before settling lightly, briefly. “And Maya? Next time someone asks about your platform? Tell them about the fireflies. Tell them about the swing. Tell them the truth. It’s the only thing on this bus that hasn’t been pre-approved by the comms team.”

He walked forward, his stride regaining its familiar, purposeful length. Maya watched him go, then looked down at her own hands, resting on her knees. Outside, the rain lessened. A sliver of moon broke through the clouds, pale and sharp, illuminating the wet asphalt. She didn’t reach for a protein bar. She just sat, breathing the recycled air, listening to the steady thrum of the engine, and for the first time in weeks, felt the weight of the bus—not as a cage, but as a strange, rolling vessel carrying something fragile, something real, somewhere she couldn’t yet name, but was starting, just barely, to recognize.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The sun was just beginning to dip below the horizon, casting a golden glow over the sprawling fields of the music festival. I clutched my backpack tightly, feeling the weight of the few possessions I’d brought with me. The air was thick with the scent of grass and the distant hum of music, a symphony of guitars and drums that seemed to pulse through the very earth beneath my feet.

I had been walking for what felt like hours, my legs aching and my stomach growling. But I couldn’t stop now. Not when I was so close. The map in my hand was crumpled and worn, but it was all I had. It showed the layout of the festival grounds, with stages and food stalls marked in bright colors. And there, in the corner, was the one place I needed to find: the main stage, where my mother was supposed to be performing tonight.

I took a deep breath, trying to calm the storm of emotions swirling inside me. Running away from home had been the hardest decision I’d ever made. But I couldn’t stay in that empty house any longer, surrounded by memories of a life that no longer existed. My father’s absence, the constant silence, the unanswered questions about why she left—it all felt like a heavy blanket suffocating me. I needed answers, and I needed them now.

As I walked, the crowd around me grew thicker. People were everywhere, laughing and dancing, their faces painted with vibrant colors. Some wore elaborate costumes, while others carried signs and flags. I felt small and out of place, a tiny fish in a vast ocean. But I pushed forward, determined not to let anything distract me from my goal.

“Excuse me,” I said, tapping a girl on the shoulder. She turned, her eyes wide with surprise. “Can you tell me how to get to the main stage?”

She blinked, then smiled. “Sure! Just follow this path until you see the big tent. You can’t miss it. Are you here for the show?”

I nodded, forcing a smile. “Yeah, I’m looking forward to it.”

“Cool! Who are you here to see?”

I hesitated, the words catching in my throat. “My… my mom. She’s performing tonight.”

Her eyes widened. “Wow, that’s awesome! What’s her name? Maybe I’ve heard of her.”

“Lila Hart,” I said, the name rolling off my tongue with a mix of pride and pain.

She looked thoughtful for a moment, then snapped her fingers. “Oh, I think I’ve seen her name on the lineup! She’s a singer, right? With the long red hair?”

I nodded, feeling a surge of hope. “That’s her. Do you know if she’s already here?”

“I’m not sure, but I think she’s doing a sound check soon. You might catch her if you hurry.”

“Thanks,” I said, my heart racing. “Thanks so much.”

I continued down the path, the sound of music growing louder with each step. The main stage loomed ahead, a massive structure with lights and banners. People were already gathering, and I could see a group of techs setting up equipment. I scanned the area, searching for any sign of her. But there was no one who looked familiar.

I found a spot near the front, leaning against a barrier. My mind was a jumble of thoughts and emotions. What would I say to her when I finally saw her? Would she even recognize me? What if she didn’t want to talk to me? The doubts gnawed at me, making my hands tremble.

“Hey, you okay?” a voice asked, and I turned to see a boy about my age standing next to me. He had curly brown hair and a kind smile. “You look a bit nervous.”

I forced a laugh, trying to appear more confident than I felt. “Just a little. I’ve never been to a festival before.”

“First time, huh? It can be overwhelming, but it’s also amazing. Trust me, you’re gonna love it. I’m Max, by the way.”

“I’m Emma,” I said, shaking his hand. “Nice to meet you, Max.”

“Emma, huh? That’s a cool name. So, who are you here to see?”

I hesitated, unsure if I should share my story with a stranger. But something about Max made me feel safe, like I could trust him. “I’m actually here to see my mom. She’s performing tonight.”

Max’s eyes lit up. “No way! That’s so cool. Is she a famous singer or something?”

I shrugged, feeling a pang of sadness. “Not really. She’s just… my mom. We haven’t seen each other in a while, and I wanted to find her.”

He nodded, his expression softening. “I get it. Family stuff can be complicated. But it’s great that you’re here. I’m sure she’ll be happy to see you.”

I hoped he was right. The thought of seeing her again, of finally getting some answers, was both thrilling and terrifying. I took a deep breath, trying to steady myself. “Thanks, Max. I really appreciate that.”

“No problem,” he said, grinning. “Hey, do you want to grab something to eat? There’s a food truck over there with the best tacos. My treat.”

I smiled, feeling a little lighter. “Sure, that sounds great. Thanks, Max.”

We walked over to the food truck, and as we waited in line, I felt a sense of camaraderie with Max. For the first time since I’d run away, I didn’t feel so alone. Maybe, just maybe, everything would work out.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The rain in Haven’s Point didn’t fall—it seeped. It clung to brick facades, blurred the amber glow of streetlamps, and turned the cobblestones of Harbor Lane into slick, obsidian mirrors reflecting fractured light and passing ghosts. Clara Vance pulled her coat tighter, the wool damp at the shoulders, her notebook tucked under one arm like a shield. She hadn’t planned to walk this route. But the old train station—now a café with mismatched chairs and the faint, persistent scent of burnt espresso—had drawn her like gravity. Ten years. Ten years since she’d boarded the 4:15 p.m. to Boston with a duffel bag, a scholarship letter, and a silence so thick it still echoed in her throat.

She paused beneath the awning, watching steam rise from a paper cup in her gloved hand. The bell above the café door jingled—sharp, insistent—and then *he* stepped out.

Not a memory. Not a trick of the rain-smeared light.

Eli Thorne.

He was taller, broader through the shoulders, his dark hair shorter, wind-tousled, a faint silver thread catching the lamplight near his temple. He wore a faded navy work shirt rolled to the elbows, forearms dusted with fine, dark hair and smudged with something pale—drywall compound, maybe. His eyes, the colour of storm-washed slate, lifted—and locked onto hers.

Time didn’t stop. It *stuttered*. A car hissed past, spraying a fan of grey water; a gull cried overhead, raw and lonely. Clara’s breath hitched, a small, involuntary sound swallowed by the downpour. Her fingers tightened on the warm cup, the heat suddenly too intense against her palm.

He didn’t smile. Didn’t look away. Just stood there, rain beading on his lashes, his gaze travelling over her face—the line of her jaw, the curve of her mouth, the way her dark hair, escaping its knot, curled damply at her nape. Recognition flared, deep and slow, like embers coaxed back to life. Then something else: a quiet, unguarded ache.

“Clara Vance.” His voice was lower than she remembered, rougher, layered with the cadence of the coast—salt and gravel and long silences.

She managed a nod. “Eli.”

He took a step forward, closing the distance between the café awning and the narrow sidewalk where she stood. Rain glistened on his collar. “You’re back.”

“Just for a story.” Her voice sounded thin, reedy, betraying none of the steady confidence she projected in boardrooms and press conferences. “The old lighthouse restoration. For *Coastal Review*.”

He nodded slowly, his eyes never leaving hers. There was no bitterness in them, not yet. Just observation. Assessment. Like he was reading a sentence he’d spent a decade trying to understand. “They’re putting in solar panels,” he said, his tone neutral. “And reinforcing the lantern room. Took them long enough.”

A ghost of the old Eli surfaced then—a wry twist at the corner of his mouth, fleeting as smoke. It cracked something open inside her, a fissure in the careful dam she’d built over ten years of measured success and unspoken absences.

“You still work at the boatyard?” she asked, the question absurdly mundane, a lifeline thrown across a chasm.
