“Own it now. Thorne & Son. Though ‘Son’ is mostly me these days.” He glanced past her, toward the harbour, where the skeletal outline of the breakwater cut black against the bruised sky. “Your dad’s still at the paper?”

“He retired. Last spring.” She hesitated, the words tasting like ash. “I saw him last week. He said… he said you fixed Mrs. Gable’s porch last summer. After the storm.”

Eli’s gaze snapped back to her, sharp, searching. “He did, did he?” A beat passed, heavy with the weight of everything unsaid—the late-night walks along the jetty, the shared thermos of terrible coffee, the way he’d held her hand when her mother died, his thumb rubbing slow circles on her knuckles until the world stopped feeling quite so hollow. And then, the morning she left. No call. No note. Just the hollow space beside her bed, the untouched mug on the kitchen counter, the silence where her voice should have been.

He shifted his weight, hands sliding into the pockets of his worn jeans. Rain dripped from the brim of his cap. “Why’d you come back, Clara?”

The directness stole her breath. Not *why are you here*, but *why’d you come back*. As if her return wasn’t just professional, but a reckoning.

“I needed to see it,” she whispered, the truth raw and sudden. “The place. The light. The way the fog rolls in off the water at dawn.” She looked down at her boots, scuffed and practical, then back up, meeting his gaze fully. “I needed to see if it still felt like home. Or if that was just something I’d made up.”

A long silence stretched, filled only by the drumming rain and the distant, mournful sigh of a freighter’s horn. Eli studied her—the slight tremor in her lower lip she couldn’t suppress, the way her knuckles whitened around the paper cup. He didn’t reach for her. Didn’t offer platitudes. He simply absorbed her, this woman who’d walked away and returned bearing a notebook and a quiet, desperate hunger.

Finally, he nodded, once. A slow, deliberate movement. “It still smells like salt and wet pine,” he said, his voice softer now, almost gentle. “And the bakery on Elm still burns the cinnamon rolls on Tuesdays.” He paused, his gaze holding hers with an intensity that made her pulse leap. “You staying at the Seaview?”

She swallowed. “For now.”

He didn’t ask how long. Didn’t say *goodbye* again. Instead, he reached into his pocket, pulled out a small, folded square of paper—slightly damp at the edges—and held it out. Not a business card. A sketch. Rough, quick pencil lines: the curve of the harbour, the jagged silhouette of the lighthouse, a single figure standing small and solitary on the headland. In the corner, in his familiar, looping script: *Where you always watched the boats leave.*

Clara took it, her fingers brushing his. His skin was warm, calloused, real. The paper felt fragile, precious, a tiny, inked bridge across ten years of rain and silence.

“Come by the yard tomorrow,” he said, turning to go. “Around noon. I’ll show you the new dry dock. And…” He paused, glancing back, rain glistening on his lashes, his expression unreadable, yet undeniably open. “…I’ll tell you about the cinnamon rolls.”

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The blizzard hit like a freight train—no warning, just white fury swallowing the horizon. Dr. Arden Finch slammed the clinic door shut behind her, breath pluming in the sudden, biting dark. Her SUV fishtailed twice before she wrestled it onto the rutted track leading to the Holloway Ranch. She wasn’t *supposed* to be here. Not tonight. But old Maggie Holloway’s border collie, Scout, had gone into sudden, violent seizures—and Arden knew, with cold certainty, that waiting until morning meant losing him.

She found Silas Holloway on the porch, boots planted, jaw set like granite, holding a lantern that cast long, trembling shadows. Snow already dusted his broad shoulders and silver-streaked stubble.

“You shouldn’t have come,” he said, voice low and rough as gravel under tires. He didn’t step aside.

“I’m here because Scout’s seizing *now*, Silas. Not ‘should’ve’—*is*.” She pushed past him, her medical bag slapping against her hip. “Where is he?”

“Barn. And don’t call me Silas. It’s Mr. Holloway. Or just ‘Holloway.’ We’re not neighbors sharing pie.”

She stopped, turned. Her green eyes, tired but sharp, locked onto his. “Scout’s convulsing in your barn, and you’re correcting my grammar? Fine. *Mr. Holloway.* Now move.”

He let out a short, humorless huff—but he moved.

Inside the barn, the air was thick with hay-dust and animal warmth, undercut by the sharp, coppery tang of fear-sweat. Scout lay on a bed of fresh straw, limbs rigid, jaw clenched, eyes rolled back. Maggie knelt beside him, trembling, her gnarled hand stroking his flank.

“He’s been like this since midnight,” Maggie whispered, tears cutting clean tracks through the grime on her cheeks. “I called you at three. You came.”

“I came because I’m paid to care,” Arden said softly, kneeling, already pulling a stethoscope from her coat. Her gloves came off with practiced speed. “But also because Scout licked my coffee cup last summer and stole half my sandwich. He’s got standards.”

A flicker—almost imperceptible—in Silas’s eyes. Then he crossed his arms. “Standards won’t stop a seizure.”

“No,” Arden agreed, pressing the stethoscope to Scout’s chest, listening past the frantic thud-thud-thud. “But phenobarbital might.” She glanced up. “I need warm water, a clean towel, and your strongest whiskey. For *me*. Not the dog.”

Silas didn’t move. “Whiskey’s for drinking, not dosing.”

“It’s for calming *me* down so I don’t scream when you hover like a disapproving thundercloud,” she shot back, her voice tight but steady. “Now, *please*.”

He stared. Then, with a grunt, he turned and strode out.

He returned with the water, the towel—and a dented tin cup half-full of amber liquid. He held it out. Their fingers didn’t touch, but the heat radiating from the cup did.

Arden took it. Sipped. Burned. Exhaled slowly. “Better.”

Silas watched her administer the IV sedative, her hands sure, efficient, gentle as she smoothed Scout’s ear. “You’re good with animals,” he said, surprising himself.

“I’m decent with scared ones,” she replied, not looking up. “People included. Though some are harder than others.”

A pause. The wind screamed against the barn walls. Snow piled against the doors with soft, insistent thuds.

“Why’d you stay?” Silas asked suddenly. “After Ben died. Everyone expected you to pack up and leave Willow Creek. It’s… quiet here. Too quiet for a city vet.”

Arden’s hand stilled for a heartbeat. Then she adjusted Scout’s IV line. “Ben loved this place. The smell of wet earth after rain. The way the light hits the ridge at dawn. He wanted to open a small practice here—not for the money, but because he believed in mending things. Broken bones. Broken fences. Broken hearts.” She met Silas’s gaze, unflinching. “I stayed to finish what he started. Not for him. For *me*.”

Silas looked away, jaw working. “Maggie says you fixed Old Man Henderson’s prize bull last spring. Even though he called you ‘that city girl with fancy gloves.’”

“He called me worse *after* I stitched his thumb back on,” she said dryly. “But yes. I fixed the bull. Because it needed fixing.”

“And you charge half what the vet in Billings does.”

“I charge what keeps the lights on and the vaccines cold,” she said, her voice softening. “And sometimes, I don’t charge at all. Like tonight.”

Silas was silent a long moment. Then he crouched, not too close, but close enough to see Scout’s breathing deepen, slow, relax. “He’s coming around.”

“Good.” She packed her kit, her movements precise. “He’ll need rest. And follow-up bloodwork tomorrow.”

Silas stood. “There won’t be a tomorrow. Not for travel.”

She looked out the barn window. The world was erased—just swirling, relentless white. “How bad?”

“Worse than forecast. County’s closed the pass. Roads buried. Power’s flickering.” He rubbed his neck. “Maggie’s got two spare rooms. One’s yours.”

She hesitated. “I can sleep in the truck.”

“The truck’s buried up to the axles. And it’s twenty below. You’ll freeze or get hypothermia. Or both.” His tone was flat, factual. Not kind. Not unkind. Just true.

She sighed, ran a hand through her wind-tangled hair. “Fine. But I’m sleeping with the door *open*. And if you so much as *look* at me sideways—”

“I look sideways at *everyone*, Doc,” he interrupted, a ghost of something—amusement?—touching his mouth. “It’s how I tell if they’re lying. Or hiding a sick calf.”

She almost smiled. Almost. “Fair enough.”

Later, in the cramped, warm bedroom—pine walls, a quilt stitched with faded blue flowers—she sat on the edge of the narrow bed, listening to the storm rage. A soft knock. Silas stood there, holding two steaming mugs.

“Maggie’s ginger tea. Strong. Said it ‘settles the nerves and the stomach.’” He didn’t enter. Just held one out.

She took it. Their fingers brushed this time. Warm. Brief. Electric.

“Thank you,” she said.

He nodded, then paused. “Scout’s going to be okay.”

“Yes,” she said, wrapping her hands around the mug. “He is.”

Silas lingered. “You know… Ben used to fix my fence posts. Always sang off-key. Drove Maggie crazy.”

She looked up, startled. “He did?”

“Yeah. Terrible tenor. But the posts were straight. And true.” He met her eyes. “So are you, Doc. Straight. True.”

The storm howled. The fire crackled. And for the first time in three years, Arden Finch didn’t feel the crushing weight of the silence left behind. She felt only the heat of the mug, the quiet strength in Silas’s steady gaze, and the fragile, undeniable warmth of something new—unfolding, stubborn as winter, tender as the first thaw.

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The streetlights cast an eerie glow on the car, making it look like a ghostly shell. Inside, tension crackled between Frank and Joey. They’d been at this for what felt like hours, but in reality, it had only been twenty minutes.

“Look, man, I’m telling you, this is our ticket out,” Frank said, his voice low and urgent. He tapped the steering wheel with his fingers, a nervous habit he couldn’t shake. “We do this, we’re set for life.”

Joey shook his head, running a hand through his greasy hair. “You’re crazy. This ain’t some small-time job. We mess up, we’re talking serious time, man. You want to spend the rest of your life in the can?”

Frank’s eyes narrowed. “And what? Keep living like this? Scrambling for chump change, looking over our shoulders every damn day? No, thanks. I want more, Joey. I deserve more.”

“Yeah, and so do I, but not like this. Kidnapping? That’s a whole different ball game. It’s not just us anymore; it’s someone else’s life. You think about that?”

Frank’s jaw clenched. “I have thought about it. And I know the risks. But the payout, Joey, it’s worth it. Think about the money, the freedom. We could be anywhere, doing anything.”

Joey’s eyes darted around the car, as if searching for an escape. “And what if something goes wrong? What if the kid gets hurt? Or worse? You think you can live with that?”

Frank’s hands tightened on the steering wheel, his knuckles turning white. “Nothing’s gonna go wrong. We’ve got it all planned out. We get in, grab the kid, make the call, and collect the cash. Simple as that.”

“Simple?” Joey snorted. “You really think it’s that easy? These people, they’ve got connections. They’ll find us. And when they do, they won’t be calling the cops. They’ll be sending their own guys, and you know what happens then.”

Frank’s face darkened. “So, what, we just give up? Go back to our crappy apartments and dead-end jobs? Is that what you want, Joey? Because I sure as hell don’t.”

Joey sighed, rubbing his temples. “I don’t want that either, but there’s gotta be another way. Something less... dangerous. We could—”

“Could what?” Frank interrupted, his voice rising. “Rob a few more stores? Bust open a couple more safes? It’s never gonna be enough, Joey. Not unless we take a big risk. And this is it. This is our chance.”

Joey leaned back in his seat, staring out the window. The city was quiet, almost peaceful. But he knew better. The calm was just a facade, a thin veneer over the chaos and danger that lurked beneath. “What if we get caught, Frank? What if the kid talks, or someone sees us, or—”

“We won’t get caught. We’re careful, we’re smart. And we’re desperate. That’s what makes us dangerous. That’s what makes us untouchable.”

Joey’s gaze shifted back to Frank, his expression torn. “I don’t know, man. I just... I don’t know if I can do it. If I can live with the guilt, the fear. Every day, thinking about it, knowing—”

“Then don’t think about it,” Frank snapped. “Think about the future. Think about the life we can have. We do this, we’re free. We’re rich. We’re out of this hellhole for good.”

Joey closed his eyes, taking a deep breath. When he opened them again, there was a resigned look in them, a mix of fear and determination. “Okay, Frank. Okay. But if we do this, we do it right. No screw-ups. No mistakes. Got it?”

Frank nodded, a grim smile tugging at the corners of his mouth. “Got it. We do it right. And we walk away clean. This is our shot, Joey. Our one shot. Let’s make it count.”

The two men sat in silence for a moment, the weight of their decision pressing down on them. Then, without another word, Frank started the car, and they pulled away from the curb, driving into the night, their fates hanging in the balance.

title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
The air in the Observation Dome tasted stale—recycled too many times, carrying the faint metallic tang of aging filters and the ghost of ozone from the ship’s humming core. Outside the curved transparisteel, stars didn’t streak. They hung, fixed and indifferent, in the velvet black. For seventy-three years, they’d been the crew’s only horizon.

Commander Elara Voss stood with her back to the view, arms crossed, her uniform tunic crisp despite the low gravity’s soft tug. Around her, the senior bridge crew formed a tight, silent semicircle: Dr. Kenji Sato, head of life sciences, fingers white where they gripped his tablet; Engineer Mira Chen, her usual calm replaced by a rigid stillness; and Lieutenant Ravi Desai, navigation specialist, staring at the central holo-display as if it might dissolve.

The display showed the *Odyssey*’s projected course—a clean, unwavering vector toward Proxima Centauri b. The destination that had been etched into every schoolbook, whispered at every memorial service for those who’d died en route, promised in every captain’s log for three generations.

Elara tapped her comm. “Captain Reyes. Report to Observation Dome. Now.”

The silence stretched, thick and brittle. Then the dome’s inner door hissed open. Captain Aris Reyes entered. He moved with his usual unhurried grace, silver hair neatly combed, the deep blue of his command insignia gleaming under the soft lights. His smile was warm, practiced. “Commander. Everyone. What’s the urgency?”

Elara didn’t return the smile. She gestured to the holo-display. “Explain this.”

Reyes followed her gaze. His expression didn’t flicker. “It’s our course. Proxima b. As scheduled.”

“Scheduled?” Mira’s voice was low, sharp as a scalpel. She stepped forward, her tablet projecting a secondary overlay onto the main display—a complex, layered data stream showing gravitational anomalies, stellar drift corrections, and a subtle, persistent deviation in the ship’s inertial guidance logs. “This ‘scheduled’ course has been drifting *away* from Proxima for the last seventeen years, Captain. Not a navigational error. A deliberate, cumulative course correction. Every single one logged under your personal authorization.”

Reyes’s smile thinned. “Course refinements are standard. Stellar dust density, minor relativistic effects—”

“Seventeen years,” Kenji interrupted, his voice quiet but cutting through the hum of the life-support systems. “Seventeen years of ‘refinements’ that shift us deeper into the interstellar void. Not toward a star system, Captain. Toward *nothing*. The nearest viable system on this trajectory is Gliese 667 Cc. And we won’t reach it for another 142 years. Our current supplies? We’ll exhaust them in eighty-seven.”

A beat passed. The stars outside seemed to press closer.

Ravi finally looked up. His face was pale. “I ran the numbers again last night. Triple-checked. The original launch vector… it was real. But the first major recalibration—Year 56, after the third reactor surge—it wasn’t about shielding. It was about *turning*. A slow, steady turn away from Proxima. Like we were… avoiding it.”

Reyes exhaled slowly, the warmth draining from his eyes, leaving behind something weary and ancient. He walked to the edge of the dome, placing a palm flat against the cool transparisteel, staring not at the stars, but at his own faint reflection. “You’re right,” he said, the words landing like stones in the quiet. “The course is false.”

Elara’s breath hitched. “Why?”

Reyes turned. His gaze swept over them—not with defiance, but with a profound, bone-deep sorrow. “Because Proxima Centauri b isn’t habitable. It never was.”

Mira recoiled. “That’s impossible. The pre-launch surveys—”

“Were wrong,” Reyes said, his voice flat. “Catastrophically wrong. The atmospheric analysis was contaminated. The magnetic field readings were misinterpreted. By the time the *Odyssey* launched, the truth was buried under layers of political necessity and institutional denial. Sending a generation ship to a dead rock would have shattered Earth’s last hope. So they sent us to a myth. And they entrusted me with the truth—and the lie.”

Kenji stared, horrified. “You’ve known… all this time?”

“Since Year Two,” Reyes said softly. “When the long-range probes we deployed—probes programmed to *confirm* the data—sent back their final transmission. Not just confirmation. Correction. Detailed spectral analysis. Surface temperature gradients. Radiation flux maps. Proxima b is a scorched, tidally locked wasteland. No liquid water. No stable atmosphere. No chance.”

Silence swallowed the dome. The hum of the ship felt louder now, a relentless, mocking pulse.

“So why keep sailing?” Ravi whispered, the question raw. “Why not turn back? Or… or find another target?”

Reyes met Elara’s gaze. There was no apology in his eyes, only exhaustion and a terrible, unyielding resolve. “Because turning back is suicide. We lack the fuel, the structural integrity, the psychological resilience to reverse course across 4.2 light-years. And ‘another target’?” He gave a humorless, brief shake of his head. “Every viable candidate within range requires decades more travel than we have life support. Gliese 667 Cc is marginally better, yes—but its biosignature is ambiguous, its stability unproven. And we are *here*. This ship is our world. Its systems, its people, its fragile, hard-won ecosystem—they are all we have. To abandon the mission *now*, to admit the lie publicly…” He paused, his voice dropping to a near-whisper. “It would fracture us. It would end us before the void ever could.”

Elara looked at her crew—the scientist, the engineer, the navigator—their faces illuminated by the cold, false light of the holo-display. She looked at the stars, no longer distant promises, but indifferent witnesses to a colossal, generations-long deception.

Her voice, when she spoke, was steady, stripped bare. “So what do we do, Captain?”

Reyes turned fully to face them, his hand still resting on the dome’s cold surface. “We keep sailing,” he said. “We maintain the lie. We preserve the ship. And we pray… that somewhere out there, in the dark between the stars, we find something real.”

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
Chapter Seven  

The bathroom door was ajar. Not *slightly* ajar—like a polite suggestion of privacy—but *gaped*, as if the hinges themselves had sighed in surrender. And there, framed by the warped oak trim and the faint, lingering scent of lavender-scented mildew remover, stood Reginald.  

Reginald the horse.  

Not a statue. Not a hallucination induced by three consecutive nights of oat-milk lattes and existential dread. A full-grown, chestnut-coated, slightly underweight, and deeply unimpressed horse, one hoof resting thoughtfully on the rim of the bathtub, his tail swishing with the quiet, rhythmic disdain of someone who has just been asked to explain quantum entanglement at 7:15 a.m.  

I cleared my throat. It came out as a squeak.  

My client, Ms. Penelope Thistledown—barrister, widow, owner of three impeccably groomed Persian cats and, apparently, a sudden, inexplicable equine tenant—stood beside me in the hallway, clutching a steaming mug of chamomile tea like it was a talisman against reality’s collapse. Her left eyebrow had achieved liftoff. Her right hand hovered near her temple, fingers twitching, as if calculating the precise millisecond before she’d need to dial her neurologist.  

“Mr. Finch,” she said, voice brittle as dried sage. “You told me you specialised in *energetic dissonance*. Not… *zoological trespass*.”  

“I did,” I said, adjusting my hemp-and-copper cufflinks (non-ferrous, obviously—they interfere with auric resonance). “And Reginald is precisely that. A symptom. A very large, warm-blooded, mildly judgmental symptom.”  

She took a slow sip. Her eyes didn’t blink. “He’s standing in my *bathtub*, Mr. Finch. With what appears to be a damp towel draped over his rump. Which I *definitely* did not place there.”  

“No,” I murmured, stepping carefully into the threshold—not crossing it yet, just *hovering*, like a man testing water temperature before committing to a metaphysical plunge. “That would be the *sacred towel*. Used only for grounding during lunar alignment. Or when a horse feels emotionally exposed.”  

Penelope lowered the mug. “Emotionally *exposed*?”  

“Observe,” I whispered, gesturing subtly—not with my hand, but with my *intention*, which, according to my third chakra, should be calibrated to gentle inquiry, not accusation. Reginald lifted his head. His dark, liquid eye swivelled toward me. Not hostile. Not friendly. Just… *assessing*. Like a librarian spotting a patron attempting to check out the Dewey Decimal System *and* the entire cookbook section.  

“He’s not *in* your bathroom, Penelope,” I began, voice softening into the low, resonant hum I reserve for explaining why the universe is both infinitely complex and fundamentally kind. “He’s *with* it. In relationship to it. The tub isn’t a vessel for water anymore—it’s become a *vessel for stillness*. He sensed the stagnation in your upper-floor plumbing—the gurgle in the pipes last Tuesday? That wasn’t a blockage. That was grief. Unprocessed. Your late husband’s favourite loofah is still in the shower caddy, yes? You haven’t touched it in seventeen months. The energy there has curdled. Thickened. Like cold honey.”  

Penelope blinked. Once. Slowly. “The loofah is *pink*.”  

“And *charged*,” I affirmed. “With memory, with absence, with the unresolved vibration of ‘I meant to ask him about the garden shed roof’. Reginald doesn’t *do* logic. He does *resonance*. Horses are walking tuning forks for the human soul’s unspoken frequencies. He didn’t *choose* your bathroom. He was *drawn* to the epicentre of your emotional static. The tile is cool, the air is humid, the mirror is fogged—*perfect conditions for mirroring*. He’s holding space for what you’re not saying aloud.”  

She stared at Reginald. Reginald stared back. A long, silent negotiation occurred. It involved nostril flares and the subtle shifting of weight. I held my breath. My own chakras vibrated sympathetically—my root chakra hummed like a contented bumblebee; my solar plexus fluttered, uncertain whether to assert dominance or offer biscuits.  

Then Penelope exhaled. A real breath. Deep. Shaky. “He… he looks tired.”  

“He *is* tired,” I said, warmth blooming in my chest. “Of carrying your silence. Of being the only witness to the way you pause before opening the medicine cabinet. Of hearing you whisper ‘Arthur’ to the kettle every morning.”  

Reginald snorted. A soft, wet, profoundly *human* sound. Then, with infinite dignity, he stepped *out* of the tub, placed all four hooves squarely on the bathmat (a plush, avocado-green monstrosity), and lowered his head to nuzzle the hem of Penelope’s cashmere cardigan.  

She froze. Then, very slowly, she set the mug down on the sink ledge. Her hand, trembling only slightly, rose—not to push him away, but to rest, palm flat, against the warm, velvety curve of his cheekbone.  

“He smells like rain and hay,” she whispered.  

“And forgiveness,” I murmured.  

She didn’t look at me. She kept her gaze locked on Reginald’s eye—the one that held galaxies and grocery lists and the quiet, terrible weight of widowhood. “So… what do we *do*?”  

I smiled. Not the knowing smile of the enlightened sage. The weary, tender, slightly absurd smile of a man who’d just spent forty-three minutes explaining equine empathic intervention to a barrister while standing barefoot on a damp bathmat.  

“Well,” I said, pulling a small, smooth river stone from my pocket—obsidian, for grounding—“first, we apologise to the plumbing. Then, we find Reginald some oats. Organic. Unbleached. And Penelope?”  

She finally glanced at me. Her eyes were bright. Not with tears. With something far more dangerous: *recognition*.  

“Yes?”  

I held up the stone. “The loofah stays. But maybe… just maybe… tonight, you rinse it. Gently. While humming. Any tune. Even ‘God Save the Queen’.”  

Reginald sighed. A deep, rumbling sound that shook dust from the ceiling light fixture.  

And somewhere, deep in the walls, a pipe stopped gurgling.  

Just for a moment.  

Just enough.

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
The neon sign outside the diner flickered, casting an erratic glow over the cracked asphalt. Inside, the air was thick with the smell of grease and burnt coffee. Jake Marston, a man whose life had been defined by shadows and silence, sat in a corner booth, his back to the wall. The worn leather jacket he wore seemed almost too big for him, but it carried the weight of years spent in places no one wanted to remember. His eyes, sharp and wary, scanned the room, a habit from days when danger lurked around every corner.

The bell above the door jingled, announcing the arrival of three men. They were dressed in dark suits, their faces hard and unyielding, like stone carvings come to life. The diner’s regulars—truckers, locals, and the occasional traveler—paused, sensing the tension that followed them in. Jake’s hand instinctively moved under the table, fingers brushing against the cold metal of his gun, hidden in a holster beneath his jacket.

“Evening, folks,” the lead man said, his voice smooth but with an edge that cut through the low hum of conversation. “We’re looking for someone. Name’s Jack Marlowe.”

A waitress, her name tag reading ‘Sally,’ looked up from behind the counter, her eyes wide. “Jack Marlowe? I ain’t seen anyone like that, mister. You sure you got the right place?”

The man’s gaze swept the room, landing on Jake. “You see, we’ve been tracking this guy for a while. He’s got some... unfinished business with us. And I think our friend here might know something about it.” He took a step closer, his eyes narrowing. “Aren’t you a little far from home, Jack?”

Jake’s heart pounded, but his face remained impassive. “I think you’ve got the wrong guy. My name is Jake Marston, and I’m just passing through.”

The second man, a towering figure with a scar running down his cheek, stepped forward. “Save the lies, Marlowe. We’ve got your file. Ex-military, dishonorably discharged. Sound familiar?”

Jake’s mind raced. He knew he couldn’t outfight all three, not in a crowded diner. But he also knew he couldn’t let them take him. Not without a fight. “I don’t know who you think I am, but I’m not Jack Marlowe. Maybe you should double-check your intel.”

The third man, a wiry individual with a cruel smile, pulled out a photograph and held it up. “This is the guy we’re after. See the resemblance?” The photo showed a man who could have been Jake’s doppelgänger, but there was something in the eyes, a hardness that Jake didn’t recognize.

Jake leaned back, trying to buy time. “Look, I get it. You’re chasing a ghost. But I’m not your man. Why don’t you sit down, have a cup of coffee, and we can talk this out?”

The lead man’s expression hardened. “We don’t have time for games. Stand up, Marlowe. We’re taking you in, one way or another.”

Jake’s hand tightened on the grip of his gun. He knew what would happen if he drew it; the diner would erupt into chaos. Innocent people could get hurt. But he also knew that these men wouldn’t stop. They would drag him out, and he’d never see the light of day again.

Sally, the waitress, seemed to sense the escalating tension. She slowly reached for the phone, her eyes darting between Jake and the men. “Maybe you boys should calm down. This is a nice place. No need for trouble.”

The lead man turned to her, his voice low and menacing. “Stay out of this, ma’am. This is between us and him.”

Jake saw his chance. In a fluid motion, he slid out of the booth, his hand still on the gun. “Alright, let’s do this. But not here. Let’s take this outside, where we won’t bother anyone.”

The men exchanged a glance, then nodded. As they moved toward the door, Jake felt the weight of the diner’s eyes on him. He knew he had only one shot at this. One chance to turn the tables and make it out alive.

Outside, the night air was cool, and the street was empty. The neon sign flickered once more, as if signaling the start of a deadly game.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The air in the Casino de Monte-Carlo’s Salon Privé tasted like cold money and old perfume—sandalwood, bergamot, and the faint, metallic tang of sweat beneath starched collars. Not the tourist-floor air, thick with cigar smoke and desperation, but this: hushed, lacquered, expensive. A place where silence wasn’t empty; it was *loaded*.  

Elias Thorne sat at the baccarat table, his left hand resting lightly on the green felt, fingers spread just so—not relaxed, not tense, but *anchored*. His right held a tumbler of Glenfiddich 18, neat, the ice long gone, the amber liquid catching the low, gilded light from the Murano glass chandelier overhead. He wore a Brioni suit the colour of wet slate, cut sharp enough to draw blood. His tie—a narrow, midnight-blue silk—was knotted with the careless precision of a man who’d tied one every morning for seventeen years.  

Across the table, Lucien Dubois smiled. Not broadly. A slow, vertical lift at the corners of his mouth, like a seam splitting. His teeth were very white. His eyes were the colour of river stones after rain—grey, opaque, unreflective. He wore a cream linen jacket, sleeves rolled to the elbows, revealing forearms corded with muscle that looked more suited to hauling rigging than signing bearer bonds. His watch was a Patek Philippe Calatrava, platinum, no date window. The kind of watch that didn’t tell time so much as *assert* its own permanence.  

Dubois wasn’t French. He was Swiss-born, raised in Geneva, educated at ETH Zurich, and had spent the last eight years laundering money through shell companies registered in the Caymans, Liechtenstein, and—according to a single, brittle source inside Swisscom—three dormant accounts linked to a logistics firm in Minsk. That firm shipped “industrial lubricants” to a decommissioned textile plant outside Grodno. Satellite imagery showed no trucks entering. Only vans. Unmarked. Grey.  

Thorne hadn’t seen the vans. He’d seen the satellite feed, grainy and cold, on a monitor in a safe house in Nice. He’d smelled the damp wool of his coat that night, heard the distant wail of a siren cutting through the Mediterranean fog.  

The dealer—a woman named Colette, with silver hair pinned tight and hands that moved like clockwork—dealt. Two cards each. Thorne’s: six, three. Seven. Dubois’s: king, five. Fifteen. He drew. A four. Nineteen.  

Thorne didn’t blink. He pushed forward a stack of €5,000 chips. Black. Not flashy. Just… present.  

Dubois mirrored him. Exact stack. Exact placement. His thumbnail, filed short and blunt, tapped the top chip once. *Tap.* Like a metronome counting down.  

Colette dealt again. Thorne: ace, queen. Eleven. He drew. A seven. Eighteen.  

Dubois: jack, nine. Nineteen.  

No draw.  

Dubois leaned back, just a fraction. His chair creaked—a dry, papery sound. He lifted his glass—mineral water, no ice—and took a slow sip. His throat moved. A pulse flickered at his jawline. Thorne watched it. Not the face. The *pulse*. It was steady. Too steady.  

A waiter appeared, silent as dust, offering canapés on a silver tray. Caviar on blinis. Smoked salmon on rye. Thorne declined with a slight shake of his head. Dubois took two blinis. Ate them slowly, chewing with his mouth closed. Wiped his lower lip with a monogrammed napkin—*L.D.* in faded navy thread.  

The next hand. Thorne: three, five. Eight. No draw.  

Dubois: seven, two. Nine.  

Dubois won. He didn’t smile. Didn’t touch the chips. Just let Colette push them across. His fingers remained folded in his lap. Thorne watched the backs of Dubois’s hands. Veins like blue pencil lines under pale skin. A thin, silvery scar ran from the base of his left thumb, disappearing beneath the cuff of his shirt. Not surgical. Not accidental. A clean, deliberate cut. Old.  

Thorne remembered a file photo—blurred, taken from a distance outside a Zurich bank. Dubois stepping into a black Mercedes. Same scar. Same cuff.  

The dealer shuffled. The cards whispered—rasping, intimate. Thorne’s knuckles were white where he gripped his tumbler. Not from tension. From *cold*. A deep, marrow-cold that had nothing to do with the air conditioning. It was the cold of knowing you’re looking at the hinge—the exact, unblinking point where money becomes bullets, and bullets become names crossed off lists written in fading ink.  

Third hand. Thorne: four, six. Ten. Draw. A three. Thirteen.  

Dubois: five, eight. Thirteen.  

Tie.  

Colette placed the tie bet—€10,000—on the centre of the table. Dubois didn’t move. Thorne didn’t move. They watched the dealer deal the tie cards. One for Thorne. A nine. One for Dubois. A four.  

Thorne exhaled. A short, soft release. Like steam from a valve.  

Dubois’s left eye twitched. Not a blink. A micro-spasm. Barely there. A tremor in the lid. Lasted half a second. Thorne saw it. Felt it land in his gut like a pebble dropped down a well.  

The dealer dealt again. Thorne: seven. Dubois: queen.  

Thorne won.  

He didn’t reach for the chips. Let Colette slide them over. Watched Dubois’s hands. Still folded. Still still. But the pulse at his jaw—Thorne saw it now—had quickened. Just a fraction. A tiny, frantic flutter beneath the skin.  

Dubois finally looked up. Not at Thorne’s face. At his left hand, resting on the felt. At the wedding band Thorne wore—not gold, but platinum, plain, slightly worn on the inner edge. A detail. A habit. A lie he’d worn for twelve years, ever since Eleanor died in a car crash outside Cheltenham that smelled suspiciously of brake fluid and silence.  

Dubois held Thorne’s gaze for three seconds. Then looked down at his own hands. Turned his left palm up. Stared at the scar.  

A bell chimed—soft, resonant—from the far end of the salon. Midnight.  

Dubois stood. Smooth, unhurried. Adjusted his jacket. Didn’t glance at the chips Thorne had just won. Didn’t say goodbye. Just walked toward the heavy velvet curtain that led to the private elevator bank, his footsteps swallowed by the carpet before they even began.  

Thorne stayed seated. Drank the last of the whisky. It burned, clean and bitter.  

He reached into his inside pocket. Not for his phone. For a small, folded square of paper—cream-coloured, thick stock. A receipt from the Hôtel Hermitage. Room 412. Paid in cash. Checked in at 3:17 p.m. Checked out at 4:02 p.m. No luggage retrieved.  

He didn’t unfold it. Just held it between thumb and forefinger, feeling the embossed hotel crest, the slight ridge of the ink.  

Then he slid it back into his pocket.  

The dealer cleared the table. The chips clinked. Somewhere, a woman laughed—too loud, too late.  

Thorne ordered another Glenfiddich. Neat.  

He didn’t look at the door Dubois had vanished through.  

He looked at his own reflection in the polished mahogany rail beside the table. Pale. Tired. Eyes the colour of London pavement after rain.  

And waited.

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The knocking stopped.

Silence rushed in—thick, wet, *wrong*. Not the usual groan of wind through broken skylights or the skitter-scrape of rats in the cereal aisle. This silence had weight. It pressed against eardrums. Made teeth ache.

Jax froze mid-sip, lukewarm coffee sloshing over his knuckles. His breath hitched. Didn’t come back.

“Did you—?” Maya whispered. Her voice cracked like dry plaster. She didn’t finish. Didn’t need to.

They all heard it. All *felt* it—the hollow, rhythmic *thump-thump-thump* against the steel roll-up door at the loading dock. Not frantic. Not desperate. Steady. Patient. Like someone testing a door handle they already knew was locked.

*Thump.*

Lena dropped her wrench. It clanged on the concrete floor, sharp and stupidly loud. She didn’t pick it up. Just stared at the heavy-duty padlock on the dock door—the one *they’d* welded shut two days ago. The one *they’d* sealed with duct tape and plywood and three layers of chain-link fencing pulled from the garden center next door. The one *they’d* reinforced after burying Eli.

Eli.

His name hit Jax like a fist in the gut. Cold sweat pricked his scalp under his greasy baseball cap. He remembered Eli’s face—pale, slack, eyes wide open and milky-blue in the flashlight beam as they lowered him into the shallow grave behind the dumpster. Remembered the way his left hand had flopped sideways, fingers splayed, *just so*, when the dirt hit his chest. Remembered Lena sobbing, not for Eli, but because she’d dropped the shovel twice and couldn’t get the hole deep enough before the first moan came from the parking lot.

*Thump.*

Maya’s hand flew to her mouth. Her eyes darted to the security monitor mounted crookedly above the register. Grainy black-and-white feed showed the loading dock bay: empty. Just rain-streaked glass, the rusted dumpster, the dark mouth of the alley beyond. No figure. No movement. Just static hiss and the slow crawl of condensation down the screen.

“Could be… could be the wind,” Lena breathed. Her voice trembled, thin as old paper. “Or a branch. Or—”

“Wind don’t knock *three times*,” Jax said. His voice was gravel scraped raw. He set the coffee cup down. Didn’t look at anyone. Just watched the monitor. Watched the empty bay. Watched the static pulse like a dying heartbeat.

Another sound cut through the silence.

A low, wet *scrape*. Like something dragging itself across concrete. Slow. Deliberate. Coming from *under* the dock door.

Lena whimpered. A tiny, animal sound.

Jax moved. Fast. Silent. He grabbed the fire axe leaning by the freezer doors—cold steel, familiar weight. Maya fumbled for her pistol, hands shaking so bad the slide rattled. Lena backed up, bumping into stacked pallets of canned beans. A can clattered to the floor. *Ping.* Loud. Stupid.

Then—a voice.

Not loud. Not shouting.

A whisper. Thin. Guttural. Like stones grinding in a throat full of mud.

*“Jax…?”*

Jax went ice-cold. Every hair on his arms stood up. That wasn’t Eli’s voice. Not the Eli who laughed too loud at bad jokes, who always shared his last protein bar. This was *wrong*. Flattened. Hollowed out. Like listening to a recording played backward through a broken speaker.

*“Maya…? Lena…?”*

Maya choked. Dropped the pistol. It clattered on the tile. She didn’t reach for it. Just stared at the dock door, tears cutting clean tracks through the grime on her cheeks.

*“Let me in.”*

The words weren’t pleading. They were *stating*. Like reading a grocery list. Like asking for milk.

Lena made a small, broken sound and stumbled toward the back exit—the one that led to the employee parking lot. Jax didn’t stop her. Couldn’t. His eyes were locked on the monitor. The static flickered violently. For half a second—*less*—the image resolved.

Not Eli’s face.

Just a hand. Pale. Swollen. Fingernails blackened and split. Pressed flat against the inside of the glass panel beside the dock door. Fingers twitched. Once.

Then the screen dissolved into snow.

The knocking started again.

*Thump-thump-thump.*

Steady.

Patient.

Right on the other side of the steel.

Jax raised the axe. His knuckles were white. His breath came in short, hot bursts. He didn’t know if he’d swing at the door. At the glass. At the whispering thing outside. Or at himself.

Because the worst part?

He *recognized* that pause between knocks.

It was exactly how Eli used to count before he threw a fastball.

Three seconds.

Always three seconds.

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
The old farmhouse creaked and groaned as the wind swept across the fields, rustling through the tall grass. The sky was a deep, ominous gray, and the air carried the scent of rain. Inside, the Carter family—John, Sarah, and their two children, Emily and Jake—were busy unpacking boxes in the living room. The house, with its high ceilings and wooden beams, felt both spacious and oppressive, as if it were watching them.

"Mom, can we go outside and explore?" Emily asked, her eyes wide with excitement. She was ten, with long brown hair and an adventurous spirit.

"Sure, but stay close to the house," Sarah replied, wiping her hands on her jeans. "And keep an eye on your brother."

Emily nodded and grabbed Jake's hand, pulling him toward the back door. Jake, who was only six, followed reluctantly, his small frame hunched over slightly. He had always been more cautious, more sensitive to the strange and the unknown.

As they stepped out into the yard, the sound of digging caught their attention. It was coming from the cellar, a small, windowless structure attached to the side of the house. The previous owners had mentioned that their dog, a large, shaggy black Labrador named Max, had developed an obsession with digging in the cellar. They had tried everything to stop him, but nothing seemed to work. In the end, they had given up and moved away, leaving the dog behind with the new owners.

"Listen, Em," Jake said, tugging on his sister's sleeve. "It sounds like Max is still digging."

Emily frowned. "Dad said Max went to live with a neighbor. Maybe it's just a stray."

They approached the cellar, and the sound grew louder. It was a rhythmic, persistent scratching, like claws against dirt. Emily reached for the handle of the cellar door, but Jake held her back.

"I don't think we should go in there," he whispered, his voice trembling. "It doesn't feel right."

"Nonsense," Emily said, though she too felt a chill run down her spine. She opened the door, and the musty smell of earth and dampness wafted out. A single bare bulb hung from the ceiling, casting a dim, flickering light. The walls were lined with shelves, some holding old jars and tools, others empty and dusty.

In the center of the room, a large hole had been dug into the dirt floor. The soil was piled up around it, and the sound of digging continued, but there was no sign of any dog. The hole was deep, and something about it made Emily's heart race.

"Jake, do you see anything?" she asked, her voice barely above a whisper.

"No," Jake replied, his eyes fixed on the hole. "But I hear it. It's still digging."

Suddenly, the sound stopped. The silence was deafening, and the air seemed to grow colder. Emily took a step forward, peering into the darkness at the bottom of the hole. Then, without warning, a low, guttural growl echoed from within.

"Let's get out of here!" Jake shouted, grabbing his sister's arm and pulling her back. They stumbled out of the cellar, slamming the door shut behind them. The sound of digging resumed, muffled now, but unmistakable.

Inside the house, John and Sarah were in the kitchen, discussing where to place the furniture. The sound of the cellar door slamming made them look up.

"Did you hear that?" Sarah asked, her brow furrowed with concern.

"Yeah, I did," John said, setting down a cup of coffee. "I'll go check on the kids. You stay here."

He walked to the back door and found Emily and Jake standing by the cellar, their faces pale and frightened.

"What happened?" John asked, kneeling down to their level.

"There's something in the cellar, Dad," Emily said, her voice shaking. "It was digging, and then it growled at us."

John looked at the closed door, a sense of unease settling in his stomach. "Stay here," he said, standing up. "I'll take a look."

He opened the cellar door, and the sound of digging immediately ceased. The light inside flickered, and for a moment, John thought he saw a shadow move at the edge of his vision. He took a deep breath and descended the steps, his heart pounding in his chest.

The hole in the center of the room was deeper than he had expected, and the air was thick with the stench of decay. As he approached, a cold, clammy hand suddenly shot out of the darkness, grabbing his ankle. John let out a cry of surprise and fell to the ground, scrambling backward. The hand retreated, and the sound of digging resumed, more frantic and desperate than before.

John scrambled to his feet and rushed out of the cellar, slamming the door behind him. He turned to face his family, his face pale and sweat-drenched.

"We need to leave," he said, his voice hoarse. "Now."

Sarah's eyes widened, and she nodded, understanding the gravity of the situation. They quickly gathered what they could, piling into the car and driving away from the farmhouse, the sound of digging echoing in their minds, a haunting reminder of the horrors that lay beneath.

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The rain in Venice doesn’t fall—it *settles*. A cold, greasy film on the back of your throat, a damp that seeps into your bones before you’ve even stepped outside. I watched it blur the canal beyond my office window, turning the distant campanile into a smudge of grey watercolour. My coffee was cold. The third cup. The mug felt like a stone in my hands.

*She’s late.*

Not by much. Five minutes. But in this city, where time is measured in tides and the slow drip of water from a crumbling cornice, five minutes feels like a held breath. Especially when you’re waiting for Elena Vianello.

I’d seen her photograph—taken at the funeral, no doubt. Pale hair coiled tight, black veil pinned just so, eyes downcast, hands folded like a saint in a chapel fresco. A widow’s mask. Perfectly applied. I’d studied it for ten minutes this morning, tracing the slight tension at the corner of her mouth, the unnatural stillness of her jaw. Not grief. Not yet. Something else. Something… calibrated.

The knock came—light, precise, three taps. Not hesitant. Not trembling. Confident. Almost courteous.

“Avanti,” I said, not looking up. Let her feel the weight of the silence first.

The door opened. She didn’t enter immediately. She stood in the frame, letting the dim corridor light halo her silhouette—a woman carved from moonlight and marble. Then she stepped in, closing the door with a soft, decisive click. No rustle of wet fabric. Her coat was dry. Impeccably tailored charcoal wool, shoulders sharp as knife-edges. Her hair, the colour of spun ash, was pulled back severely, revealing the elegant, unlined curve of her neck. Her eyes—pale green, like shallow lagoon water over limestone—met mine. Direct. Unblinking.

“Commissario Rossi,” she said. Her voice was low, clear, devoid of tremor. Like a cello note held perfectly, without vibrato.

“Signora Vianello.” I gestured to the chair opposite my desk. “Please.”

She moved with quiet economy, settling into the chair without a whisper of friction. She placed a small, structured leather bag on her lap, fingers resting lightly on its clasp. Not clasped. Not fidgeting. Just… resting.

I didn’t offer more coffee. Didn’t ask about the weather. The silence stretched, thin and taut, filled only by the distant, mournful groan of a vaporetto engine churning through the fog-shrouded Grand Canal. I watched her. Watched the way her gaze swept the room—not searching, not nervous, but *assessing*. The framed photo of my daughter on the shelf (a rare lapse in protocol, but I’d left it there after her last visit). The stack of reports beside my keyboard. The faint, stubborn stain on the edge of my desk where ink had bled through a report months ago. She noted them all. Catalogued them.

*Relieved*, I thought again. The word echoed, hollow and insistent. Not relieved *that he’s gone*. That would be monstrous. But relieved *of something*. Of a weight? A vigil? A performance?

“You received the preliminary findings?” I asked, my voice deliberately neutral, flat as the surface of the lagoon at dawn.

She nodded once. A small, precise movement. “Yes. The fall from the balcony. The broken railing. The… absence of defensive wounds.” Her lips barely moved on the last phrase. *Absence of defensive wounds.* She knew the terminology. Knew what it implied. Not a struggle. Not an accident fought against. Just… surrender. Or acceptance.

“Did you see him that evening?” I asked, leaning forward slightly, resting my elbows on the desk, steepling my fingers. A posture of attention, not accusation. Yet.

“I saw him leave the apartment around seven-thirty,” she said. Her voice hadn’t changed pitch. Hadn’t wavered. “He said he was meeting friends for a drink at Florian’s. He often did.”

“Often?” I repeated softly.

A flicker. Not in her eyes, but in the very corner of her left nostril. A minute, involuntary flare. Like steam escaping a valve. “Yes. Often.”

“And you stayed home?”

“I read. A novel. By Simenon.” She offered the title as if it were evidence. Proof of ordinary domesticity. *A novel. By Simenon.*

I picked up a pen. Not to write. Just to hold it. To give my hands something to do while my mind raced. *Simenon.* The master of quiet despair. The architect of perfect, suffocating marriages. Did she choose it for irony? For camouflage? Or because it mirrored the air in her own home—the thick, silent pressure before the storm broke?

“The railing,” I said, setting the pen down with deliberate softness. “It was old. Corroded. We found traces of fresh paint near the break point. On the underside. As if someone had tried to cover the rust recently. But not well enough.”

Her gaze didn’t waver. It held mine, steady, green and cool. But her knuckles, where her fingers rested on the bag’s clasp, whitened. Just a fraction. A tiny, tell-tale tightening in the tendons.

“Rust,” she murmured. Her voice was still calm, but a new texture had entered it—thin, brittle, like ice over deep, dark water. “Venice eats everything. Stone. Wood. Metal. Even… people.” She paused. A beat longer than necessary. Her eyes didn’t leave mine. “Especially people who forget how fragile things are here, Commissario. How easily the foundations shift. How quickly the water rises.”

She leaned back, just a fraction, the sharp line of her collarbone stark against the charcoal wool. A small, almost imperceptible sigh escaped her. Not a sob. Not a gasp. A release. A long, slow exhalation, as if she’d been holding her breath for weeks, months, years.

And in that sigh, I heard it. Not grief. Not shock. Not fear.

Resignation. And beneath it, a terrifying, chilling echo: *Finally.*

The rain streaked the window behind her, blurring the world outside into a watercolour smear of grey and brown. Inside, the air felt suddenly, profoundly still. Heavy. Charged. Like the hush before lightning strikes the campanile.

I didn’t speak. I just watched her breathe. And wondered, with a cold certainty that settled deeper than the Venetian damp, what exactly she had just released.

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
The dust in the air tasted like burnt copper and old blood. Inside the *Iron Maw*, Sergeant Vanya Rostova wiped grease from her temple with the back of a gloved hand, leaving a smudge of cerulean coolant across her skin. Outside the reinforced quartz viewport, the sky over Helios-7’s Mare Obscura wasn’t sky at all—just a bruised, churning ceiling of ochre cloud, lit from below by the sickly orange pulse of the colony’s geothermal vents. Below that, the mining complex sprawled: skeletal ore-sifters, pressurized hab-domes like cracked pearls, and the long, low hump of Refinery Gamma—her objective, her tomb if she failed.

“Thermal bloom at three o’clock,” said Kael, voice flat, fingers dancing over the sensor console. His eyes hadn’t left the thermal overlay projected onto his visor. “Eighteen… no, twenty-three contacts. Main body’s still beyond ridge-line Alpha. But the scouts—*they’re moving fast.*”

Vanya leaned forward, her spine creaking inside the armored harness. On the main display, heat signatures bloomed like spilled mercury: lean, angular shapes skittering down the basalt scree—Scythe-class assault crawlers, each one barely larger than a grav-bike but bristling with phased plasma cutters and micro-missile pods. Behind them, the ground trembled—not from seismic activity, but from the deep, resonant thud of heavy walkers. Three Goliath Mk.IV chassis, their articulated legs punching craters into the regolith with every stride. Each carried twin railgun turrets, their barrels glowing faintly violet with capacitive charge.

“Twenty-three scouts,” Vanya repeated, her voice low, almost conversational. She keyed the comm to the other two tanks—*Rust Hound* and *Black Anvil*—hunkered in camo-net trenches fifty meters apart. “They’re not probing. They’re *herding.*”

A pause. Then Jax’s voice crackled back, tight with static and tension: “Herding us *toward* Gamma. Or toward the vent shafts. Either way, they want us pinned when the heavies roll.”

“Pinned?” Kael snorted, adjusting the magnification on the lead crawler. Its ceramic carapace shimmered, refracting the dim light. “We’re *already* pinned, Jax. We’re the only thing standing between those bastards and six hundred miners sleeping in zero-G dorms under Gamma’s blast shield. And we’ve got three rounds left in the main gun. Two HEAT, one APFSDS.” He tapped the ammo counter. *003.*

Vanya didn’t flinch. She watched the lead crawler halt thirty meters from the perimeter fence—a rusted lattice strung with proximity sensors now blinking amber, then red. A hatch hissed open. Not a soldier emerged. A drone—no bigger than a dog—scuttled out, its optical array whirring as it scanned the ground, then lifted, locking onto *Iron Maw*’s turret.

“Laser designation,” Kael breathed.

Vanya triggered the countermeasure suite. A burst of magnesium-flare smoke erupted from the hull’s port side—not to blind, but to scatter the targeting lock. The drone jerked, optics flaring white. For three seconds, it hesitated.

That was all she needed.

“Gun up—elevation minus twelve. Traverse left ten degrees. Fire.”

The *Iron Maw*’s 120mm smoothbore recoiled with a sound like a mountain breaking. The shell screamed—deafening even through the tank’s acoustic dampeners—and struck the drone’s base just as it reacquired lock. The explosion wasn’t fire; it was a concussive *crack*, vaporizing the drone and sending a shockwave that rattled the fence posts. Shrapnel pinged against the turret like hail.

Silence, thick and sudden.

Then the comms erupted.

“*Rust Hound* hit! Left track shredded!” Jax’s voice was ragged. “They’re flanking—two crawlers on the gully edge!”

Vanya slammed her palm against the console. “Kael—switch to coax. Full auto. Suppress that gully. *Now.*”

The coaxial 7.62mm spat fire, tracer rounds stitching a molten line across the dark gully rim. Sparks flew where bullets struck ceramic armor. One crawler lurched sideways, its leg hydraulics shrieking as a round punched through its actuator housing. It toppled, spilling black coolant onto the grey dust.

But more were coming. From behind the ridge, the first Goliath appeared—twenty meters tall, its armored carapace scarred and pitted, its railguns humming as they spun up. A low, subsonic thrum vibrated through the hull, making Vanya’s teeth ache.

“Range?” she asked, her voice steady.

“Twelve hundred. Closing.”

She exhaled, slow. Checked the ammo counter again. *002.*

“Jax,” she said, calm as glacier ice. “You and Lien get your people clear of Gamma’s east corridor. Seal the blast doors manually if you have to. Don’t wait for the alarm.”

“Vanya—”

“*Do it.*” She paused, then added, softer, “Tell Anya… tell her I kept my promise about the orchids.”

Static. Then, quiet: “Copy that, Sarge.”

Kael didn’t look up. “Second Goliath’s deploying support drones. Swarm pattern. Twelve units. They’ll be on us in ninety seconds.”

Vanya watched the lead Goliath raise its right railgun. The violet glow intensified, coalescing into a searing point of light at the muzzle. Targeting solution painted across her HUD: center mass. Her crosshairs settled on the joint where the gun mounted to the torso—a hairline fracture in the plating, visible only because of the thermal bleed from overheated capacitors.

“Kael,” she said, “when I say *now*, dump all remaining power to the gyrostabilizer. Even the life-support reserve. Give me one clean shot.”

He nodded once. His fingers hovered over the override.

Outside, the wind died. Dust hung suspended. The Goliath’s railgun fired.

The world turned white.

Not fire—but light, blinding, silent, tearing through the air like a god’s scalpel. It missed *Iron Maw* by three meters, shearing off the top half of the observation tower beside Refinery Gamma. Concrete and rebar disintegrated mid-air, raining down in glittering shards.

Vanya didn’t blink. Didn’t breathe.

She waited for the recoil tremor to fade from the ground.

Then she whispered, “*Now.*”

Kael slammed the override.

The tank’s internal lights dimmed. Alarms wailed—low, urgent, ignored. Every watt surged into the turret ring, locking the barrel with impossible precision.

Vanya squeezed the trigger.

The shell left the barrel not with a roar, but a deep, guttural *thoom*. It struck the fracture. The Goliath didn’t explode. It *unzipped*—a seam of white-hot plasma erupting along its spine as the railgun’s own capacitors detonated inward. One leg buckled. Then another. It fell not with a crash, but a slow, terrible groan, like a dying leviathan sinking into the earth.

Dust rose. Smoke curled.

On the comm, Kael’s voice was raw. “One down. Two to go.”

Vanya stared at the burning wreck, then at the horizon, where the second Goliath’s silhouette advanced, unblinking, unstoppable.

She reached for the last round’s loading lever.

Her knuckles were white. Her breath, steady.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The sun was setting, casting long shadows over the fields as I trudged along the dusty path, my backpack feeling heavier with each step. The festival grounds were just ahead, a kaleidoscope of colors and sounds that seemed to pulse with an energy all its own. I could hear the distant thump of bass, the excited chatter of people, and the occasional burst of laughter. It was like stepping into another world, one where anything was possible.

My name is Mia, and I'm fourteen. I've been on my own for three days now, ever since I left home with nothing but a backpack, a few dollars, and a crumpled photo of my mom. She left when I was five, and I haven't seen her since. But I know she's here, at this music festival, because I found a flyer in her old room, hidden behind a poster of some band I'd never heard of. The flyer was for this very festival, and it had her handwriting scrawled across the back: "This is where I'll be. Love, Mom."

I had no idea what I would say to her when I found her, or if she even wanted to see me. All I knew was that I needed to find her, to understand why she left, and maybe, just maybe, to have her back in my life.

As I got closer to the festival, the crowd thickened, and I had to weave my way through groups of people. Some were dressed in wild, colorful outfits, others in simple t-shirts and jeans. The air was thick with the smell of food, sweat, and something sweet and herbal that made my head spin. I felt a little out of place, like a kid who had wandered into a party for adults, but I kept moving, my eyes scanning the faces around me, searching for any sign of my mom.

I finally reached the entrance, where a guy with a clipboard and a lanyard around his neck was checking wristbands. I didn't have one, and I knew I couldn't afford to buy a ticket. I hesitated, my heart pounding in my chest, and then I saw a gap in the fence, partially hidden by a stack of wooden pallets. I took a deep breath and slipped through, trying to look like I belonged there.

Inside, the festival was even more chaotic. Stages were set up everywhere, and bands were playing, their music blending together in a cacophony of sound. People were dancing, laughing, and singing along, and I felt a pang of loneliness. I had no one to share this with, no one to hold my hand and tell me everything would be okay.

I walked past a row of food stalls, the aroma of grilled cheese and funnel cakes making my stomach growl. I hadn't eaten much in the last few days, and I was starting to feel weak. I fished a couple of crumpled bills from my pocket and bought a slice of pizza, savoring the warm, gooey cheese as I continued my search.

As the night fell, the festival lights came on, casting a magical glow over everything. I wandered from stage to stage, listening to the music and watching the people, hoping to catch a glimpse of my mom. But as the hours passed, my hope began to wane. Maybe she wasn't here after all. Maybe the flyer was just a coincidence, a cruel trick of fate.

I found a quiet spot near the edge of the festival, away from the noise and the crowds. I sat down on the grass, hugging my knees to my chest, and let the tears fall. I was tired, hungry, and more alone than I had ever been. I wondered if I had made a huge mistake, if I should have stayed home and tried to forget about her. But I couldn't. Not yet.

Just as I was about to give up, I heard a familiar voice. It was soft, almost lost in the din, but I recognized it instantly. I looked up and saw her, standing a few feet away, talking to a group of people. My mom. She looked different, older, with streaks of gray in her hair, but it was her. I stood up, my legs trembling, and took a step forward.

"Mom?" I called out, my voice barely a whisper.

She turned, and for a moment, her face was a mask of confusion. Then, her eyes widened, and she gasped, "Mia?"

We stood there, staring at each other, the world around us fading away. I didn't know what would happen next, but for the first time in years, I felt a glimmer of hope.

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
The bathroom door creaked open—not with urgency, but with the deliberate, unhurried sigh of someone who’d just finished aligning their chakras mid-steam.

Lila Chen stood barefoot on the cool tile, wrapped in a hemp-cotton robe the colour of dried sage. Her silver-streaked braid hung over one shoulder, and she held a ceramic mug steaming with ginger-turmeric tea. Behind her, filling the entire doorway like a misplaced myth, stood Barnaby—a chestnut gelding with soulful, amber eyes, a faint dusting of lavender-scented oatmeal shampoo clinging to his forehead, and one very damp hoof resting politely *on* the bathmat.

Mr. Thaddeus Finch—silk tie askew, eyebrows permanently fused into a single skeptical arch—stared. His knuckles were white where he gripped the doorframe. “Ms. Chen,” he said, voice tight as a violin string tuned too high. “I hired you to find my missing heirloom pocket watch. Not to… *curate equine interior design*.”

Lila took a slow sip. “Barnaby isn’t *in* the bathroom, Mr. Finch. He’s *with* the bathroom.”

Thaddeus blinked. “He’s *standing in my bathtub*, Ms. Chen. With his head *over the shower curtain rod*.”

“Precisely,” she murmured, stepping aside so Barnaby could nudge past her—gently, respectfully—into the hallway. He paused, lowered his muzzle, and delicately nudged Thaddeus’s left loafer with his nose. Thaddeus flinched.

“See?” Lila said, lowering her mug. “He’s checking your root chakra alignment. You’ve been clenching your jaw since you walked in. Your shoulders are up by your ears. Your breath is shallow—like you’re holding onto something that’s already gone.”

“I’m holding onto *sanity*, Ms. Chen! And possibly the lease agreement!” Thaddeus gestured wildly toward the bathroom. “That horse was *in my guest powder room* five minutes ago. I heard him *snorting* at my monogrammed hand towels!”

Lila smiled—not condescendingly, but with the quiet certainty of someone who’d watched dandelions push through cracked pavement for thirty-seven years. “Barnaby doesn’t snort *at* things, Mr. Finch. He *resonates with* them. Your towels carry traces of synthetic fabric softener—phthalates, artificial musk. Dissonant frequencies. He was trying to neutralise them. With his breath. It’s a form of energetic fumigation.”

Thaddeus rubbed his temples. “Energetic… fumigation.”

“Yes. And before you ask—no, he didn’t eat your soap. Though he did *taste* the lavender-vanilla bar. Not for nourishment. For olfactory calibration. Your nervous system’s been running on cortisol since Tuesday. The vanilla note grounds it. He knew.”

Thaddeus froze. “…Tuesday? That’s when my accountant called about the audit.”

Lila nodded. “Barnaby felt the tremor in your floorboards when you paced past the stable door at 3:17 a.m. He also noticed the faint metallic scent clinging to your cufflinks—old sweat, stress, and trace iron from that vintage watch you keep in your top drawer. The one you haven’t wound in six weeks.”

Thaddeus went very still. “How did you—?”

“I didn’t.” She tilted her head toward Barnaby, who’d settled onto the Persian rug in the hallway, blinking slowly, one ear swivelling toward them like a satellite dish. “He did. Horses don’t lie, Mr. Finch. They don’t speculate. They *perceive*. Your watch isn’t lost. It’s *muted*. Buried under layers of anxiety, rushed decisions, and that awful ‘stress-scent’ you emit when you skip breakfast.”

Thaddeus exhaled—long, shaky. “So… you brought a horse into my home to… *smell my watch*?”

“To *reconnect you with its resonance*,” Lila corrected softly. “You haven’t *felt* time in months. You’ve only *counted* it. Barnaby remembers the weight of brass, the hum of a coiled spring, the warmth of human skin against metal. He stood in your bathroom because the acoustics there—the porcelain, the tile, the steam trapped in the air—amplify subtle vibrations. Especially those tied to memory.”

She stepped closer, her voice dropping, warm and low as honey stirred into warm milk. “Your father gave you that watch, didn’t he? On your eighteenth birthday. He told you, ‘Time isn’t something you chase, Thaddeus. It’s something you hold gently—like a bird’s wing.’ You haven’t held anything gently in years.”

Thaddeus looked down. His throat worked. “It’s in the bottom drawer of my desk. Under the tax files. I… I forgot it was there. I thought it was broken.”

“It’s not broken,” Lila said. “It’s waiting for you to remember how to listen.”

Barnaby lifted his head. Softly, deliberately, he blew air through his nostrils—not a snort, but a long, warm, rhythmic exhale. A sound like wind moving through tall grass.

Thaddeus closed his eyes.

And for the first time in months, he *felt* the silence between heartbeats.

When he opened them, Lila was holding out his watch—not the tarnished, forgotten thing from the drawer, but the one *now*, gleaming softly in the hallway light, its second hand ticking with quiet, unwavering certainty.

“How—?”

“Barnaby nudged the drawer open this morning,” she said, handing it over. “Then he stood in the bathroom until the resonance aligned. The steam helped. So did your lavender soap. And your suppressed grief. And your stubborn, beautiful, terrified hope.”

Thaddeus turned the watch over in his palm. Felt its familiar heft. Heard its steady, patient tick.

He looked from the watch to Barnaby—who gazed back, calm, ancient, utterly unimpressed by pocket watches or property values—and then to Lila.

“…Do you take credit cards?”

Lila smiled. “We accept barter. Local honey. Hand-knitted socks. Or fifteen minutes of silent sitting—barefoot, on grass—while Barnaby stands nearby.”

Thaddeus stared at the watch. Then at the horse. Then, slowly, he loosened his tie.

“…I have some lavender soap left.”  

Barnaby flicked an ear.  

Lila nodded. “Good start.”

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
The air in Hut 3 smelled of damp wool, stale tea, and the faint, metallic tang of overheated vacuum tubes. Outside, rain lashed the slate roof of Bletchley Park like impatient fingers. Inside, Eleanor Vance traced a finger over the latest intercept—Message 742-B, decrypted just hours before, its Japanese naval cipher rendered into precise, unblinking English: *“…fuel reserves nominal. Typhoon expected near Okinawa. Recommend delay of Operation Kikusui until after 18th.”*

She’d read it three times. Not for meaning—everyone knew the typhoon warning was routine—but for the rhythm beneath it.

Eleanor leaned back, the wooden chair groaning. Her eyes flicked to the wall above her desk, where she’d pinned a grid of twelve messages, all from the past six weeks, all bearing weather reports. She’d transcribed them herself, cross-referencing time stamps, sender call signs, and the precise phrasing of wind speeds, barometric pressure, and cloud cover. To most, they were filler—noise between real intelligence. To her, they were a metronome.

She tapped the corner of Message 742-B. “Nominal,” she murmured. Then she pointed to Message 729-D: *“Fuel reserves adequate.”* And 715-F: *“Fuel reserves satisfactory.”* And 703-A: *“Fuel reserves acceptable.”*

All synonyms. All appearing only in messages that also contained a weather report. All placed in the same sentence position—third clause, always following the location and preceding the operational recommendation.

Her pencil hovered over a fresh sheet. She wrote: *“Nominal = High Priority / Imminent Action”*, then underlined it twice.

A shadow fell across her notes. Lieutenant Davies stood there, rainwater darkening the shoulders of his greatcoat, a steaming mug in hand. “Still at it, Vance? Thought you’d have gone home by now. Or at least stopped staring at the weather.”

“I’m not staring at the weather, sir,” she said, voice quiet but steady. “I’m staring at what’s *behind* it.”

Davies sighed, setting the mug down with a soft clink. He glanced at her grid. “Ah. The typhoon files. You know what Commander Ashworth said. ‘Weather is camouflage, not code.’ And frankly, he’s right. We’ve got Enigma bleeding through the floorboards, and you’re charting cloud formations.”

“It’s not camouflage, sir. It’s insertion. A consistent, deliberate insertion.” She tapped the grid. “‘Nominal’ appears only when fuel is full *and* an operation is scheduled within seventy-two hours. ‘Adequate’ means action in four to six days. ‘Satisfactory’—seven to ten. I checked the logs. Every single time. Even the ones dismissed as ‘routine maintenance alerts’.”

Davies took a slow sip of tea. “And the typhoons?”

“They’re real. But the *timing* of the reports isn’t. Look—Message 731-C mentions ‘light squalls near Formosa’—but the Met Office confirms no squalls occurred there that day. Yet two days later, a destroyer squadron left Keelung. Coincidence? Or signal?”

He frowned, stepping closer. “You’re suggesting the Japanese are embedding operational tempo in weather verbiage?”

“Yes. Not just tempo—location, too. See here?” She flipped to a second sheet, pointing to underlined phrases: *“northwest quadrant of the South China Sea,” “southern edge of the Philippine Trench,” “eastern approaches to Palau.”* “They’re not describing weather. They’re naming coordinates—approximate, yes, but directional. And every one aligns with known fleet movements *within forty-eight hours*.”

Davies rubbed his temple. “Eleanor… we run statistical analyses on this kind of thing. Twice a week. Nothing’s flagged.”

“Because you’re looking for letter substitutions, not semantic layering. They’re using *meaning*, not cipher wheels. It’s linguistic steganography—hiding intent in plain sight, in the language itself.”

He was silent for a long moment, watching the rain streak the grimy window. Then he said, quietly, “Show me the next prediction.”

She didn’t hesitate. “Message 745-E will arrive tomorrow afternoon. It’ll contain a weather report for the Bonin Islands. It’ll use the word ‘optimal’. That means a major operation—carrier-based—is launching from Chichi Jima within thirty-six hours. Likely against Midway supply lines.”

Davies exhaled sharply. “Optimal? That’s not even on your scale.”

“It is now. I added it last night. After cross-checking the carrier logbooks from Pearl Harbor intel. ‘Optimal’ appeared once before—in Message 688-G. Three days later, the *Shōkaku* launched strikes on Efate.”

He stared at her—not with dismissal, but with the slow, dawning weight of possibility. “You haven’t told Ashworth.”

“No. He’d call it speculation. Or worse—wishful thinking.”

“He’d be right to demand proof.”

“I know.” She slid a thin envelope across the desk. Inside were three carbon copies: her grid, her correlation table, and a list of seven past predictions she’d written privately, dated and sealed, each matched to subsequent naval activity confirmed by Ultra intercepts or aerial reconnaissance. None had been shared. Not even with her supervisor.

Davies opened the envelope. His thumb brushed the paper. He read the first entry—*“Predicted: Submarine patrol shift near Truk, 12 Oct. Confirmed: USS *Sealion* sighting, 13 Oct.”*—then the second, the third. His jaw tightened.

“You kept this to yourself?”

“I needed confirmation. Not theory. Fact.”

He looked up. Rainlight caught the grey at his temples. “If this holds… if *optimal* means what you say…” He didn’t finish. He didn’t need to. The implications hung between them—vessels spared, convoys rerouted, lives measured in minutes saved.

Davies picked up her pencil. For a long moment, he held it, then pressed the tip firmly into the margin beside *“optimal”* on her sheet. Not a question mark. A single, decisive checkmark.

“Bring me 745-E the moment it lands,” he said. His voice was low, but certain. “And Eleanor?”

She met his gaze.

“Don’t tell anyone else. Not yet.”

Outside, the rain softened to a hush. Inside, the hum of the machines deepened—not louder, but different. As if, for the first time in months, the room held its breath, listening—not to the wires, but to the silence between the words.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The lights of the casino were a blur, a kaleidoscope of gaudy colors that seemed to mock me with their garishness. I took a deep breath, trying to steady my nerves as I approached the baccarat table. The air was thick with the scent of expensive cologne and the faint, almost imperceptible aroma of cigar smoke. My heart pounded in my chest, a relentless drumbeat that threatened to drown out all other sounds.

I had been briefed on this mission for weeks, but nothing could have prepared me for the reality of it. The man I was about to face was not just any financier; he was the linchpin of an enemy network that had been causing havoc across Europe. His name was Viktor Kovalenko, and he was a master of deception, a man who could charm his way out of any situation and into any bank account. Tonight, I had to play him at his own game—literally.

As I approached the table, I caught sight of Kovalenko. He was a tall, imposing figure, with a chiseled jaw and piercing blue eyes that seemed to see right through you. He was dressed impeccably in a tailored suit, exuding an air of confidence and wealth. I felt a shiver run down my spine, but I forced myself to maintain my composure. This was no time for weakness.

"Good evening, Mr. Kovalenko," I said, my voice steady despite the turmoil inside me. "I hope I'm not interrupting anything."

He looked up, a sly smile spreading across his face. "Ah, Mr. Blackwood. I was wondering when you would join us. Please, take a seat. We were just about to start a new round."

I nodded and sat down, my eyes scanning the table. The dealer, a young woman with a professional demeanor, was already shuffling the cards. I could feel the weight of the room's gaze on me, a mix of curiosity and suspicion. Everyone here knew that Kovalenko was a high roller, and they were eager to see how I would fare against him.

"May I offer you a drink, Mr. Blackwood?" Kovalenko asked, his voice smooth as silk. "Perhaps a glass of champagne to celebrate our little game?"

I shook my head. "No, thank you. I prefer to keep a clear head."

"Very wise," he said, raising an eyebrow. "But then, I suppose you must be a very cautious man, given your line of work."

I met his gaze, refusing to flinch. "Cautious, yes. But not afraid. I know what I'm getting into."

Kovalenko chuckled, a low, rumbling sound that sent a chill down my spine. "Of course, of course. But let's not forget, this is a game of chance, Mr. Blackwood. And in games of chance, even the most cautious can fall prey to the whims of fate."

The dealer began to deal the cards, and I focused on the task at hand. Baccarat was a simple game, but it required a sharp mind and a steady hand. I had practiced for hours, running through every possible scenario, but nothing could replicate the pressure of the real thing.

"Your bet, Mr. Blackwood," Kovalenko said, his eyes never leaving mine.

I placed a stack of chips on the table, my hands steady. "Banker."

Kovalenko smiled, a predatory gleam in his eyes. "Interesting choice. I'll match it, of course."

The dealer turned over the cards, and I watched as the game unfolded. The first round was a draw, and I felt a flicker of relief. But I knew better than to let my guard down. Kovalenko was a master, and he would not be so easily defeated.

As the night wore on, the tension in the room grew. The stakes were rising, and I could feel the weight of the world on my shoulders. Every move, every decision, could mean the difference between success and failure. I had to stay focused, to keep my wits about me.
